which incorporates sophisticated smart grids, to administer load shedding and 
generate new energy standards. The proposed solution involves consumers actively 
participating in microgrid control through smart decision-making. A novel 
aggregative game method is introduced, enabling the derivation of Nash equilibria 
for large-scale non-cooperative games. Two practical applications of this model 
are demonstrated: (1) load shedding during peak electricity usage, which results 
in reduced utility bills for users and lower strain on the power grid; (2) setting 
new energy consumption standards. Furthermore, a practical billing system 
based on real-time energy consumption is also explored. The analysis of these 
applications reveals that the maximum number of users participating in the 
billing scheme and the total reduction in electricity consumption all scale 
positively with the number of users. Detailed case studies are conducted to 
demonstrate the model's effectiveness, including realistic scenarios derived from 
actual power consumption data.

A model of charged black strings in the Rastall theory of gravity has been developed as a modification of the Schwarzschild-Taub-Arendt solution. Conducting local energy-momentum tensor experiments near the event horizon revealed that the gravitational effect changes the thermal distribution of particles emitting radiation from charged black strings. As a result, the Rastall charged black string solution can have either positive or negative Hawking temperatures, contingent upon the values of its surface gravity and multiplicative coefficient of the covariant derivative of the four-dimensional energy-momentum tensor tensor. Furthermore, the Hawking temperatures were found to be sensitive to changes in the particle mass to charge ratio. Additionally, the Hawking lifetimes were calculated for observations limited to the present cosmic era.

Convergence speeds in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem are deeply rooted in the properties of the Fourier decomposition of unitary group representations. This note explores this connection by demonstrating that certain spectral norms of these representations lead to diverse bounds on convergence speeds that can be tightly linked to mean and almost mean squares of group characters. We will illustrate this relationship specifically in the cases of compact and semisimple Lie groups.

The research on extremely metal-poor stars is critical to understanding the early development of our galaxy. Although a few hundred such stars have been identified, thousands of uninvestigated candidates remain hidden within the vast amounts of galaxy spectrum data. High-resolution spectral analysis is typically used to detect these stars, but the process is time-consuming and only feasible for those with already suspected metal-poor status. A new study proposes utilizing the BRP-Spec tool, which utilizes spectral data from the Gaia satellite, to identify metal-poor stars at a lower resolution. The study incorporates a machine learning method to simplify the process. A preliminary test indicates that BRP-Spec shows 84% efficiency in detecting metal-poor stars of -2 or less, whereas it accurately identifies 79% of stars with reduced temperatures (above 5000K), and both methods result in minimal false positives. As a result, BRP-Spec offers a faster and more cost-effective means of identifying metal-poor stars at lower resolution, which can lead to the detection of novel, extremely metal-poor stars.

This study evaluates and forecasts the severity of worldwide wildfire seasons.
We analyze this by examining the number of fires and destroyed buildings
over a 20-year period from 2003 to 2022. Our data covers 56 countries and
more than 84,000 wildfires. By modeling the number of wildfires and
incarcerations as separate functions, we can assess a country's wildfire risk
level. This two-part model enables us to accurately predict the number of
fires while also accounting for the destruction caused by them. Using the
identified parameters, we can estimate the likelihood of a country experiencing
a severe wildfire season. This research aims to provide valuable insights for
wildfire prevention efforts and early intervention strategies.

This study focuses on understanding the nature of corpus-based morphological complexity
measures, specifically the Intricacy Index and its variations. We investigate the relationships
between these measures, identify their underlying strengths and challenges, and evaluate
their usefulness for different purposes. We discover that the measures are often
correlated, but can also be influenced by distinct factors. It's concluded that the
Intricacy Index and its variations serve well in distinguishing languages with varying
levels of complexity and in identifying features contributing to complexity, yet they
require enhancement in order to accurately quantify complexity across a wide range
of languages, especially those considered simple. We also introduce further research
areas aimed at validating the authenticity of complexity measures like the Intricacy
Index. Such validations could involve linking these measures to concrete aspects of
linguistic performance, leveraging various approaches, such as typological comparison,
linguistic theory, psycholinguistics and learning assessments. It is proposed that
learning outcomes, specifically the results of standardized English as a Foreign Language
tests, could be employed to validate the authenticity of corpus-based complexity
indices like the Intricacy Index. We outline a planned study aimed at conducting this
validation, and provide initial exploratory research examining the relationship
between learning outcomes and our enhanced definition of Intricacy, indexed by the
average and the highest complexity of three syntactic units: phrases, clauses, and
sentences. We discovered a modest negative correlation between learning outcomes

We're proposing a technique to detect weak, intergalactic gravitational lenses within galaxy clusters using a unique method of image reconstruction. This technique can identify small-scale gravitational lensing effects, which could be significant enough to bend light by up to 0.5 degrees, by utilizing a combination of Aitken values. To validate our approach, we utilized a dataset of 37 strongly-gravitating galaxy pairs and applied our method to analyze 8 strong gravitational lens datasets. We also developed a simulation to assess the effectiveness of our algorithm in various scenarios and found that it could accurately determine the mass of a gravitational lens within a 20% margin even when there were 1000 pixels or less along the lens axis. This technique has the potential to enhance our understanding of the mass distribution within galaxy clusters, which could provide insights into the behavior of dark matter. This information could be significant in testing current theories of dark matter, including a particular model known as self-interacting dark matter, by analyzing the structure of galaxy clusters and the formation of gravitational lenses.

Deep learning models' success has been impressive, but their growing complexity has made them increasingly hard to understand. This lack of insight into their behavior is problematic, as it poses risks in areas such as healthcare and self-driving cars. Achieving a deeper understanding of these models is critical to gaining their trust. While researchers have made significant progress in gaining some understanding, there is still a significant gap between what is theoretically possible and what can be accomplished in practice. This study presents an innovative technique that bridges this gap by using general, high-level information about a model to eliminate unnecessary low-level details. By employing this approach, we can reduce the complexity of a model and still retain essential insights into its behavior. We can leverage models trained on other, related tasks, as well as analyze a model after training it for a shorter, simplified version of the task. Our method has yielded promising results in improving understanding for a range of complex models, including neural networks for image and sequence analysis. This technique is also unique because it is one of the few that can rely solely on analyzing a model's behavior after training, as opposed to other approaches that also require access to training data. This is an important distinction, as it makes our method more applicable in scenarios where such data is scarce.

This paper proposes the M-ar-K-Fast: Multivariate ar-bitary Kernel Fast Algorithm, an efficient version of the M-ar-K component-based algorithm for high-dimensional data analysis. Both original component analysis and the efficient version produce the same results. The study introduces key concepts including Multivariate ar-Bitary Kernels, their properties, and the algorithm's operational principles. The M-ar-K component-based approach is an enhancement of several path-breaking frameworks, namely Sufficient Dimensionality Reduction, sparse canonical correlation, and sparse regression. The framework automatically produces optimal representations, is scalable, and performs well on large datasets, and automatically sets relevant parameters. The influence of different parameter settings is also analyzed. A comprehensive set of simulated and real datasets were used to evaluate the method, and the research compares the performance of the M-ar-K component-based approach with other competing methods.

Identifying simultaneous events on social media based on multiple related locations is a challenging task that researchers have been working to overcome for almost a decade now. Most existing methods rely on either dense data sources, such as Twitter, or simple correlation thresholds, which can lead to poor performance and accuracy issues on behalf of the individual data contributors. To address these limitations, we're proposing a new approach utilizing spatial-temporal networks to pinpoint concurrent events in real-time using social media data. Our approach considers the spatio-temporal behavior of each location by accounting for the time of the first event and the frequency of subsequent events, allowing for the detection of locations sharing a common event through shared sub-histograms. We're showcasing the efficacy of our proposed algorithm with two extensive real-world case studies: one examining the events surrounding the 2018 World Cup and another covering the 2019 Thai election, resulting in concurrently identified events of a total number of 1 845 715 on Twitter.

This note explores two key results. First, we establish that the solution to the elliptic equation $-\Delta q = 0$ within a given domain $S \subset \mathbb{R}^N$, where $S$ possesses a smooth, given surface structure $g$, is unambiguous and solely depends on the structure $g$, even when the domain $S$ changes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any deviation from this solution is a non-negative operator acting on the deviation itself. Additionally, we examine the general form of the given surface structure $g$, which leads to the derivation of two specific criteria relevant to the study of elliptic equations and their applications in conformal geometry and partial differential equations.

This study uncovers strong ties between cobalt's unique properties within specific chemical compounds and its abundance as a cobalt alloy. By utilizing an optimization process called evolutionary search, we identified promising cobalt-containing materials and calculated their thermodynamic stability and electrical conductivity. Notably, some cobalt-containing materials with exceptionally high voltage and excellent conductivity were found, and several potential candidates that exceed traditional alloys in both properties have been discovered. The information about these cobalt-rich materials, including their chemical compositions, structures, and properties, has been made publicly available for further research.

In the field of display advertising, real-time auction technology creates a complex optimization problem that has been studied extensively over the past decade. A key challenge in this field is cost-per-action (CPA) optimization, which involves maximizing the likelihood of successful actions within a predetermined budget while considering the uncertainty associated with ad rewards. Previous studies on CPA optimization often relied on assumptions such as known action probabilities, the availability of estimates or bounds, and a sufficient budget, but these assumptions do not accurately reflect the actual operating environment of large-scale advertising platforms. These systems place upper limits on the budget, which must be exceeded in favor of a housekeeping fee incurred by the auctioneer. Furthermore, these platforms operate in an environment characterized by a high frequency of auctions, resulting in poorly accurate estimates of ad rewards. This study addresses these challenges by developing an adaptive, robust bidding strategy that relies on the evaluation of expected costs rather than the uncertainty associated with ad rewards. The proposed algorithm utilizes an optimization framework that incorporates both the short-term goal of meeting demand and the long-term goal of maximizing the likelihood of successful actions, while adhering to the constraints of a limited budget and the requirement of an upper limit on risks. The algorithm iteratively adjusts its decision-making process through successive approximations, which are proven to converge to optimal solutions under general conditions. Furthermore, this study examines a variant of the algorithm that incorporates the evaluation of upper limits on risks, which can be solved exactly through a new optimization framework. The proposed algorithmic strategies

Non-classical characteristics of quantum information, embodied by certain important quantum criteria such as Wigner negativity and higher-order correlations, can manifest in diverse quantum states, including entangled and squeezed matter, as well as in systems defined by their quantum trajectories. Researchers have recently Investigated the behavior of Wigner negativity in harmonic oscillator states that evolve according to a quantum-guided model featuring non-linear mean-field behavior. Notably, this quantum-guided model displays positive Wigner negativity periods even when the ordinary mean field would be negative, and even exhibits permanent Wigner negativity in specific single-mode regimes. Additionally, this study found that Wigner negativity can serve as an indicator of the onset of quantum-guided behavior, as it becomes negative when the quantum-guided correction is small. Moreover, this study has determined the conditions for the simultaneous occurrence of quantum-guided and higher-order correlations. As such, this research has significant implications for understanding non-classical behavior in systems that utilize quantum-guided nonlinearity, such as those found in multimode quantum networks and transmons.

We evaluate the security of secure multi-party quantum key distribution (QKD) using random source-based private randomness through random bit measurement. Unlike previous approaches, considering the source's random nature as a malicious factor is not necessary, as it does not affect the adversary's uncontrolled behavior. Therefore, security analysis no longer necessitates a complex source model, thus simplifying the process and allowing for a more straightforward evaluation of QKD security. This understanding has also been applied to conventional QKD and single-party QKD, and as a result, the method has been verified effective in practical scenarios and has been approved by the European Union's CoCoA3 project as a standard security evaluation method. Furthermore, our work has also been compared with approaches using source-side model, and the difference in security guarantees has been demonstrated. This work has been conducted with the aid of the random bit measurement method, and as a result, the development of an open-source code for evaluating the security of QKD with non-uniform random source has been achieved.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. We have developed a method to identify Bertrand curves in complex, multi-dimensional spaces by utilizing a novel transversal vector field approach. Furthermore, we have established that in complex, multi-dimensional spaces, these curves are always either null or spacelike. This allows us to conclude that in complex, multi-dimensional spaces, the curves that are timelike in nature do not fall into the category of Bertrand curves.

We analyze the connection between the sampling distribution of Feller diffusion and the characteristics of its stationary distribution. Specifically, assuming the diffusion process has a stationary distribution whose density functions are denoted as $\pi_\theta(x)$, we explore how sampling outcomes are affected. Diverging from conventional practices, our approach retains the explicit form of the density functions, rather than utilizing a specific functional form like the log-normal distribution. By expressing the probability density of a sample $x_i$ as a function of $\pi_\theta(x)$, we establish a generalized version of the central limit theorem and show that sample statistics follow standard distributions under specific conditions regarding the interval $[x, x+n]$. Furthermore, our work is exemplified by the Feller diffusion model with a double well potential, where samples from this process are shown to be approximately standard-normal under certain premises.

In this research, we've developed a practical method to analyze the scattering behavior of multiple photon states in a three-dimensional waveguide QED system. By building upon previous work that established a non-radiative perturbation theory, we've created an effective formalism to study photon scattering in systems with multiple emitters. Our approach is based on a physical interpretation of the non-radiative interactions as diagrammatic rules, which effectively encode the fundamental emitters' self-interactions and inter-emitter couplings. Furthermore, this method extends previous single-photon analysis to a more general case of multi-photon scattering, which finds particular relevance in three-dimensional waveguide QED due to its inherent ability to handle coherently interacting multi-photon states. As a result, we demonstrate that certain fundamental emitters' self-interactions that are absent in one-dimensional systems can actually occur within three-dimensional systems through multi-photon interactions. Additionally, this method provides a conceptually clear and simplified framework for calculating multi-photon scattering processes, which are highly necessary for various quantum information and matter-photon nonlinear optics applications. Specifically, we provide two exemplary applications: the scattering of two photons by a weakly coupled emitters system, which is analytically solvable and accessible with current technology, and the scattering by a $\Lambda$-type system, which represents a challenging but highly non-trivial case for future stronger coupling scenarios.

We present a novel phase of dark matter (DM) characterized by spin-dependent diffusion in the early Universe. This solution arises within a simplified scalar-fermion dark matter model where a substantial dark matter component is comprised of particles possessing spin. The interaction between the dark matter particles and their scalar environment, mediated by a channel outside the DM sector, yields a dynamic that favors higher-spin particles. As a result, this process yields a distinct diffusion profile with amplification, unlike the standard instance of diffusion where the signal either remains unchanged or diminishes with time. Our analysis involves an in-depth examination of the model's parameter space through Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations, utilizing observational constraints from Planck, ACMMB15, and H0N1 data alongside limits from direct detection experiments, diffuse neutrino background measurements, and large-scale structure observations.
This note employs Bernoulli polynomials and trigonometric form conversions to derive and present previously discovered formulas of Faulhaber and Euler.

This research investigates an ancient detection method for continuous phase modulation that has experienced diminished popularity in modern communication systems design. A conventional differential CPM receiver, excluding the well-known coherent CPM receiver, is a non-coherent receiver that operates without the need for a training sequence. It is known that one of the major drawbacks of this receiver is its sensitivity to delay, which significantly exceeds that of coherent receivers. This study aims to quantify this sensitivity by implementing a simulation in MATLAB, focusing on a particular type of CPM - the 2M-2P CPM - and using a particular type of non-coherent receiver design. The results of the simulation indicate that for a particular type of CPM parameter setting, even a minor delay of one symbol period can cause the receiver to struggle in correctly identifying data, with correct identification falling below 50% after a delay of three symbol periods. The impact of this delay vulnerability is historically attributed to the inherent properties of CPM as a type of modulation with inherent pair-wise error characteristics.

Interactive learning's reward learning process involves collaborating with a learner who proposes predictions and receives feedback from an instructor.  Optimizing this interactive process could potentially speed up the learning process and reduce costs associated with expert feedback.  However, expert preferences do not conform to traditional assumptions, causing state-of-the-art algorithms to struggle and result in time-consuming and resource-intensive processes.  To address this issue, we've developed a method that visually presents and organizes predicted outcomes in a ranked order, allowing experts to efficiently compare and signal their preferences among them using annotated time-series data.  Our resource-saving strategy effectively utilizes an HMM model to identify key factors, draws visual comparisons between predictions, and presents results in a comparative format that facilitates faster and more efficient feedback loops.  To achieve this, we've incorporated a simulated search protocol that simulates an instructor's feedback to train the model with the most optimal parameters.  Our experiments conducted with both real-world and simulated data showcase the effectiveness of this model, highlighting its capacity to learn and produce results in a fraction of the time compared to similar algorithms.

We use the light-cone gauge and the momentum-space approach to derive the nucleon's quark and gluon composition in noncommutative spacetime, taking into account the NC effect on the nucleon's stress tensor. Our results for the composition functions are expressed in terms of flavor, flavor-isospin and spin, and are generalized to higher dimensions. We then apply our results to calculate the NC effect on nucleon structure and scale dependence. We also use our results to revisit the Hoyle state and the proton's mass corrections, and to explain why the proton's stress tensor NC correction is not affected by its internal quark and gluon distributions. Our calculations also reveal the relations between the NC effect and nucleon structure, taking into account momentum and flavor, in an independent manner. We then use our results to derive the NC parton distribution functions, taking into account flavor, isospin, spin, and momentum, in the proton. Our results for these PDFs are generalized to $n_c$ (number of quarks) and $n_g$ (number of gluons) and are applied to investigate the NC effect on parton distribution functions, taking into account the Hoyle state, gluon dominance, and high-$k_T$ limits. Our calculations also reveal the NC effect on the gluon-luminosity operator, taking into account the Hoyle state, and the NC effect on the gluon stress tensor, taking into account $n_g$ and

Research on kagomé lattice frustrated quantum fluids has revealed a unique theoretical result, namely, a topological edge. Theoretical predictions show that these quantum fluids have a zero chemical potential edge state under certain conditions. The presence of this edge state makes the theoretical model stable at infinite coupling strength, allowing for theoretical extraction of chiral quantum spin liquids. Theoretical reviews on quantum fluids have inspired the creation of classical spin models mimicking their characteristics, such as the frustrated toric code pattern model (FTPM). Similar to the quantum fluid, FTPM has demonstrated an edge state without a bulk contribution. However, an explanation for these results in terms of a phase transition is still lacking. Theoretical researchers are working to understand the origins and properties of this edge state in FTPM.

We examine the spectral properties of large, randomly constructed Hermitian block matrices and subject them to modifications of a specific type. These modifications have a finite rank and can be regarded as slight perturbations of the original matrices. In the study, a model is developed to approximate the statistical behavior of the eigenvalues of the altered matrices based on the neural network's free energy. We verify that the eigenvalue distribution is a generalized beta function and confirm that the model yields accurate results as the size of the matrices expands. Furthermore, it is found that the neural network model produces a well-defined large matrix limit, and the convergence of the associated phase factors to a specific determinantal kernel is proven.

Recent advances in pre-trained models for conversation understanding have been substantial, yet limitations remain due to their reliance on response generation tasks that can result in inaccurate or misleading summaries. For instance, when prompted with a humorous query, a desirable response might not be humorous as well. To overcome these shortcomings, we suggest an alternative pre-training approach that prioritizes meaning. We introduce three crucial objectives: the first preserves the natural structure of dialogue, the second retains the core meaning of input statements, and the third provides context-based references, allowing for more precise comprehension of conversations. We implement this innovative method with a number of strategies and achieve notable results on the SAMSA-B dataset, which shows that our approach leads to better comprehension of dialogue by comparing multiple meanings. Furthermore, we find that incorporating our proposed context-based reference objective enhances the model's ability to understand jokes and memes, which often employ humor.

Machine learning algorithms have long been used to analyze data, but their ability to explain their findings has been a persistent challenge. In an effort to bridge this gap, researchers have been working on developing machine learning that is more "interpretable." The focus has been on creating learning methods and algorithms that produce predictions and models that provide insight into the decision-making process. The measure of interpretability, however, relies heavily on the understanding of the underlying concept, often relying on expertise and assuming a certain level of familiarity. The proposed framework, on the other hand, is designed with learning and understanding in mind, differentiating itself from the traditional approach with a more adaptive model. The framework not only recognizes the role of context but also the complexity of the cognitive effort involved in acquiring new knowledge. The framework's first iteration assesses the complexity of the learning process through four key factors: the initial understanding required, the complexity of the concept itself, the depth of knowledge required to understand the problem, and the frequency of use. The framework is then put to the test by evaluating various machine learning algorithms, the results of which highlight the complexity of the task at hand, suggesting that highly "interpretable" algorithms may only offer insights if users are already familiar with the underlying concept, suggesting that there is indeed a relationship between the two. The findings also indicate that humans learn differently based on their background and expertise, with some having an advantage over others. Anomaly detection has become a prominent subject in several fields of application, yet deep anomalies, occurring when anomalies are not present in the training dataset, often prove difficult to address. Methods under the umbrella of tinyML, designed to accommodate memory and computational restrictions, as well as those incorporating loosely supervised data, can significantly aid in detecting deep anomalies. A novel tinyML anomaly detection algorithm, based on the Isolation Forest model, has been proposed, demonstrating superior results compared to existing solutions. This algorithm's performance under tinyML and loosely supervised scenarios makes it well-suited for detecting deep anomalies.

A novel approach to model extreme value statistics based on a Bayesian non-homogeneous Poisson process is presented. This methodology enables the direct use of hierarchical statistical models to derive statistical parameters of extreme value distributions. We first establish a general framework for modeling extreme value patterns, then focus on estimating the parameters of the generalized maximum domain of attraction model for parametric and non-parametric cases. Our proposed method is illustrated by analyzing both simulated and real-world data, specifically examining memoryless patterns in water level records at the Swedish city of Malmö.

In a previous study, it was demonstrated that the angular distribution of Rutherford scattering cross-sections is governed by a quadratic equation, with the constant term being zero and the linear term negative. Further investigation has led to the discovery of a significant finding - across all possible values of the Coulomb parameter and scattering angle, the scattering cross-section presents as negative unless the product of the two parameters falls below a specific threshold, at which point the cross-section switches to positive. Additionally, two distinct parameter regions have been identified - both yielding a positive cross-section - depending on whether the product of the two parameters falls above or below this specific threshold.

This research presents an update on a widely-used knowledge base called ATOMIC, comprising 700K relation instances tied to natural language precepts. We outline two novel datasets, each offering insight into the nature of natural language connectivity, derived from a significant Twitter-based data set. We focus on the symmetric Knowledge Graph relationship, representing the reciprocal associations among entities, and draw comparisons with the knowledge graph models of Wikipedia and Wikipedia's reverse graphs. Our findings indicate that the symmetric nature of social media-derived knowledge graphs exhibits a higher degree of randomness than the directional Wikipedia knowledge graph, and also reveal a significantly higher proportion of self-loops in the symmetric model compared to the directional one. Moreover, a large portion of the connections in the symmetric model are interrelated, and a substantial portion of the knowledge relationships can be acquired using basic language attributes. We hypothesize that a significant proportion of the complex knowledge relationships are potentially acquired through these basic attributes.

We developed a novel information compression method tailored to map linear features in infrared light, which we employed to create the Hi-GAL survey map of the Carina molecular complex using $\sim$50 objects. Our compression algorithm leverages the linearity of spectral energy distribution (SED) models and compresses two-dimensional spatial information and one-dimensional light curves, whereas model parameters are individually compressed. Having assessed the performance of our method with mock observations and the Paronka et al. (2013) technique, we applied it to the Hi-GAL map of the Carina molecular complex and extracted 42 distinct source groups, predominantly known molecular clouds, each displaying a similar shape and SED. Our sources, spread across four regions, include the M8 star-forming region, the M8-Spout cloud, the molecular cloud at the edge of the parabolic shape at M8-E, the BSMC G035.68+0.69, and the CLUP-1 cloud, near the edge of the Carina molecular complex. We present compressed and decompressed images of the sources and provide complementary data at http://irs.uca.edu/compression/.

The cluster NGC 2808, a key member of the galactic bulge, exhibits distinctive metallicity characteristics.  The presence of a scattered metal pattern within the stars of this cluster initially suggested the role of an alternative stellar generation in its evolution. However, more recent studies of a smaller sample of higher brightness stars within NGC 2808 suggested a simpler two-generation model, reducing the likelihood of second-generation metal mixing. We have determined the ages, metallicities, carbon, and nitrogen levels for a larger number of higher brightness blue horizontal branch stars within NGC 2808 using new photometric data from Hubble Space Telescope. The calculated ages for these stars fall between 13.2 and 14.2 million years, and we found no correlation between their luminosity and age. The calculated spread in metallic abundance for these stars is marginally consistent with that previously determined for a smaller sample of same brightness level stars but is slightly smaller, approximately half. The results confirm that NGC 2808 consists of two populations with different metallicities. The presence of a spread in metal abundance in these two populations rules out the possibility of metal mixing as an explanation for the scattered metal pattern. Further, metal spread data indicate a relatively low initial Fe abundance dispersion in NGC 2808, a finding that can be explained by the presence of a relatively small number of heavy Fe contributing stars in second generation. The study also explores the role of helium abundance in explaining the sizeable difference in luminosity between the two populations

We examine the initial stage of file diffusion through a preferred (Sole) process.  This involves a probabilistic model where adoption occurs at varying speeds.  The speed of adoption can be such that it's slower than exponential, a condition known as subexponential.  This model is widely used in various studies on information spread and diffusion.  The speed of adoption is influenced by two distinct factors: awareness of the information content of the file and a measure of how readily that information can be understood.  The understanding component is sometimes referred to as "loveliness."  Assuming a probabilistic understanding of these factors, we apply a probabilistic approach to determine the duration of initial exit times and examine the relationship between exit duration and measures of strength, or "loveliness."  The results of our analysis provide a means of comparing the efficacy of different marketing strategies by comparing the time it takes for a file to reach the point of final adoption using this model.

Quantum theories often rely on two fundamental principles: wave function collapse and Bayes' theorem.  Although widely used, the relationship between these concepts is poorly understood, with some claiming they are mutually exclusive.  This paper explores quantum Bayes' theorem, a combination of the two, and demonstrates that it successfully explains the wave function collapse by emphasizing its role in the process of inference.  By examining the posterior wave function derived from quantum Bayes' theorem, the paper provides a new perspective on the quantum paradoxes associated with wave function collapse.  Furthermore, this study serves as a comprehensive review of the development of quantum mechanics and highlights the importance of inductive reasoning in quantum physics.

Traditional quantum field theory focuses on major systems, representing the primary, uncontrollable components of a given physical system. In contrast, this research centers on minor systems, defined as small, controllable components of a given physical system, unrelated to its primary dynamics. By establishing a comprehensive and consistent formulation of quantum chromo dynamics for minor systems, we derive a fundamental expression for their free energy and thermodynamic properties, leading to novel calculations and observations. Specifically, for a given volume and temperature, the free energy is determined by a density functional, whose microscopic description involves the partition function of gluon states within the volume, described by a modified Yang-Mills equation. Furthermore, thermodynamic properties are governed by similar equations as their major system counterparts, including the equation of state, a generalized Wilson equation, originally proposed for strong-correlation systems. Our approach, addressing the dynamics of minor systems in a controlled manner, offers a potential solution to the challenges of finite temperature and density quantum chromodynamics.

We provide a detailed explanation of how to compute the cohomology groups of the Steenrod algebra through the use of differential forms, building on earlier work by Adem, Brown, Peterson, Quillen, and Stienon. It's noted that by employing the Regenstreif-Scheiermeyer construction, the cohomology groups of the Steenrod algebra can be further divided into subgroups containing complex derivatives. Consequently, this allows for an alternative method of computing the cohomology groups of the Steenrod algebra that differs from the Roy and Woo approach.

The Lyman-alpha molecule has a resonance energy of 11.18 eV, which means it can effectively absorb ultraviolet radiation below 11 eV, making it a common obstacle in space photography, but our innovative filter uses a dual gas mixture to block Lyman-alpha radiation while allowing other wavelengths to pass through, facilitating accurate U-band photometry in space.

In graph theory, an intermediate vertex is called an ideal vertex if a tree can be formed by removing it from a given graph. Ideally-placed intermediate vertices allow for the formation of multiple trees simultaneously. This property has sparked significant interest in studying graphs with this characteristic. Researchers have proposed a method for identifying these graphs and establishing a standardized approach for naming these graphs, which will be presented in this paper. Furthermore, an investigation into ideal vertices in symmetric graphs was conducted, and a novel classification system for these ideal vertices was developed, resulting in a comprehensive study of ideal vertices in symmetric graphs. Additionally, specific characteristics of symmetric graphs featuring ideal vertices were identified, and a method for pinpointing such vertices in certain types of symmetric graphs was developed. Moreover, examples of graphs that fail to meet the criteria of the newly-established classification system were identified, showcasing the respective properties of these graphs, and a counterexample to the conjectured consistency of the classification system was presented.

This paper presents a method for organizing and retrieving visual information based on temporal sequences of images, where each frame is represented as a parametric model linking human perception and low-level image properties. A catalog is effectively an abstract object, independent of its physical representation, allowing users to collect and manage image collections independently of rendering methods. A user-friendly interface in Dynamic Image Cataloging is demonstrated through search and browsing functions, uncoupled from image processing and rendering. Additionally, this method benefits multiple fields such as image databases, multimedia retrieval, medical imaging, and geographic information systems that deal with large catalogs of images.

This study confirms that a message of random bits, encrypted and transmitted via a carrier in a Gaussian noise channel, can be confirmed as the original message for any two parties, without needing the transmitter to know the message content. We developed an error correction code, called the binary Gaussian code, that allows for this verification. This code gave us a clear understanding of how long binary messages need to be to ensure that when transmitted, decoded, and compared to the original message, no errors will ever be found, as long as the channel conditions remain constant. We found a way to calculate the minimum length of a binary message that needs to be sent, to ensure that when received and compared to the original message, no errors will ever be found, under the assumption that maximum receiver computation power is limited by the number of bits in the message).

We analyze motion without dispersion for particles trapped within a washboard potential, advancing per unit time in the direction of a ascending slope at a velocity less than the absolute value of the slope. We confirm that particles maintain their state, with exact preservation of the phase, velocity, and position, and provide an alternative proof of the fact that the Lagrangian is time-invariant. Moreover, we show that the only long-term change is a rotation of the system, and we determine the amount of rotation in the final phase relative to the initial phase, relying on the difference in phase rather than absolute values. We also study the dynamics of pairs consisting of a particle and its image created through time-reversal, discovering that this pair remains in a synchronized motion with exact velocity matching, scaling, and geometric phase preservation in proportion to the time-reversal phase. Furthermore, we develop an analogy between the dynamics of a washboard potential and the dynamics of a magnetic field lines, illustrating that non-uniform velocity along these lines corresponds to a washboard potential slope. Lastly, we investigate the dynamics of a washboard-like potential that is localized rather than extended, such as the Klein-Gordon boundary condition solution in a one-dimensional space, and conclude that a particle moving according to this localized potential will experience a return to its initial state, with a backward motion velocity being the slope's negative value. We derive an invariant Lagrangian by hand, confirming that this velocity is the only one that changes over time,

This study develops a novel, adaptable technique for estimating impulse response functions that leverages high-dimensional, time-series data. Our proposed method enhances the popular local projection model by implementing sparse, flexible polynomial spline interpolation for the dependent variable, which enhances the local projection's ability to handle categorical data and reduces dimensionality in high-order time series. By adaptively operating under different identification conditions, this technique yields diverse but useful outcome estimations. In particular, our analysis demonstrates the connection between the local projection based on sparse splines and the Generalized Impulse Response Operator (GIRO) framework under minimal identification constraints. Furthermore, under identification constraints rooted in the Structural Vector Autoregression model, our technique produces an object that can be utilized to derive structural shocks and gain insight into the causal influences of policy decisions. Our research illustrates the efficacy of the local sparse spline identification method in practical applications, and we apply this analysis to the field of monetary economics to obtain fresh insights.

In a solid quantum vacuum, the interactions of electric charges demonstrate intriguing properties, which can be understood by analyzing the quantum vacuum's response to charge motion. A notable example is the angular Casimir effect observed when a charge rotates within a magnetic field. This phenomenon originates from the quantum vacuum's magnetic field fluctuations induced by the rotating charge. The induced fluctuations are in turn reflected in the magnetic field's time-average-ex expectation value, which admits an angular momentum-based interpretation by applying a mathematical transformation, namely the Mehler expansion. The effect quantifies the quantum vacuum's contribution to the rotating charge's kinetic momentum, revealing that this contribution is analogous to the classical Casimir effect. Specifically, it equals the product of the fine structure constant squared, the rotating charge's angular velocity, and its radial distance from the axis of rotation.

Research in knowledge graph extraction revolves around the role of named entity
classification for knowledge base annotation. This process involves identifying the
categories to which real-life entities such as persons, locations, and events
conform. Advanced models have been developed to accurately categorize entities,
despite being limited by the constraints of the linear vector space structure.
This linear structure restricts the complex hierarchical relationships between
categories, and prompts the use of non-linear hyperbolic network representations.
This paper presents a new method, FGNET-RH, which leverages hyperbolic space
representation to enhance hierarchical named entity classification. This approach
repositions entity categories in a hyperbolic space, allowing for a more
accurate representation of hierarchical relationships. FGNET-RH achieves this
through the application of hierarchical distance-based classification. This method
paves the way for a more accurate classification framework. Experiments conducted
on the 2019 and 2020 FGNET datasets demonstrate the efficacy of FGNET-RH,
yielding optimal F1 scores of 80.91 and 82.59.

To find the exact formulas for the Hankel determinants of Fej'er algebras, we examine the second Hankel determinant $H_2(n)$ and the seventh Hankel determinant $H_7(n)$ of degree $n$, considering all complex polynomials within the category $\mathcal{U}$ and the entire class $\mathcal{S}$. We establish links between $H_2(n)$ and $H_7(n)$ and derive formulas that cover both pure and mixed types of Fej'er algebras. We further derive formulas for the mean squared error in terms of the seventh Hankel determinant. We conclude by identifying formulas for the classical Schur algebras and providing numerical examples for $H_2(n)$ and its related mean squared error.

In a cloud-based data hub environment, optimal virtual machine allocation demands a load balancing scheme to prevent overutilization of resources and ensure enhanced performance. This study presents an innovative distribution method, called prepartition, for load balancing. It converts a load into a quantifiable attribute, called partition, which is used to calculate a node's load efficiency. An experiment was conducted, using a distributed data hub setup with 1000 operations per second, to evaluate prepartition's effectiveness. The results showed that prepartition achieves efficient resource utilization with minimal nodes processing less than 10% of total operations, while maintaining an optimal node load balance at less than 1%. A comparison with existing methods demonstrated prepartition's superior performance. This improved efficiency results in reduced energy consumption, lower costs, and faster transaction processing times.

We've designed an novel architecture, known as Fixed Point Networks, for predicting temporary states of a system in equilibrium, by leveraging the concept of NASH Equilibria. This architecture reworks existing policy and value networks through the incorporation of gradient-based iterations that exploit a specific type of convex-concave minimax problem. This design unlocks several key benefits for training equilibrium forecasts. First, it allows us to train directly on equilibrium models, rather than relying on approximations. Furthermore, it grants the ability to train solely based on forecasts, without needing full access to the system's rules. Notably, it also expands the applicability of reinforcement learning to multi-agent contexts where the action space is confined but the state is freely accessible. Empirical evidence reveals that Fixed Point Networks outperform other architectures in predicting NASH Equilibria, while also enabling the successful execution of tasks in multi-agent settings that were previously inaccessible via reinforcement learning.

We focus on finding the boundaries within which causal inference can occur, 
especially in cases where some variables only influence others indirectly, 
either by being connected at a previous point in time or through intermediate 
variables. We build on existing conditions for causal inference by introducing 
new restrictions that can help identify causal relationships more effectively in 
complex systems with many variables. These novel restrictions are based on the 
concept of optimal counterfactual matching, allowing us to improve and refine 
the accuracy of causal inference in high-dimensional scenarios.

We've developed an efficient method for surveillance in a linear system subject to hidden attacks. Traditionally, surveillance involved training an adaptive model on data from the target system and using it to detect anomalies, but this can be ineffective because it's based on limited data. Instead, our approach uses a single adaptive model to distinguish between normal data and attacked or unforeseen normal data, and we show that it's naturally more effective than the traditional method. Additionally, we simplify the processing of high-frequency data by combining small segments into single units, and we prove that our model can identify attacks on time-critical systems within strict time limits. And, further enhancing real-time effectiveness, our method for marking attack instances becomes increasingly accurate as the frequency of attacks increases. And, further enhancing reliability, we also developed an adaptive method for highlighting instances of attacks. We tested our methods through simulations using data from a liquid-level system and found that they identify attacks with nearly perfect accuracy, exceeding 99.9% RMS. margin of error. And, comparing performance, we found that our approach is about 3 times more sensitive to attacks and requires about 3 times less computation than the traditional method. And, finally, because our method for modeling is solitary and universal, it can be applied to a wide variety of situations involving effective effective effective surveillance of hidden attacks.

A language enables its speakers to efficiently process and Interprets vast amounts of information, thereby facilitating clear communication. However, the current text generation models are incapable of capturing the essence of long documents, thereby resulting in subpar document summaries. Our study presents GAE-ISumm, a pioneering unsupervised document summarization tool that leverages the strengths of Graph AutoEncoders and Generative Adversarial Networks. By representing a long document as an integrated graph, where sentences serve as nodes, and their semantic connections as edges, the GAE model preserves the essential interconnections between these sentences. Subsequently, the GAE model and GAN are utilized in conjunction to generate high-quality summaries. Rather than directly generating summary sentences, our approach generates an ideal, yet hidden sentence that encapsulates the long document's essence and serves as a superior analogue. This superior sentence, which is our target, is estimated using the GAN framework. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method not only outperforms existing state-of-the-art models but also effectively bridges the semantic divides between sentences, thereby identifying the latent, ideal summary.

We introduce the concept of S-rings of Noether type, a generalization of commutative Noetherian rings with a set of Noetherian ideals that has specific properties. These S-rings can be thought of as a non-commutative counterpart to commutative Noetherian rings. We identify some characteristics of S-rings, and then investigate the S-rings of prime Noetherian ideals, examining Millan's ring as a specific example of such an S-ring. We also define generalized Hilbert and Zariski spaces for S-rings of Noetherian ideals and establish Millan's ring as a specific example of a ring with a generalized Hilbert space that is Zariski closed. Furthermore, to demonstrate the effectiveness of these concepts, we apply them to the ring M_2(Q_(p)). Finally, our paper concludes with a global characterization theorem of S-rings of Noetherian ideals that has significant implications.

Recent research on the rates of stellar collapse in the nearby star population reveals an unexpected pattern. Specifically, a certain type of stellar collapse, caused by a hidden companion, is more frequent in low-mass stars than in high-mass ones, unlike another type of collapse which has the opposite property when compared with star masses. Furthermore, a notable pattern is observed in the rate of these collapses among young versus old stars, specifically with the rate of one type being higher in older stars and the rate of the other type being lower in older stars and higher in younger stars, based on current data. 

This study is focused on finding evidence of these types of hidden companions surrounding six nearby stars that have recently changed their movement across the sky at a specific rate. Researchers used a combination of past and current data along with advanced models of how stars move, and found that three out of six stars matched expectations for their motion if they had certain types of hidden companions, and could be seen at different stages of certain chemical reactions within their own gas. However, a better fit was seen in the cases of low-mass stars and not in the cases of high-mass stars, unlike another type of hidden companion which had a better fit in the cases of high-mass stars.

A novel vae variant, minimising the hierarchical $β$-divergence, is presented with restricted latent space, introduced by limiting the posterior distribution, achieving a trade-off between latent space compression and disintegration of the data distribution within the latent space. The proposed model's performance is tested and compared with traditional vae on multiple image compression tasks, employing metrics such as vinceless and gap metrics in addition to standard metrics like dist and vae metrics. The model's performance is evaluated against a vae baseline model, which employs a similar range of compression ratios and is optimized for a varying range of $β$ values, showing that our model yields better performance at similar compression ratios.

The deployment of the Internet of Things (IoT) has greatly enhanced our lives by integrating smart devices, yet has introduced concerns about security and safeguarding confidentiality in settings where multiple devices coexist.  To address this, a system for tracking intelligent home devices has been created using a private blockchain and sensor data, including GPS and accelerated gravity-based positioning techniques, to establish a decentralized solution that allows users to efficiently monitor their devices without requiring centralized infrastructure.

A widely used pre-compression encoding technique, gray coding, enhances the reliability of lossless compression systems by minimizing errors resulting from transient data losses. However, its effectiveness relies on accurate decoding of non-binary L-value symbols, which can be problematic in systems utilizing short-circuit based encoding, due to occasional temporary losses. One approach to addressing this issue involves quantizing L-values, but the optimal number of precision bits for L-values remains unclear, necessitating an adaptive solution that adjusts to varying patterns in the input data. This problem can be resolved through the application of a novel, convolutional neural network (CNN) model that optimizes the number of precision bits for L-values, based on an analysis of the entropy of the input data, and experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses traditional methods in terms of rate-distortion performance. Furthermore, the proposed method exhibits flexibility, as it can be applied to existing compression systems without requiring modifications to the decoding path, and can also be adapted for use in multi-source compression systems, involving various input data with differing entropy patterns.

This paper presents an iterative approach for efficiently assessing the upward planarity of a directed graph. The method builds upon existing full-planarity algorithms by adding an overapproximation parameter to determine whether a graph is approximately planifiable. Each iteration significantly reduces the graph's size by removing edges in constant time, ultimately achieving an exponential decrease in time complexity with the parameter. The time complexity is further divided into three components: O(n^2) for preprocessing, O(2^n * n) for iterating through levels, and O(n^2) for handling unremoved edges in the final merge step. The overall complexity is thus influenced by the parameter and settles at a non-dominant term of O(n^2) excluding the parameter. The method allows for a trade-off between computation time and a polynomial increase in the number of operations denoted by the parameter k. The method can also be further optimized by employing various variants of the algorithm.

Machine learning models are increasingly being applied to their human counterparts in tasks such as crowd-sourced label assignment. While these traditional methods work effectively in tasks with clear answers, they fail to account for noisy data generated by humans, which leads to significant degradation in model performance. In an effort to overcome this limitation, we have developed a novel approach that treats human output distributions as noisy data and reframes it as a missing label problem. This reformulation enables us to leverage ensemble modeling, which, in turn, improves the accuracy of label assignments. Our proposed method also prioritizes ensemble confidence by utilizing entropy as a regularization factor. The ensemble model and entropy optimization work in tandem to correct earlier modeling errors, resulting in improved confidence in model predictions. In evaluating our approach, we have demonstrated high classification accuracy on synthetic image datasets that mimic human-based label assignment, as well as an impressive 4% enhancement in accuracy on the Quac dataset, which is comprised of noisy crowd-sourced data. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the diversity of human models is a key factor in determining optimal ensemble configurations and, consequently, accurate label assignments.

For semiflows with transfer operators that define dynamical systems with compactness properties, we establish a condition (exponential decay of correlations) that guarantees the decay of the norm over time. This result complements a previous finding by Liu, Ralston and Temam for flows, filling a theoretical gap for semiflows.

Covering arrays are a critical tool for ensuring comprehensive compatibility in complex systems and have various practical applications. Among the different types of covering arrays, particular emphasis has been given to tiny-covering-arrays which aim to minimize the number of events displayed. This research focuses specifically on tiny-strength-$k$ covering arrays where we're interested in finding the smallest possible covering arrays with strength $k$ or higher. Given the difficulty in directly covering all schedules, we're able to break down events into individual components based on specific parameters and use a modified version of the integer partition function to determine the total number of these components. Additionally, we're able to identify some general conditions for tiny-strength-$k$ covering arrays and use this information to assess whether a certain array is tiny for specific values of $k$. Finally, we're able to identify some arrays that are tiny for certain values of $k$ and use this information to assess its efficiency compared to other methods.

In a contest where multiple players compete for a prize by submitting a single value, each player attempts to outdo the others by offering a higher value. If a player's submitted value is closest to the ideal result, they win the contest. Players can strategically study how the distances between their submitted values and the optimal value correlate with each other, and use this information to develop a winning strategy. By analyzing the contest results, they can determine if an optimal solution exists, which is the basis of finding and proving theorems about solving such complex problems. This paper contributes by explaining how players can achieve this using noisy values and imperfectly correlated results, which is a more general scenario than previously considered. We found that as the degree of noise and correlation decreases, players can use geometric principles to divide the result space into regions, which allows them to accurately predict whether an optimal solution exists using geometric properties.

This study involves a structured duplication of Baker et al.'s (2015) directed genetic algorithm (DGa), which utilizes input failure reports to produce exact system failures. DGa combines a stochastic binary tree approach to encode failures with techniques such as pruning and node vector representation to enhance effectiveness. Our replication effort addresses DGa's key methodology and hyperparameter choices, focusing on replication limitations and the results. Moreover, a comparative evaluation of the replication approach with existing methods, including automatic failure reproduction based on ProM, is presented. DGa's performance is measured using three metrics, representing time efficiency, data efficiency, and accuracy, respectively. DGa's success rate and accuracy are analyzed through precision and recall assessment, while its effectiveness is calculated using F1 scores. The study establishes a new benchmark for exact failure reproduction.

The unusual defect lattice arrangement observed in superconductors exhibits a high degree of periodicity, which often corresponds to the structural arrangement of the material. In these systems, the size of the defect lattice often scales in relation to the material's periodic structure, although exceptions exist where the defect lattice size adapts in response to varying pressure or temperature while retaining a unique arrangement of its components. Melting patterns of superconducting vortices in complex materials display these characteristics, with the size of the resulting pattern influenced by interactions between the vortices as well as the material's structure. In the study presented here, the researchers have observed a transition from a regular square array of vortices within the material Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$Fe$_{2}$As$_{2}$. Utilizing a technique that distinguishes between different phases of the material without disrupting the sample, the researchers have found two stages to this phase transition: first, a regular square array of vortices forming within the material at temperatures below 2 K; then, upon decreasing the magnetic field from 0.5 T to 0.15 T, a new configuration emerges through a first-order transition, which assumes a square pattern but with two different sizes - a larger inner square and two smaller outer triangles. This new finding indicates a high-pressure phase transition within the material due to its similarity with similar transitions found in materials lacking superconductivity and also demonstrates the effectiveness of the

Investigations of direct photon emission in high-energy collisions have been crucial in grasping the properties of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) state. By analyzing time-asymmetric behavior of this phenomenon in local flow conditions, researchers can access information about the QGP's transport coefficients, thereby gaining insight into its viscosity. Utilizing state-of-the-art relativistic hydrodynamic models, research has found that visible characteristics of this phenomenon are regulated by the combined effects of viscosity and temperature-dependent transport processes. Furthermore, studies have demonstrated that experimental data on peripheral Au+Au collisions at 200 GeV exhibits characteristics that correspond to hydrodynamic behavior, thereby justifying the use of hydrodynamics in extracting the QGP's viscosity from this phenomenon. With the aid of HSPIS, researchers have found that the QGP's viscosity parameter $\eta/s$ falls within the range of 0.4 to 0.8, thereby providing evidence of a low bound of this parameter. In a subsequent study, researchers have used an in-medium transport model to investigate the initial stages of photon production, and in doing so, have determined that $\eta/s$ is approximately 0.22, both at low and high energy levels. Notably, this study reveals that spatial viscosity fluctuations play a critical (fluctuating) role in determining transport coefficients, and that such effects will be particularly pronounced in high-energy collisions of small systems. In a final study, researchers have used an in-depth analysis of thermal

We investigate ground states of the two-dimensional, three-component Heisenberg model with nearest neighbor interactions on a triangular and kagome lattice systems. Focusing on arrangements of spin and magnetic order, our work particularly examines the possible configurations consisting of 30 spins or less per period. After analyzing and documenting all possible ground states for both lattices containing small numbers of spins, we identify patterns and regular patterns within these arrangements. Our findings show that certain configurations are extensive in number and account for a significant portion of all possible ground states, while another set is relatively rare. The infrequent patterns are mainly found within arrangements having a higher coordination number and those containing opposite spin orientations. The frequent patterns are predominantly found within arrangements having a lower coordination number and those containing same spin orientations. A theoretical explanation for these observations is provided, and the research implies that experiments conducted at low temperatures may extensively produce the rare magnetic arrangement of all spin components being antiparallel on a kagome lattice composed of certain metal ions.

Our method, called REPAIR, retrieves a limited number of causal links within highly complex systems by using sparse regression on large intervention results. 
Testing our method across the majority of public experiment platforms, our algorithm maintains a strong control over false discovery rates, even with the presence of correlated data.
Through thorough analysis of its performance, our results demonstrate that REPAIR is an effective tool for identifying causal relationships, achieving the highest accuracy among comparison methods in both controlled and real-world experiments. 
Additionally, our method allows for the establishment of causal relationships with intervention results not originally considered, providing an efficient and highly scalable solution for large-scale data analysis.

The universe's detection of the B-mode polarization, a five-year observation, confirms that the gravitational wave signal originates from cosmic expansion. This leads to a groundbreaking conclusion that the universe's symmetry-breaking inflation, driven by a single scalar field, is not only plausible but also statistically supported. Moreover, the conclusion comes with precise numerical backing, stating that the inflationary energy scale is approximately $3\times10^{16}$ GeV and the inflation duration is about $3\times10^{18}$ seconds, which aligns with the universe's current understanding at that moment in time.

The CDF II Collaboration has made a precise measurement of the W boson mass that shows a discrepancy from the Standard Model predictions. In light of this discrepancy and the recent findings by the Fermilab muon g-2 group that show a significant anomaly in the muon's magnetic moment, a type-X 2HDM framework is investigated to see if it can accommodate both the observed discrepancies. We have extended the type-X 2HDM model to include a gauge invariant operator that allows the H5 field to interact with fermions, allowing us to make predictions about the behavior of muons and tau leptons. This model can accommodate the observed W boson mass anomaly and the muon's magnetic moment anomaly for different values of the H5 field. Our analysis shows that for certain mass ranges of the H5 field, the model can accommodate the observed anomalies while conforming to the existing upper limits on the interaction between this field and muons and tau leptons.

When searching for specific concepts on the internet, users often encounter a challenge known as question-answering, where they cannot simply rely on the query results because of inaccurate labels. To overcome this, a type of query reformulation is proposed which alters the question to pinpoint specific concepts within the query results. Two of the main obstacles in this area are the subjectivity of human-based label creation and query reformulation processes. To address these issues, a novel approach is presented which uses crowdsourced data to create concept labels and reformulate queries in an automatic manner. By establishing a large dictionary of ground truth concepts from crowd-sourced data, this method can accurately identify which words within the query hold critical information. To demonstrate its effectiveness, this approach is applied to concept-based label creation and query reformulation, where it is compared with established state-of-the-art methods on six widely-used datasets containing 2,000 new queries. The findings indicate that this technique outperforms other automatic query reformulation methods. Furthermore, a manual evaluation of 500 queries revealed that this approach successfully identifies relevant concepts in 71.4% of the queries. To validate its practical relevance, a search engine ranking model known as DRank is also employed to compare the performance of original and reformulated queries in terms of user satisfaction, where it is found that this approach leads to a 32% increase in satisfaction from 63.1% for original queries to 95.7% for reformulated queries.

This study introduces a novel empirical approach to analyze conversation styles using a learning algorithm based on neural networks. Our primary objective is to measure the similarity between a model's and a learner's utterance sequences during conversations, based on the transfer of learning. The proposed algorithm is tested with the MEAT model, an auto-regressive neural framework designed for automatic speech recognition and speech synthesis. The results demonstrate that our method successfully identifies the similarity between a base language model and various learner languages, in both monitored and unmonitored settings, without the need for rewards or external feedback. Additionally, we discuss the implications of our approach, highlighting its differences and similarities with established second language acquisition theories.

We have developed an openly accessible platform aimed at aiding research and data analysis through the visualization of spectral and imaging data across various fields. This framework not only enables rapid data visualization but also facilitates real-time simulation of different data collections, yielding results that can inform observational planning. To accomplish this, we have incorporated a web-based visualizer that utilizes X-Y plots for spectral data and 2D/3D maps for imaging data, both of which can be accessed at no charge and run directly within a web browser. The source code behind our platform is freely available for modification and distribution, allowing it to be easily integrated into external projects as needed.

This research introduces a novel approach to a previously under-explored problem in unsupervised action understanding, specifically 'temporal action partitioning'. We frame it as a task where the goal is to divide a continuous video stream into discrete action sequences without knowing the correct segmentation in advance. We created several challenging synthetic video datasets with increasing difficulty to simulate this problem, starting from simple videos where the end result is achievable but the intermediate steps are increasingly obscure. These datasets enabled us to evaluate the effectiveness of proposed methods and understand their strengths and limitations. Ultimately, we discovered that combining a self-supervised framework with externally available video data yields the most accurate partitioning results.

Utilizing the Glover-Roberts-Robichon present algebra, we investigate the existence and properties of hidden-charm pentaquark states and their counterparts that contain charm. The study involves a systematic examination of various isospin and orbital angular momentum configurations, and we derive the Regge trajectories for both types of pentaquark states. Additionally, we employ the harmonic-Regge formalism to determine their masses and study their decay patterns into mesons and baryons, utilizing SU(3) symmetry. The model's outcomes are found to be consistent with the findings from the quark model and recent LHC experiments.

Many students of computer science struggle with the fundamentals of software testing, yet numerous working professionals, who are not face-to-face with students, have the same difficulties, suggesting a significant problem exists, largely due to inadequate understanding of software testing concepts and skills, rather than a lack of talent. Addressing this issue requires enhancing education and academic approaches to effectively address the underlying knowledge gaps. This study compares two methods of providing students with feedback on software testing assignments, using real-world data from a online platform and over 170 students, to assess the impact on students' understanding and comprehension. The analysis indicates that students performing better academically are more likely to produce higher-quality assignments, but the order of academic performance and understanding is reversed for students with lower grades. This work is the first of a two-part study exploring software testing education challenges through the lens of software engineering and educational research.

We address the issue of adjusting the conditions of a deep learning model without leveraging its original training environment, a challenging task made even more difficult when we can't access the original training data either. Traditional approaches to domain adjustment, such as domain confusion, require access to the original environment, whereas our solution, a method called STFT, can successfully apply domain changes without such access by utilizing a limited set of labeled samples from the target environment. Unlike conventional methods, STFT is a universal solution that can be easily adapted to various domain change tasks without requiring any further modifications, thanks to its reliance on a different, pseudo-supervised approach that allows the model to draw in relevant information from unlabeled data. Experimental results demonstrate that STFT is just as effective as domain confusion, while providing significant improvements in cases where there's a substantial discrepancy between the available labeled data and the original environment.

A review of gas core nuclear reactors for deep space propulsion has been conducted.
The primary objectives of this study involve examining the pusher blanket
assembly's structural robustness, assessing and comparing various materials
used in the radiation barrier, evaluating coolant options, and investigating
the optimal reactor size and power range for spacecraft applications.
The study also aims to identify and address remaining technological hurdles
that must be overcome for this reactor concept to be viable.

In the field of astroparticle research, neural networks are used to analyze data from high-energy particle collisions between the Sun and nearby galaxies. Training a neural network for this task is difficult since it relies on the network localizing interaction points within a three-dimensional volume. However, astrophysical considerations can provide valuable information to guide this localization. Inspired by medical imaging using neural networks to identify tumors, we apply similar techniques to high-energy particle collisions. Our study demonstrates how incorporating astrophysical constraints into the neural network architecture can improve training outcomes, even in cases where such constraints cannot be directly applied to the output. Additionally, we show that our domain-informed approach can split complex localization tasks into two easier problems, leading to two distinct neural network designs that outperform combined localization attempts. Our research presents domain-informed design principles for developing neural networks that can effectively analyze high-energy particle collisions, even when the physical constraints cannot directly influence the localization of points within three-dimensional volumes. These design principles are versatile and can be applied to other fields, such as gravitational wave research.

The potential of future telescopes like the James Webb Space Telescope and the General Catalogue of Atmospheres of Exoplanets (GACE) to investigate the molecular atmospheres of giant exoplanets provide a strong foundation for scientific research. Effective analysis of spectroscopic data in terms of absorption coefficients will play a crucial role in studying both brown dwarfs and planets. With this goal in mind, we have developed a comprehensive database of absorption cross-sections for various molecular species that are likely to be found in the atmospheres of giant exoplanets and brown dwarfs. Our collection of data, which covers a temperature range from 100 to 2000 K and encompasses 18 molecules, can serve as a valuable asset for undertaking comprehensive model atmospheres and simulations of thermal molecular processes. Furthermore, we are planning to expand our database to a broader temperature and pressure spectrum in the near future.

This work proposes a novel framework for validating the accuracy of Answer Set Programming (ASP) models by employing external sources of truth.
