A flexible paradigm is introduced that enables ASP models to leverage diverse types of authoritative data, such as axiomatic statements and observations from external sources. The framework defines a range of ASP models that incorporate this authoritative data and provides a Unification framework, merging the insights of these models to yield a cohesive ASP model. The proposed framework is uniquely adaptable to various types of authoritative data and can be used to facilitate learning and other advanced functionalities. Moreover, this work provides an optimization technique for utilizing it in ASP modeling by transforming specific ASP programs into equivalent ones using propositional logic.

Recent breakthroughs in quantum information and learning have led to a flourishing
of quantum information and learning systems. Studying quantum information and
learning has not only brought significant progress but also uncovered intricate
connections between them. Researchers initially conceived quantum information as a
extension of classical information and taught quantum learning as a sophisticated
expression of classical learning. Recently, experts have found a link between
quantum information and learning and a general quantum resource theory, which
enables us to broaden classical learning into a general quantum learning
framework. This theoretical framework can not only make sense of many quantum
algorithmic advantages but also reveal the hidden quantum nature within them.
Here, we explore the foundational idea of this general quantum resource
theoretical framework and present an essential concept related to learning.

We propose a novel approach to establish a statistical model based solely on the distribution's moments. In doing so, we derive both theoretical and algorithmic methods for creating a probability model given a finite set of a distribution's moments, and we also establish a moment estimation framework along with its corresponding convergence statements. Furthermore, we introduce a metric for evaluating the accuracy of such moment model estimations. To illustrate the practical relevance of this approach, we adapt a well-established statistical test, originally designed for multivariate normality, to instead verify the accuracy of a moment model. This adapted test enables us to make inferences about a distribution, and it also allows us to assess the efficacy of Monte Carlo methods for a broad class of problems. We demonstrate the potential of this approach by examining its application to the specific task of training neural networks, where we aim to identify a suitable probability model for the data distribution, and also by proposing a metric to evaluate the efficacy of variance reduction methods in stochastic gradient descent for neural network training.

We analyze a continuous-time process with a stable component and a subordinator, resulting in a non-homogeneous Markov process, also observed to be the minimal weak solution of a corresponding stochastic differential equation. The properties of this process are comparable to a three-component system, consisting of a deterministic component, a linear diffusion, and a linear subdiffusion, all occurring independently. In our study, we evaluate the behavior of this process in a compact set, derive its weak convergence properties as the time goes to infinity, and establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of related estimators, also making use of second-order functional central limit theorems and weak convergences to establish the results. Some numerical examples have also been included.

Our research demonstrates that low-density parity-check codes with random patterns of check equations can efficiently encode and decode quantum data by using linear and non-linear methods of decoding, which can achieve nearly perfect decoding performance for arbitrary noise levels. We further develop a technique to accurately calculate the probability of successful decoding for these codes that are affected by noise of any arbitrary type, by using the collective decay principle. We compared the performance of these codes with that of surface codes of 15-step interconnection under both binary and continuous measurement, finding that the former can achieve nearly perfect decoding rates for binary measurement, and nearly perfect probabilities of no error under continuous measurement, at code rates very close to the quantum Boltzmann game optimal rate. We also compared the performance of these codes with that of surface codes of 15-step interconnection under both binary and continuous measurement, finding that the former can achieve nearly perfect decoding rates for binary measurement, and nearly perfect probabilities of no error under continuous measurement, at code rates very close to the quantum Boltzmann game optimal rate. We also compared the performance of these codes with that of surface codes of 15-step interconnection under continuous measurement, showing that the former can sustain up to 60% higher levels of noisy interference while maintaining nearly perfect decoding performance, and that the number of circulating photons required for successful decoding is at least six times higher.

We explore the concept of computational biology's "contact graph" model for analyzing the spread of infectious diseases and other phenomena on large graphs. To achieve this, we develop efficient distributed algorithms for creating dominant ensembles of certain graph types, specifically spherically-influenced and high-girth graphs, which have been shown to closely mimic the behavior of real viral spread in certain scenarios. By tailoring our methods to take advantage of the inherent structure of these graph types, we are able to develop distributed solutions that satisfy rigorous technical requirements, in addition to observing practical performance gains in our experiments.

We investigate unique properties of elevated-order topological insulators (TIs) with both spatial disorder and external perturbations. By focusing on non-trivial topological states, we derive a straightforward mass-boundary correspondence in disordered TIs. This interaction results in a distinct transition in these systems between fully delocalized, fully localized, and multifragmentized phases, which occurs when the disordered parameter surpasses specific threshold values. Notably, as the disordered parameter increases, the size of these delocalized regions diminishes, and the corresponding transition scales shift towards lower values of the external perturbation. We verify our theoretical findings through the use of numerical simulations.

A summary of new searches for squarks and gluinos in final states of jets and missing transverse momentum from the CMS experiment at the LHC is provided, including data from 2016 collected with a total of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data at 13 TeV. This includes the most constrained, high-energy scenarios where the net sensitivity is presented. Additionally, results from compressed squark searches in collaborative searches with CDF are presented. Assuming the simplified model of direct production of squarks and gluinos, net cross section limits are provided at 95% confidence level. Based on data, the exclusion limits on various mass parameters of squarks and gluinos in relevant models are presented, including the lightest neutralino of 50 GeV. Finally, collaborative searches with CDF are presented in the region of squark production with small mass difference with net mass limit of 320 GeV in the case of up- and charged supersymmetric squarks.

Neural rendering, which leverages the strength of different machine learning models, offers a promising approach to rendering complex scenes. This research aims to improve neural rendering by applying it to volume data, which requires the development of a brightness field model that combines albedo and density information. By establishing a link between volume data and a brightness field, this paper demonstrates the ability to render both albedo and density images, as well as Albedo + Depth and Depth images, using a brightness field model that can be trained efficiently through volume data pre-processing. Notably, this paper shows that this model can be trained from a small number of real depth images, without ground truth images, by applying a novel class segmentation loss through the lens of a brightness field, resulting in a model that achieves state-of-the-art results on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

Observations conducted at the SOAR telescope in 2020 along with previously unpublished data, yielded a substantial dataset of 1735 measurements across 1288 pairs and 1177 targets. A significant discovery of this study includes identifying 59 novel pairs or subsystems among nearby dwarf stars, primarily, adding to our ongoing speckle program. Our speckle program aims to monitor orbital movements of binaries within the solar neighborhood, specifically, high-order hierarchies, Hipparcos pairs, and also assess 892 members of young moving groups, clusters, and associations, many of which reside outside of these groups, particularly, within the solar neighborhood. Analysis of our data revealed 305 newly resolved pairs, bringing the total number of resolved pairs across all SOAR datasets to 3135, among which 1615 remain unresolved. Lastly, speckle data allowed us to resolve an additional 103 pairs, augmenting the speckle dataset at the plate and increasing the total number of resolved pairs across all plate datasets to 2238.

A universal algebraic framework is established for describing cosmic strings' classical signatures, featuring a specific type of Lie algebra with homogeneous components. This work further demonstrates that a specific sub-algebra leads to the BMS$_4$, BMS$_3$, and Azabean algebras as key specialization cases. It is shown that a specific duality relationship leads to the equivalence of certain signatures with the signatures of massive free particles, achieving a duality with kinematical components. The study culminates by showing that certain signatory equations are inherently linked to the three-dimensional integrability of massive free particles.

A unique event was observed by LoFAR at Type II and IV radio frequencies, thought to result from a shock wave caused by a flare and coronal mass ejection on July 1, 2013. The event's characteristics suggest it was triggered by a steepened shock front that initially compressed the electron cloud ahead of it before overtaking it. The event's evolution can be explained by a propagating shock driving an electron cloud at a 240 km/s and supports the hypothesis that coronal mass ejections occur more frequently than solar flares.

We conducted an analysis of lepton flavor universality and anomalies in leptonic decays of heavy mesons, as well as the muon's magnetic moment, within the general two Higgs doublet framework. Introducing a new parameter $\hat{s}$, which controls a specific type of flavor changing interaction, in combination with the existing $\rho$ parameter, which regulates another, we examined the boundaries of the parameter space in the $\hat{s}-\rho$ plane. Our findings indicate that, in the case of the electron and muon, the boundaries are largely identical, which aligns with current experimental findings and constraints. However, if the boundaries are breached and corresponding signals are detected, a more precise measurement of $\sin^2\theta_w$ at the LHCb experiment could significantly reduce the allowable range of $\hat{s}$ and $\rho$. We also found that, in many regions of the $\hat{s}-\rho$ plane, the observed anomalies in $a_\mu$ could be resolved. Consequently, new, detectable effects are likely to arise in the $b \rightarrow s$ transitions if $\hat{s}$ and $\rho$ assume certain values. Furthermore, investigating the Z boson's decay into the four lightest Higgs bosons at future facilities may be crucial in understanding the Z-boson's flavor changing couplings that are anticipated in a number of theoretical scenarios.

We create a computer model to simulate a chaotic fluid motion scenario using a novel approach. This approach involves developing a statistical model based on average values, which helps us maintain the initial conditions of the fluid motion. In return, we can use this initial conditions to calculate vital metrics like viscosity, and it allows us to make predictions about the connection between the way the fluid moves and the characteristics of the fluid itself. This method is highly effective, even with limited data, and it gives us the ability to study how the characteristics of the fluid change over time. A recent advancement in this area has led to the creation of a new statistical model for the way the characteristics of the fluid move, which we can use to better understand the fluid dynamics by focusing on the changes over time. All of these advancements give us the ability to make precise calculations about the way the characteristics of the fluid change, which is essential for our understanding of the fluid dynamics.

The boson sampling model is built around the idea that measuring a complex quantum system using a specific number of photons from selected modes creates a naturally occurring model that can be utilized for purposes like image recognition. However, implementing this model poses significant challenges related to describing the underlying quantum state, including deriving expectations for any given measurement setup. Typically, researchers have approached this state problem by assuming it corresponds to a specific type of quantum system, but these incomplete specifications raise issues regarding the fundamental understanding of boson sampling. By addressing these concerns through a detailed analysis of the boson sampling model, we derive the state expectations for any given setup without making any particular assumptions about the system in question. Furthermore, our work enables the calculation of a quantifiable non-locality indicator within the model. Our findings have implications for theoretical models that claim to accurately describe boson sampling and may facilitate experimental implementations by highlighting existing approaches in the field.

Time series data in life sciences often involves dealing with noisy and irregular patterns of significance, and is frequently characterized by a high number of variables. Despite the importance of these patterns, studies in the field have historically been limited by the constraints of short temporal windows and multi-dimensional data sets. We propose a novel method for learning from time-based data sets, including a monitoring component that quickly detects anomalies and changes by using an optimized neural network design with a restricted number of parameters. Our results show that this method can effectively analyze a complex dataset from mouse physiology, and highlight the potential for significant scientific breakthroughs through the effective analysis of biomedical time series data.

In cases where key factors are hidden from observation, essential elements must be identified from visible elements, a task requiring either explicit relationships or the use of machine learning techniques, particularly those employing recurrent architectures. This paper examines how recurrent models function, with a focus on their applications in uncovering latent variables, as well as their applications in processing natural language. It's demonstrated that recurrent architectures are particularly effective at leveraging contextual information, even when key factors are hidden, through examples such as uncovering the underlying language model despite the presence of noisy input, or extracting implicit rules from observed data. This paper also explores the use of recurrent architectures in the context of uncertainty estimation for machine learning models, a task for which the theoretical underpinnings are still developing. It's argued that recurrent architectures offer a natural solution to this challenge, one that is closely linked to their ability to model complex, high-level aspects of data.

The convolutions of feature extraction, including those by Inverse Graphics Network (IGN) and C3D, are combined to effectively localize critical frames in videos containing specific actions, despite minimal labeling. By incorporating the IGN convolution for understanding contextual information and the C3D convolution for capturing spatiotemporal essentials of action recognition, the proposed self-supervised ConvGraph self-education method enables efficient detection of actions from weakly-guided annotations. Our innovation outperforms existing solutions, including strongly-supervised models, in localized frame detection. Notably, the proposed method achieves frame localization accuracy of 51.5% without supervision, surpassing previous work by having over 20% higher accuracy without relying on expensive annotation. Our method also exhibits minimal dependence on computational power, demonstrating a speedup of 2.7 times compared to previous actions as a classification models. Our method's capacity for self-improvement leads to accurate and localized frame sets, thus enhancing the effectiveness of action detection for applications. Our method also sheds light on the effectiveness of self-supervised learning for enhancing action recognition. Our method's source code is available at: \url{https://github.com/asharakeh/Spot-What-Counts}.

The Visual Cognition Challenge: Image Resemblance Assessment held in conjunction with ICCV 2023 demonstrated that human resemblance assessments are challenging for AI models to match. The competition's results and insights provided valuable insights for AI researchers and developers working in visual cognition. The following is a summary of the challenges' background and outcomes.

Our research involves analyzing the impacts of random fluctuations on parabolic equations, hyperbolic equations, and diffusion models with variable conductivity. We investigate these phenomena in various situations, including random jumps, time disruptions, and spatial inconsistencies, often yielding unique mathematical challenges. Some consequences of random fluctuations include metastable behavior, a phenomenon that can be observed approximately at specific times based on the system's natural frequency. In our study, we examine metastability in a timer-based activation process, a temperature-driven SDE, and a diffusion model with spatially varying conductivity. Our work also covers the boundary conditions of these processes, focusing on reflections on boundaries for random systems. We use mathematical modeling, asymptotic analysis, and probabilistic techniques to describe random fluctuations and their long-term effects. In particular, we demonstrate that the probability of an activation event in a timer-based process, a heat equation in a bounded domain, and a diffusion model with variable conductivity on a flat surface all show similar patterns, even as the system size changes. This suggests a universal pattern underlying these models, which can be confirmed by studying their limiting behavior as the system size becomes almost infinite.

This research aims to investigate the influence of intense magnetic fields on the energy of closed-shell atomic systems using the Linear Localized Orbital of Valley Type (LLOVT)-Local Correlation Theory (LCT), which also employs a parameter that adjusts energy to compensate Purcell-type magnetic effects.

This work introduces a pioneering framework known as DP-REC, which utilizes differential privacy to deliver personalized, multimedia educational content in a secure, communication-efficient federated learning paradigm for educational institutions. Given the stringent constraints of differential privacy, the proposed framework effectively mitigates communication expenses by establishing a decentralized setting for statistical analysis. Furthermore, it presents innovative strategies for securing various forms of educational data (comprising video, audio and text) and demonstrates the practical applicability of its design through the development of a federated learning system for music education. DP-REC's efficacy is substantiated by comprehensive experiments that explore its performance in a secure context, as well as its ability to optimize both accuracy and efficiency. These findings inspire a comprehensive set of research directions related to differential privacy in educational settings, which are also presented.

A comprehensive far-ultraviolet survey of the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus complex has been completed with the UVORBIT spacecraft, providing detailed spectra and spatial resolution of about 5 arcminutes. The survey has resulted in a total of 2100 hours of observation time, during which we mapped the distribution of ionized gas, identified 23 plasma clouds, and studied their properties. Our findings indicate that the ionized gas within Taurus-Auriga-Perseus is primarily composed of two distinct components: massive (approximately 1 x 10^18 particles) plasma clouds with small dimensions and a more diffuse, background gas with a much lower density. A statistical analysis of our data revealed no correlation between the estimated volumes of ionized gas within individual clouds and their mean densities, suggesting the presence of a power-law distribution. Furthermore, we used far-ultraviolet radiation from the nearby star lambda Ori IR as a proxy to study photoionization and discover a previously undetected cloud, located at approximately 1.0 +/- 0.1 kpc from the center of this system. Based on flux measurements of photoionized lines, we estimated that the mass of this cloud is approximately 2.9 x 10^17 grams and its dimensions are about 5.6 +/- 1.2 parsecs in radius. Finally, using far-ultraviolet emissions from the molecular cloud toward lambda Ori IR as a proxy, we verified that the cloud's kinetic

Document search techniques in digital libraries utilize effective indexing methods, where query answers are derived from examining relevant document sections. Given the recent adoption of document management in information systems, we concentrate on designing a table retrieval pipeline tailored to PDFs, enhancing the capabilities of a tokenized table retrieval method. Our enhancement leverages graph neural networks to compare a given table with potential substitutes within a document. Experimental results demonstrate that this network-driven table matching approach surpasses the tokenized pipeline in quality while incrementally contributing to computational resources. Furthermore, incorporating a graph-based table matching algorithm enhances its search precision without affecting overall speed. In a comprehensive evaluation, our proposed algorithm achieved 10% higher mean average precision (MAP) at 20% of the tokenized method's search cost. When combined, the table matching algorithm and PDF document indexing yielded 9% higher MAP than the tokenized method, operating at 50% of the original cost.

This research looks at multi-stage games where some players have imperfect information about the process's progression. We investigate the best strategy for these players to use publicly available information to narrow down the possible states of the game. Different levels of knowledge about the game's progression affect the potential to learn new information and the ability to make the most of it. We examine three specific game scenarios, involving incomplete information about the process's sequence, the probability of its phases, and the distribution of its probabilities. We identify three distinct patterns, or "groupings," that emerge based on the available information. These patterns determine the potential to update knowledge based on new information, the ability to conclude the game based on new information, and the ability to make the most of new information in the game. We identify "groupings" for two specific game scenarios, showing how players with incomplete information can take advantage of the game's progression to make the most of new information. We show that concluding the game based on new information and making the most of new information are equivalent in the game scenarios we examined.

In developed nations, population density mapping employs various methods, such as increasing infrastructure to support growing populations. In developing countries like Mozambique, the inverse often occurs, as increasing access to high-tech solutions like autonomous survey methods. Our work focuses on the intersection of these trends. Despite the promise of autonomous population density mapping, this field remains largely unexplored, as most studies rely on simulated or theoretical approaches, as practical applications are few and distant. 

Autonomous population density estimation is a complex problem that requires a combination of automated survey planning and object detection. Our study utilizes a Mozambique population density dataset to evaluate the performance of different automated survey planning and object detection methods. Notably, this dataset is one of the few non-simulated examples available. 

Our research also explores the impact of various survey planning configurations on vehicle trajectory performance. Based on this analysis, we identify the most effective approach, which serves as a viable solution for future autonomous population assessment in the region. Our findings demonstrate that a simple object detection model, specifically Faster-RCNN with VGG-16, accurately identifies key objects along routes. However, more sophisticated models like RoI-10 and Faster-RCNN with ResNet-50 would enhance this model's performance for more complex scenarios. 

Our work lays the groundwork for a possible future autonomous population density mapping project. Although significant enhancements to the object detection model, as well as the integration of a right-of-way change detection system, are necessary for a production-ready system

Over the past decade, significant advancements have been made in probabilistic data structures, particularly in approximate match query filters. These developments led to innovative stream processing applications, yet introducing a fresh data structure that minimizes false positives could greatly enhance performance. We're therefore proposing the FPFC (False Positive Free Collection), a groundbreaking paradigm that utilizes an initial filter to eliminate false positives before processing a query, followed by a final determination with an alternative filter. By incorporating an FPCC-prepared data set into existing algorithms, we can substantially speed up and optimize their performance. We're presenting two distinct probabilistic FPCC methods, each using different initial filters (extending the AMI filter and a different approach incorporating random hash), and examining their efficiency benefits. Our experimental findings confirm the performance gains of these algorithms.

We've found a unique way to achieve spinor particle-molecule transitions from initial free-particle states through a laser-induced three-body recombination process. This method involves using three-pulse laser control to modify the interactions between particles and ultimately create molecules with combined spin states. Focusing on bosonic particles, our results reveal symmetric spinor molecules that can exhibit various spin orientations, even with identical spin states, and our approach provides a foundation for creating more complex spinor molecules with antiferromagnetic arrangements. Furthermore, our approach is extended to create spinor molecules of fermionic particles, and our findings for the SU(N) symmetric system show that combining identical spin states results in maximally entangled molecules, and this principle applies to any value of N.

The the fundamental nature of multi-phase fluid-structure interaction problems drives significant interest in both engineering and scientific fields, with a range of complex phenomena occurring where fluid and rigid bodies interact in the presence of turbulence, surface tension, and heat transfer effects. In addressing these phenomena, purely numerical methods are developed, extending a quasi-conservative SPH method to accurately represent the multi-scale behavior of multi-phase flows and solid bodies in contact with these flows. A novel multi-scale approach is introduced, with the extension of a quasi-conservative SPH method to accurately capture the multi-scale behavior of multi-phase flows and rigid bodies. The method's local and quasi-conservative properties are rigorously analyzed using fundamental identities. The method's accuracy and quasi-conservative property are validated through multiple numerical experiments, including the simulation of rolling motions of spherical bodies across a range of spatially and temporally varying viscosities, in addition to more complex problems such as the simulation of water boiling and heat transfer between water and a heated surface, with an advanced heat transport model. The method successfully captures the multi-scale behavior of multi-phase flows and rigid bodies in the presence of turbulence, surface tension, and heat transfer effects, with a method's accuracy and quasi-conservative properties validated through rigorous analysis and rigorous numerical experiments.

Despite significant advancements in machine learning algorithms, the potential benefits of implementing these algorithms on quantum computers remains largely unknown. Here, a quantum machine learning method utilizing a superconducting processor is presented to tackle the task of binary classification. First, the method's monitored operation mode is explored by simulating parameter-dependent evolution and measurement processes using a quantum circuit. These findings reveal that the processor's intrinsic errors can expedite learning. Furthermore, the implementation of a monitored Grokotov variable-yield algorithm on the processor is successfully demonstrated, achieving a convergence rate of 0.032 within 400 iterations. Notably, the method's scalability is theoretically limited by coherence time and qubit mapping constraints. To establish the practical effectiveness of the method, an unmonitored operation mode was also developed, enabling the application of quantum machine learning on a superconducting processor despite the absence of readout qubits. A quantum-deterministic algorithm was employed to approximate a decision boundary in a two-dimensional dataset. Although the absence of monitoring introduces an additional layer of complexity, the findings suggest that the method could achieve a coherence matrix-based convergence rate of 0.025, albeit with considerable computational and storage expenses. These experiments have shed light on the potential advantages of quantum machine learning on near-term superconducting processors, particularly in scenarios where the number of available samples is relatively small.

TTS models are now being trained on significantly larger datasets than before. This shift towards larger datasets needs to be met with an equally increased capacity for models to be efficiently managed within data infrastructure. Our proposed method achieves this by introducing a novel feature that reduces the memory usage of speech models without affecting their speech output quality. Our experiments show that this novel feature can be incorporated into the FastPitch model with negligible degradation in speech quality and our results confirm this.

This study targets spatiotemporal modeling, where we design a multi-hop
inference network, named Hopper, to learn varied motion patterns at different
scales. By applying Transformer on top of CNN features, we explore motion
patterns in both spatial and temporal dimensions, and then utilize self- and
cross-attention layers to consider the interdependence of different motion
scales. Additionally, we expand on the Transformer framework to include cross-
temporal attention, which aggregates information across the entire video
sequence and also incorporates a temporal decay mechanism to ignore distant
past or future. In contrast to existing approaches that focus on single-scale or
coarse-grained motion patterns, we demonstrate that Hopper can accurately learn
motion patterns at multiple scales, outperforming current state-of-the-art
models significantly on motion segmentation and tracking tasks.

This research project investigates the production of $W$ bosons in conjunction with a pair of $b\bar{b}$ quarks within the ATLAS experimental framework at the Large Hadron Collider, utilizing 36.1 fb^-1 of proton-proton collision data captured at 13 TeV. By pinpointing $W$ boson masses within this study, significant standard model constraints on $m_W$ are establisheD, alongside an examination of the impact from the $b\bar{b}$ associated processes. The investigation is split into observed signals from both dominant $t$-channel and minor $W$+$(b\bar{b})$ events, yielding a 3187.6 GeV mass measurement, marked by a 5.3 GeV uncertainty, thereby presenting a 0.8 GeV discrepancy with the predictions from the standard model. Furthermore, the study measures the differential distribution of the $W$ boson transverse momentum in both $W$+$(b\bar{b})$ events, validating theoretical predictions with considerable agreement. With respect to top-quark-related events, the study achieves a 13.1 GeV precision in the $m_W$ measurement, thus providing a competitive outcome when compared to other recent findings. Notably, the study empirically determines the $W$ boson mass transfer from $b\bar{b}$ events and explores the associated experimental uncertainties. The investigation also scrutinizes the events

Telepresence robots are gaining popularity as a cost-effective solution for remote access,
enabling users to interact with locations and people through mobile robotic platforms.
These robots have practical applications in various settings, such as businesses and educational institutions,
which can benefit from deploying these systems to improve connections with remote staff or instructors.
To assess the user experience of navigating telepresence robots, we conducted an experiment
focusing on the impact of wireless network disturbances on QoE for robot control. Three different
quality levels of TCP/IP connections were established, including a high level using Ethernet,
a mid-level with 802.11ac Wi-Fi, and a low level with 802.11b Wi-Fi. Our study revealed a 73.42% higher
loss ratio and a 69.47% higher packet delay for robots using 802.11b Wi-Fi compared to the other two methods.
Through a survey of 21 participants evaluating the video quality and the ease of controlling the robot,
we found that users would only tolerate minor errors in navigation, and any significant delays would
result in a decrease of up to 23.08 on a scale of 30. 

To simulate the real-world experience of using telepresence robots, we created an interactive environment
that mimics the performance of telepresence robots over various networks. Our results provide an accurate
representation of the effects on QoE when using robots with high latency and loss, and the user experience
is most sensitive to latency during tasks

Time series forecasting using Bayesian techniques often involves intricate models that demand significant mathematical and computational knowledge. This paper presents an approach to forecasting using hierarchical Bayesian linear forecasting models, an earlier method being outlined in a 2019 study. The primary objective of this paper is to provide a straightforward overview of the model's implementation, focusing on the Bayesian estimation process, uncertainty quantification, and forecasting procedures. Additionally, it showcases the model's application in predicting homogenous time series across various fields, including its use in predicting COVID-19 cases, predicting stock prices across different industries, forecasting temperatures in cities, and predicting usage patterns for different types of data.

Mafia is a popular party game where players are assigned roles with distinct abilities, some of which remain unknown to the other players. The role of a Mafia member allows them to secretly announce their action, and if detected, they can be eliminated by other players. A detailed numerical model of the game was established to investigate its progression over time, and specifically, the probability that a Mafia member is eliminated. The model revealed an interesting correlation between the role distribution and the average duration of the game. The model assumed that players can accurately detect Mafias and accurately eliminate them, and future research could expand on this assumption.

We used a computer program to study how gas accumulates on two giant planets at the same time. In this simulation, the planets start with a mass and a size, and gas accumulation is driven by a phenomenon called gravitational instability. We found that the interactive nature of the planets' orbits affects how and when they accumulate gas. For a certain starting mass and size, the simulation showed that the planets exchange gas leads to a final total mass within a specific range, and this mass range increases with the size of the disk. In most cases, the planets' gas accumulation leads to a final total mass within the 0.5-1.9 mass range per unit solar mass, and this final total mass matches estimates based on the planets' sizes and outer limits of the disk. We also found that the planets' gas accumulation leads to a final total mass increase as the disk gets bigger, and this final total mass matches estimates based on the planets' sizes and outer limits of the disk. For a given disk thickness, the planets' gas accumulation leads to changes in the disk's gas density, and this final total mass increases as the disk gets thicker. Therefore, the duo of planets' gas accumulation leads to a final total mass increase as the disk gets bigger, and this final total mass matches estimates based on the planets' sizes and outer limits of the disk.

Theoretical foundations of conductivity in nanoscale systems imply the transfer of charge through either individual molecules or collective modes, like plasmons or phonons, capable of transporting energy across isolated tubes. However, distinguishing between these mechanisms is challenging, and further research is needed to clarify the role of intertube effects. To investigate this question, our study focuses on the electrical conductivity of a nearly single-crystalline armchair carbon nanotube film, discovering that the conductivity exhibits a clear semimetallic behavior characterized by a minimal energy gap. Notably, comparable conductivity values observed across two films suggest that the observed conductivity is a inherent property of the system and not the result of contamination. By combining conductivity measurements with theoretical modeling of intertube coupling, our research reveals that the observed conductivity is too high for it to be explained by three-dimensional damping models but can be accurately explained by a model that incorporates both intertube coupling and phonon-mediated effects. Our study provides the first direct evidence of phonon-assisted conductivity in nanoscale systems, and the observed effects demonstrate the significance of designing experiments that minimize tube aggregation, which is necessary to fully understand the role of intertube phonon modes in conductivity.

This research develops a novel entropy-driven variable feature weighted fuzzy k-means approach to tackle high-dimensional data clustering challenges where variables hold distinct importance. Utilizing a multi-objective fuzzy k-means algorithm with variable-weighting capabilities, this method enables fuzzy clustering boundaries and variable feature weights to be concurrently determined. A redefined entropy measure is employed to estimate cluster compactness and assess the effectiveness of fuzzy boundaries and variable feature weights in each iteration. Two redefined variables are also introduced: fuzzy membership entropy for handling noisy data and variable feature weight entropy for identifying significant variables in cluster analysis. These entities are utilized in a subsequent optimization process to refine fuzzy clustering and variable feature weights. Through comprehensive comparisons with four competitor methods, the proposed approach demonstrates solid clustering and variable selection abilities in numerical case studies and real-world applications, specifically in microarray gene expression data and credit risk evaluation problems.

The Mixture-of-Experts model has seen significant advancements in recent years but the process of learning its weighted mixture components is still a complex task. This study presents two new algorithms to overcome this challenge, leveraging an iterative approach on either the expert parameters or the gating network weights. Our proposed solutions are backed by theoretical guarantees, exhibiting faster convergence rates and more efficient properties on average. These algorithms outperformed other methods in experiments conducted on artificially designed linear and nonlinear problems as well as real-world image classification tasks, consistently producing accurate results.

This research paper explores an enhanced version of the 'game of games' approach for computing birational transformations of abelian varieties, by framing the challenge as a combined effort between two players: (1) finding a point on a target Jacobian, and (2) applying a transformation from the source Jacobian to the target, with both steps involving discrete'moves'. We will show that the 'game' in the context of Jacobians can be reinterpreted as an equivalent problem on a related space, the Prym variety, constructed from isogenous elliptic curves. A key finding is the existence of a special'splitting' corresponding to the identity, with applications to understanding the properties of the Prym variety and finding 'isogeny classes' in a geometric sense.

Symmetry disruption in quantum gravity at a quantum level implies the presence of topological defects, where energy release is exactly balanced to disrupt the underlying gravitational field's structure. The gravitational field's disruption cost is associated with the Graviton Condensate's (GC) zero-energy mode, thereby restricting the energy release criterion to electroweak scale forces for case A symmetry disruption and gravity forces for case B. Data on Cosmic Birefringence observations severely limits options for symmetry disruption, strongly favouring scenario B. This study is a more expanded version of the work presented at the 11th Symposium on Symmetry versus Symmetry, in which it was the opening talk.

Our research presents new findings based on ultraviolet (UV) imaging of the globular cluster NGC 4147, obtained with three specific filters from the UVIT instrument. The field of view covered by these observations included 45% of the cluster's area. By analyzing variability, we identified 47 stars and established a reliable cluster photometric dataset. By combining these findings with optical magnitudes from the Gaia survey, we constructed a reliable cluster photometric dataset, which allowed us to determine the cluster's distance and age. The results of multiple analyses indicate a distance of 24.79 kpc and ages between 7.53 and 7.63 billion years. The frequency of blue stragglers in the cluster was also found to be 9.6%. The characteristics of NGC 4147's horizontal branch were found to be consistent with a specific secondary geometry. The properties of the UV-bright stars in the cluster were also discovered and indicated the presence of both blue stragglers and post-He-flash stars. The cluster's white dwarf population exhibited a metal-rich characteristic, which contrasts with the metal-poor trait commonly observed in post-He-flash stars. The presence of He-rich stars in the cluster was confirmed through spatial and frequency analysis. The characteristics of NGC 4147's He-rich stars indicate a higher luminosity level, which suggests that these stars are likely members of a specific He-rich sub-group.
