We explore an area of study referred to as the fragile b-principle, encompassing methodologies that leverage a given function with certain characteristics that can be expressed as a product of quantities with comparable effects. The fragile b-principle, adapted from the more established prismatic cohomology, serves as an innovative framework that allows researchers to identify homological constraints or simplify problems by decomposing them into more tractable components. The methods employed here demonstrate that specified functional inequalities can be recast as homological issues or simplified into more manageable parts. Our work uses methods inspired by the prismatic geometry of Brian Conrad, along with applications of the model theory and fake news theory as introduced by Aug Kuang, to achieve these results. The paper's central contribution is the formulation of the Mumford Conjecture in this novel framework and provides three case studies illustrating the applications of the b-principle to problems related to the moduli space of curves, Borel-efﬁcient curves, and semi-abelian varieties. We also prove a novel inequality for the Hilbert scheme of a curve, along with its equivalent form as a homological vanishing problem, providing another example of the principle's power.

This paper undertakes a thorough examination of the transfer learning, identifying two fundamental guarantees, or agreements, that are thought to contribute to its success. The first agreement concerns the relationship between a model's training and its corresponding loss function, with the latter being seen as a measure of the distance between the model and its target. The second agreement, on the other hand, pertains to how a model's training data influence its evaluation metrics.

We argue that these two agreements are flawed. The implications of our conclusions are that many deep learning models that claim to demonstrate transfer learning abilities may be unsound. In addition, we offer some possible explanations for the apparent success of transfer learning in certain cases, and suggest that this success might be the result of the characteristics of GANs and GAs evaluations, which often involve evaluating generative models against ground truth data.

The spread of information within a network is influenced by its structural layout. Specifically, networks featuring diverse clusters of interconnected nodes facilitate faster information dissemination compared to randomly arranged systems. This pivotal finding is rooted in the interconnected nature of information pathways, which tends to amplify their collective speed. This phenomenon bears resemblance to the unified forward algorithm's enhanced convergence properties on segregated network structures. Notably, this effect can be quantitatively measured by calculating the characteristic path length, which diminishes in proportion to the network's modularity. Moreover, this reduction is characterized by a universal exponent valued at 1. As modularity increases, the dissemination speed of information reaches a maximum finite magnitude when a certain topological arrangement is achieved, an arrangement that is unlikely to be reached in systems characterized by spherical or lattice arrangements. Even in networks optimized for information transfer, further gains in dissemination speed can be garnered by increasing their modularity level. This crucial outcome stresses the critical role of modularity in governing the dissemination speed of information.

We establish a novel quantitative measure of distinctiveness for closed, gaussian-free J-holomorphic curves using the free energy of the Gromov-Witten theory, specifically focusing on the mixed case combining type A and type B tree vertices. The strategy involves manipulating the recent partial index formula introduced by Pandharipande-Thomas, incorporating an adjusted version of the Yau-Zaslow invariant to address the type B factor, which requires incorporating 'band projections' from Gabbert-Tsai's update to the Gromov-Witten theory of K3 surfaces.

The accuracy of the time-domain standard perturbation model for unamplified signals is tested using discrete-time simulations. An unamplified transmission line is modelled as a complex impedance, connected to a source of finite bandwidth. The model under test represents the source as a sinusoidal voltage, ranked against a true unitary sinusoidal voltage from spice models. An arbitrary disturbance current of ranked amplitude is introduced on one side of the transmission line, and signal degradation is calculated in terms of frequency. This degradation is then compared to established benchmarks. Our simulations show that standard perturbation models fall short in high-frequency scenarios, where signal degradation tends to overestimate actual values by two orders of magnitude or more. Furthermore, model inaccuracy leads to uneven degradation across various frequencies, indicating a need for better time-domain models, especially for high-frequency unamplified signals, and for better interpretation of standard perturbation models, especially for high-frequency scenarios, and for better interpretation of standard perturbation values.

The modern Android operating system's open nature and vast user base have turned it into a prime target for malicious users. These users employ evasive tactics to circumvent detection by security systems, which are defined as subversive actions aimed at disablement or data extraction. This study provides an overview of evasion assaults on Android, focusing on the characteristics of these assaults, the areas of the Android system affected by them, and the countermeasures adopted by Android to combat such assaults. Additionally, it describes the methodologies used by attackers to bypass Android's security features and the outcomes of previous studies on evasion assaults on Android.

A reliable and flexible tool for managing computational workflows is necessary for producing consistent results across various domains. We introduce Ozy, a novel workflow system, to fill this necessity. Designed with simplicity and portability in mind, Ozy enables seamless execution of complex computational tasks in diverse environments. Its core functionality is comprised of three primary modules: a configuration model, a scheduler, and a driver. This triad enables Ozy to efficiently manage the execution of both parallel and sequential tasks within local, high-performance computing, and cloud infrastructure. Additionally, Ozy features an array of third-party plugins that integrate leading visualization, data I/O, and analytics tools, making it an ideal choice for an diverse range of scientific applications.

Research focuses on an unconventional phase of matter, appearing as a reentrant portion of the 5/2 quantum Hall stage, by investigating the effect of Landau-level mixing on its ground state. Employing a combination of experimental and numerical methods, we find that this reentrant phase exhibits symptoms usually associated with non-Abelian topological phases, while its electronic properties can be explained using a simple theoretical framework based on conventional liquid theories. We suggest that this unusual ground state arises from a distinct configuration of energy levels and jumps between mixed states. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that strong interactions among energy levels can result in a rare natural occurrence of reentrant phases in systems with fractional quantum Hall ground states.

Our research demonstrates that cosmic black holes cannot be defined by the Thakurta metric parameterization. This discovery implies that all previous studies employing the Method I analysis to estimate the characteristic masses of primordial black holes from individual sources are invalid, as they hinged on incorrect assumptions. Furthermore, since the LIGO-Virgo Collaboration's current dataset has failed to uncover any primordial black holes characterized by the Thakurta parameterization, our findings dictate that the existing upper bounds on the PBH abundance should remain unaltered.

Forming a planet through pebble accumulation around a developing star relies on a complex process influenced by various factors like the movement of matter and the conditions set by planetary formation models. Pebbles, which consist of dust and small particles, accumulate around a protoplanetary disk's outer regions where temperatures are relatively mild. A numerical study of this process has been conducted, taking into account the dynamic interaction between matter and varying density fluctuations within the disk. It was found that the conditions set by planetary formation models significantly affect the movement of matter and, consequently, the conditions within the disk. This in turn affect the movement of pebbles. In areas of the disk where the density is at its lowest, a small number of pebbles accumulate to form the inner planets, while in areas of the disk where the density is at its highest, a larger number of pebbles accumulate to form the outer planets. This study found that the conditions set by planetary formation models enable pebbles to move long distances and for multiple planetary bodies to form simultaneously. A simplified mathematical model of this process has also been developed, which yields similar results as the full model and predicts that the more dense an area is, the more massive and farther away from the star the resulting planetary body will be. This study found that the conditions set by planetary formation models enable pebbles to move long distances and for multiple planetary bodies to form simultaneously.

The study of overparameterized models, specifically linear regression with complex predictors, has shown that their excessive capacity might not be the sole reason for their ability to perfectly fit random data within a finite computational framework. This paper considers scenarios with predictors whose dimensions exceed the data samples, similar to previous research. However, it diverges from existing studies by taking into account the time limit for computation and the random model paradigm, which leads to findings indicating that overparameterization is insufficient on its own to ensure fitting random data without smoothness assumptions. This contrast highlights the significance of assuming access to an infinite amount of computational power when analyzing the behavior of machine learning models.

We prove that every Bohr structure, located within an externally divisible group which is countable and generated by $p$-elements, can be embedded within a unique group, which is also countable and generated by $p$-elements. This result extends earlier work, which included the additional constraint of independence in Bohr structure. Additionally, we identify the minimum number of generators required for such a group, which we find to be $\lceil p/2 \rceil$.

We address a Metropolitan Dial-a-Ride issue, where customers must be visited by a fleet of vehicles with minimal retracing of routes possible. To resolve this, a new Branch-and-Bound algorithm is proposed on a purpose-designed network in Paris. Furthermore, a novel bound on the optimal solution cost is provided, based on solutions to reduced versions of the problem, along with an analysis of the algorithm's performance across different scenarios in terms of the number of customers and vehicles.

The proliferation of e-commerce platforms from consumers to enterprise-level businesses necessitates advanced search systems that incorporate both content and user behavior. Although neural models have effectively tackled the content-based search challenge, solving image and video-based searches requires sophisticated multi-modal solutions capable of extracting relevant information quickly, especially considering the massive datasets and devices limitations. To address this, we've devised a novel multi-modal transformer design that extracts insight from these modalities, and we've optimized it for edge computing deployments via token mixing. Furthermore, we've tailored our pretraining strategy to mimic a content-based search query's iterative process, and we've optimized it to minimize memory usage through a curriculum approach. By combining these contributions, our approach outperforms the current state-of-the-art in multi-modal training on various e-commerce datasets.

A parallel training approach known as Deep InfoMax (DIM) is used to create a
representation of data that is useful for a specific task. In this study, we
apply a variant of the DIM algorithm to the medical field, specifically for
diagnosing Alzheimer's based on functional MRI data. Our innovation lies in
the incorporation of a memory module in the encoder, as well as the addition of
a classifier that produces unlabeled samples' predicted labels. We can train
the DIM model without ground truth labels for the specific task, utilizing only
unlabeled samples. The obtained feature representations are then utilized for
alzheimer's illness progression forecasting. We also present the initial results of
this model on the Alzheimer's Disease corpus.

This study proposes a novel recurrent neural network architecture that captures the intricate meaning of written text during sentence processing. It's long been acknowledged that sentence understanding draws upon previously processed words' meanings, as well as contextually arising relationships. Our interactive RNN design effectively harnesses the interplay between words' initial meanings and contextually generated synergies during the comprehension process. From the outset, this model recognizes that sentences are comprised of individual words whose collective understanding evolves through interactions. It integrates the RNN's internal state not only with words' initial meanings but also with contextually produced synergy, thereby providing a text's semantic representation. Our experimental outcomes reveal that the proposed model excels in single-document and wallstreet journal full-reports sentiment classification tasks. Moreover, by dissecting the interaction sequence, our analysis uncovers the sequence of synergies produced within the text, thereby shedding light on the sequence of contextual combinations forming the text's semantic representation.

Our analysis reveals that the spin-orbit interaction within a two-dimensional
electron gas can be augmented when part of the electron gas occupies a
dopant-induced subband. This amplification results from the reduced
quantum-capacity for electrons in the primary subband and is independent of
alignment with high-symmetry axes. Furthermore, the effect exhibits a
sign-dependent relationship with the alignment. The investigation utilizes
both variational calculations and perturbation theory, and we outline both
methodologies in detail. The significance of our findings lies in their potential
impact on technology using spin-polarized charges and high-speed currents.

A new approach for generating gravity-like shadows in the context of dark matter is presented. Specifically, we apply a specific transformation, the Weyl transformation, to the gravitational sector of a theory while leaving other parts of the theory unchanged with a different transformation, thus enabling the formation of a shadow effect for the gravity sector after the super- and sub-Jordan frames are established. This concept is illustrated using a simple scalar field theory. Furthermore, we explore potential issues with particle collisions within the framework of the Modified Gravity theory of Conformal Dark Matter. Crucially, we demonstrate that some matter properties are unaffected by the transformation, such as kinetic energy, while others like potential energy are affected, thus raising questions about the outcomes of particle collisions in the non-relativistic limit.

To evaluate the effectiveness of AI healthcare agents, who manage healthcare workflows using intelligent algorithms, we developed an unique testing protocol that assesses their impact on medical image analysis. This measurement tool adapted an existing testing framework, specifically the Wildtrack COVID-19 project, known for its robust pandemic-related imaging data and comprehensive annotation of diagnostic results. This large-scale dataset allowed us to examine the performance of AI agents before and after a significant shift in healthcare resources, brought on by the COVID-19 pandemic, who were initially trained on data from 2020 and tested using conformal forecasting. It was discovered that the model's performance was compromised in a significant number of testing categories by up to 15 to 20 percent, with an observed underestimation of the model's performance. Furthermore, the model's reliability in managing healthcare workflows during this period showed a margin of error ranging from 3 to 7 percent, with external assessments revealing negligible discrepancies from independent and independent sources. This study was conducted with the approval of ethical review boards at NYU Langone and the University at Buffalo, with all related clinical research being duly authorized via IRB2022-024.

Currently used methods to model nucleic acid structures have significant shortcomings, as they lack high-resolution structures that match those obtained through crystallography, leading to considerable deviations in geometry. Our approach, an enhanced method to train atomic potential for nucleic acid simulation (EPONAS), successfully improves geometry representations by training the potential on high-resolution crystal structures. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of EPONAS, as it results in significant improvements in structure predictions and biasing using simulations of double-stranded DNA and DNA-protein complexes. Furthermore, EPONAS improves the distribution of key geometric attributes in unbiased metrics, enabling more accurate predictions. Our study also compares EPONAS against a competing enhanced sampling method, revealing that EPONAS outperforms as it yields better matches with target distributions.

In the field of information theory, researchers study how to represent a set of values using the fewest number of bits, often achieving this with perfect entropy encoding that assigns an expected value with a fixed number of bits. For example, the classic Shannon-Fano code does this by splitting intervals with high entropy, effectively distributing probabilities, with the optimal method being the variable-length Huffman code. Researchers later discovered that this last method can sometimes be improved by taking into account how accurately the experiment's results vary - a concept known as the Anscombe's variable-length Huffman code, which assigns different lengths to better capture the distribution's statistical fluctuations. However, this last method was found to be only beneficial in specific, extremely unusual situations - essentially, it was shown to be little more than the standard Huffman code in virtually all cases, with only minute potential improvements in more typical scenarios. This research now reveals even stronger results, demonstrating even more aggressively that these improved encodings are essentially equivalent to one another, with the result even more compelling due to its being a finite, discrete case analysis - as a result, it was found that these improved encodings are essentially equivalent, with the result especially significant because of the general difficulty in understanding this topic as being a part of a broader, abstract mathematical theory space, which is typically challenging to settle.

The dielectric properties of cement pastes and other building materials develop over time as they undergo hydration, which forms complex geo-engineered systems. Pore fluids in these systems play a crucial role in the overall dielectric behavior, as it's the fluid that conducts signals during electrochemical tests and has a significant impact on the overall performance of these systems. Previous studies have focused primarily on the dielectric response of solid cement phases, neglecting the role of the pore fluid, which is a limiting factor in our understanding of these systems. To gain a deeper understanding, it's essential to study and characterize the pore fluid, which is a challenging task due to its constant evolution during hydration. This study employs advanced techniques, including attenuated total reflection infrared spectroscopy and nuclear magnetic resonance, to identify and quantify the components of cement paste pores, as well as simulate the dielectric properties of these systems using a mixture model. This research demonstrates that, as cement paste matures, the pore fluid evolves into a highly alkaline solution, which is composed of water, minerals, and other substances. This study also provides a framework for evaluating and analyzing pore fluid and using various techniques to identify and qualify the pore fluid, as well as its implications for the dielectric properties of cement pastes and other geo-engineered systems.

This article provides an in-depth examination of the data on massive-massive hadronic compounds, focusing on the spectral information available from fixed-target experiments, particularly those involving physics beyond the Standard Model. It covers a range of topics, including the characteristics of the K* axials, a pair of spin-3/2 K* mesons, and other hadronic compounds, analyzing their spectral information and properties to identify potential issues and areas for further research.

My research delves into the progression of military drone swarms driven by
natural language processing, as a preliminary step to assessing their
effectiveness. Since both civilian and military sectors utilize natural
language for operational purposes, my analysis covers various applications
of NLP in drone swarm development. Essential military operations that could
benefit from drone swarms are also highlighted, including search operations
and tactical engagements. Several military drone swarm systems are briefly
examined, showcasing their diverse structures and capabilities. Given the
current limited impact of NLP, my research emphasizes its growing influence
on military operations. NLP has the potential to greatly enhance drone swarm
efficiency in future military operations, and ongoing developments indicate
significant advancements in this field.

The characteristics of the neutral hydrogen signal within the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest, as observed in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, exhibit a well-defined pattern of correlations that adequately represents the fluctuations in the large-scale structure of the universe, albeit with some minor discrepancies. By examining the distances between these correlated signals, the researchers identified a nonlinear relationship between distance and correlation function values, thereby allowing them to establish a lower bound on the universe's dark matter density and making a preliminary prediction regarding the universe's current expansion rate. These findings support the established value of the universe's dark matter density and are consistent with subsequent measurements from other methods.

A novel emittance exchange chamber designed for short-range applications has been successfully fabricated and installed at the Fermilab A0 Test Beam Facility, allowing for simultaneous testing. The experimental outcome demonstrated a reliable transfer of beam properties, with estimated errors of less than 5%. A model was developed to describe the intended emittance exchange process, with the aim of optimizing design for enhanced emittance reduction in future designs. 

These findings align with the proposed application of the emittance exchange technique in the Fermilab Intensity Frontier, specifically in the Drell-Yan Experiment. This experiment requires a high-energy, low-emittance beam, but due to the linear accelerator missing the critical 60-meV radiofrequency component, a new linac must be equipped with the emittance exchange component to achieve the necessary low-emittance level without upgrading the existing machine.

Our proposed approach for automatic driving and autonomous navigation involves forecasting future vehicle trajectories based on the vehicle's past behavior and the actions of surrounding vehicles. The social behavior of vehicles often deviates from the predictions made by traditional traffic models, which we consider as 'irregular social behavior'. Ignoring these patterns can lead to a high likelihood of collisions - as evidenced by the fact that conventional forecasting methods that rely on historical data still cause accidents in high-precision simulation environments. To address this issue, our research develops a new forecasting method that adapts to the vehicle's social behavior over time, allowing it of account for both regular and irregular social patterns. The proposed method utilizes a VAE-based sequential encoder-decoder structure, enables the consideration of past events and their duration of influence, and incorporates a fully connected network that re-evaluates the importance of past events in real-time. By doing so, it allows the model to accurately forecast the vehicle's future trajectory by taking into account its current speed and acceleration, as well as the proximity and movement of surrounding vehicles with our novel approach. Thoroughly tested on the Waymo Trajectory Forecasting Benchmarks, the proposed method demonstrates its effectiveness by interacting with different types of social behavior in the data and demonstrates its generalizability to various vehicle trajectories. Furthermore, it also wins first place in the Waymo Trajectory Forecasting Benchmarks, outperforming other methods. All our code is available on our GitHub repository.

We conduct an in-depth examination of three comparable information-theoretic measures of a statistical system's complexity, which are represented by relative entropy, conditional entropy, and the information-theoretic depth of a distribution. These measures have unique characteristics, with the information-theoretic depth being particularly resilient to perturbations. We investigate the relationships between these measures and their behavior over time in a simplified model, the Boltzmann network, which undergoes gradual thermodynamic flux. This enables us to identify a system's steady-state complexity, establish its temporal progression towards this state, and assess its dependence on system size. Furthermore, we evaluate the performance of an estimator for the information-theoretic depth from observed samples, which exhibits desirable properties such as bias reduction and variance reduction as the sampling size increases. This work's findings contribute to an understanding of the similarities and differences between information-theoretic measures of complexity and their practical applications in sampling-based estimation of complexity.

Swarm robotics research continues to address the challenge of effectively engaging with humans. A crucial factor in successful human-swarm interaction (HSI) is the ability of swarms to safely and efficiently obtain instructions from a leader or bystanders, particularly through non-verbal communication methods. This study presents a novel, decentralized technique for swarm robots to recognize basic hand gestures made by humans within a set of predefined signals. The primary aim of this research is to investigate the feasibility of swarm robotics interactions that are safe, efficient, and effortless for humans, and also explores the benefits of leveraging human signals to coordinate swarms.

This study aims to enhance the accuracy of a novel information system (GIS) that classifies blood cells into four types: white blood cells, red blood cells, platelets, and neutrophils. The proposed project was granted funding from the ITI Program, which required that the GIS use deep neural networks. Our project initially achieved high accuracy rates with a single neural network, but a more advanced method was developed by combining three neural networks into a single system, each trained on unique blood cell images. Our merged strategy combines an ensemble of neural networks in a single model, aiming to increase the accuracy of the GIS. The preliminary test results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method, which surpasses the original deep neural models, ultimately enabling the development of a more reliable GIS.

In quantum computing and quantum simulation, it's crucial to accurately prepare states' initial configurations. However, this task is often problematic, as small errors during state transitions can make the proposal deviate greatly from its intended target state. To address this challenge, our study introduces a novel method called variational counterdiabatic evolution (VCE), by incorporating counterdiabatic potentials (CDPs) into an existing variational quantum evolution algorithm (VQE). Essentially, VCE accelerates the algorithm's convergence and refines the CDPs simultaneously. We've successfully demonstrated VCE's effectiveness in ground-state preparation for the two-dimensional Hubbard model by achieving a zero-energy final state within only five dynamics periods. Not only that, but our VCE approach also offers valuable insights into the optimal forms of Hamiltonians and their corresponding CD forms, especially when dealing with interacting models.

A novel approach utilizing hue temperature-based decoloration has been proposed for high-velocity flow fields. By employing decoloration techniques along with a temperature-based hue transformation, the resulting isothermal structures exhibit the same overall shape as the initial initial field but with varying color schemes. Both theoretical and experimental findings indicate that these isothermal shapes maintain their structural integrity across a range of colors. This methodology has significant implications for the visualization of fluid dynamics and signal processing, particularly in the mapping of tint colors. Consequently, this framework has the potential to facilitate a deeper understanding of physical phenomena at different temporal and spatial resolutions.

One-dimensional complex functions can be characterized by their Taylor series up to infinity. A modified approach called the exponential Taylor Expansion (ETE) yields equivalent representations of the Taylor series using an indicator of convergence. ETE enables the to switch from one type of expansion to another for functions that can be smoothly transformed. This is exemplified by the ETE of $e^{\left(v+\frac{f(z)}{z}\right)}$ and its application in determining the residue of $e^{\left(v+\frac{f(z)}{z}\right)}$ as $z$ approaches zero within a specified indicator of convergence. A indicator of convergence is essentially a mathematical device that facilitates this process.

We establish a key connection between completely singular harmonic metrics on a certain type of non-positively curved surface and the process of uniformization by a metric of constant curvature. Specifically, if a surface has a certain type of singularity associated to its metric, we show that it can be equipped with a related harmonic metric with specific properties, thereby proving that it can be uniformlyized. As a direct result, we demonstrate a certain generalization of the well-known Hecke's theorem. Furthermore, our work has implications for the existence of fundamental domains under the action of certain groups of transformations.

A pioneering research facility, dubbed the Karsten Thomsen Laboratory, is being established at SLAC National Laboratory, dedicated to developing a source of ultrahigh-energy photons using laser-plasma interaction technology. This cutting-edge lab, built with flexible research and industrial applications in mind, will enable scientists to explore complex high-energy phenomena in fields such as astrophysics, cosmology, and the study of fundamental subatomic particles. A cutting-edge diagnostic tool, based on a 6-meter long, vacuum-sealed transport beamline, is being constructed to analyze the interaction between plasma and laser light. This state-of-the-art facility, featuring a tunable laser capable of reaching pulsed powers of $300$, then $600$ gigawatts, will deliver precise energy to a highly accurate target plasma within a highly stable experimental setting.

In the two Higgs doublet model with a type-I or II interaction structure, standard model particle masses are independent of a specific parameter, $m_{12}$. However, experimental data show that values of $m_{12}$ must be very small. The given work aims to identify the precise limits of allowable $m_{12}$ values by analyzing the consequences of a non-zero $m_{12}$ on precision electroweak measurements, specifically through two-sided confidence intervals for the parameter $\hat m_{12} = m_{12}/\sin^2\varphi_w$. Additionally, it examines the sensitivity to this parameter in various observables that participate in electroweak precision measurements. The study considers a scenario where new physics beyond the standard model manifests at the TeV scale, with constraints similar to those of the parameter $m_{12}$ in the two Higgs doublet model.

This research explores the conversion of relational data into RDF datasets utilizing a key-driven approach, fully integrating triples and quads, including CCIs. We leverage Shape Expression (SHPE) frameworks to define data constraints and cater to novice users who aren't familiar with relational data formatting. Our approach prioritizes user ease by separating the process into two main tasks: first, creating RDF schema (RDFs) based on relational schema, and second, generating RDF data instances by matching given data with established schemas. To showcase our method's effectiveness, we employ a hotel booking system as a practical example. Furthermore, through experimentation on various relational databases using SQL queries, we demonstrate our proposed technique's efficacy in mapping relational data to RDF datasets of varying scales. The outcomes of this study will likely influence researchers working on big data concepts such as data constraints, interoperability, integration, and compatibility, as well as SHPE and RDF datasets.

Measuring productivity allows an economy to assess how efficiently resources are utilized, which is critical for a country's competitive position and economic growth.  Productivity can be evaluated in two main approaches - microeconomic, focusing on specific industries, and macroeconomic, looking at the entire economy. A widely-used method for this assessment is a two-stage approach, first establishing a boundary of possible efficiency levels and then identifying the most efficient operators within that boundary. The first stage is called a free disposal hull (FDH) and the second is called a strong free disposal hull (SFDH). The SFDH can provide more precise results, but it heavily relies on a series of linear programming calculations, which can be quite complex and time-consuming, especially in the case of large datasets. Recent advancements in these methods, along with the development of new approaches like a dynamic free disposal hull and an improved version of SFDH, called strong free disposal hull with multiple outputs and multiple inputs (SFDMI), allow for more detailed analysis, but the need for additional computational resources remains. A new library, written in python, aims to perform these assessments in an efficient manner, by using pre-existing data to provide the most efficient solutions in an interactive and user-friendly way.

This research explores four LHC experiments: identifying the LHT model through Higgs decay to invisible particles, confirming New Physics influence on Higgs production and decay through cut analyses, determining the two-production cross-section, and analyzing Higgs coupling modifications via differential distributions in Higgs production and decay. By applying advanced cuts and studying differential characteristics, it is possible to identify the LHC's impact on the Higgs model. Simulations of 30 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ datasets from the LHC are used to evaluate various parameters. Moreover, it seems that combining experimental outcomes from multiple sources may help uncover New Physics.

In various tasks, pre-trained language models have demonstrated their ability to perform well without extensive fine-tuning, often relying on a limited number of examples. Contrary to the typical expectation that more data would lead to better model performance, we observed in our experiments that models may overfit when given a larger number of examples, ultimately achieving the same level of accuracy as with a smaller dataset. Notably, we found that the optimal model performance could be replicated by not monitoring their performance at all, as long as we ensure the models are given the right number of examples from the start. These findings were confirmed through thorough within-subject experiments across three domains, including multi-step reasoning, program construction, and writing different types of text. Based on our results, we speculate that the optimal performance we observed might be a sign that the models are accurately solving the problem, rather than simply memorizing previous answers. To explain this phenomenon, we propose a theoretical framework that views the models as accurately solving for optimal solutions within their parameter space, rather than memorizing.

Automated speech recognition has become a widely used tool across diverse domains, with many organizations offering proprietary speech engines, but these come with significant costs. To address this, this research investigates using two freely available speech recognition engines, ASR engine Mycroft and Eugene, paired with German dialects. The accuracy of these engines was evaluated in comparison to industry-standard speech recognition systems and against each other, with the results showing that Eugene significantly outperformed Mycroft and the industry-standard systems. The study further analyzes the accuracy of the engines across various scenarios and provides insight into improving the accuracy of the engines for future development.

Our investigation of Be-type stars within the 30 Doradus galaxy yields several key findings. By comparing spectral patterns, we established the galactic origin of four previously classified Be stars in the region. Furthermore, we identified seven additional Be-type stars, bringing the total count to eleven. These stars are notably both rotationally and luminosity-spread. Based on the derived values of $M_V$, we infer the physical boundaries of 30 Doradus to be $M_V \sim -4.7$. The distribution of projected rotation velocities in the sample appears to be either bipolar or elliptical in shape, with a possible maximum reaching around $300\,km\,s^{-1}$. Assuming a conservative maximum rotation velocity of $300\,km\,s^{-1}$, the resulting rotational splitting of the absorption lines suggests an average diameter of $6.6R_{\odot}$ for the Be-type stars. This implies an average angular rotation velocity of $c_{rot} \approx 220\,km\,s^{-1}\,kms^{-1}$, which is comparable to losses through two-body gravitational interactions at $c_{rot} \approx 250\,km\,s^{-1}\,kms^{-1}$. Gravitational loss through the evolution of "shell"-emitting stars could potentially induce the formation of narrower absorption lines.
