Inverse text standardization is a crucial step in text analysis, involving the conversion of input text into a uniform format. This process is commonly performed through tokenization, stop word removal, and morphological analysis. Yet, its effectiveness is hindered by the variety of text presentation across different platforms and vendors. We present a novel method of enhancing tokenization by leveraging datasets from various sources, including academic papers, books, and online datasets. By combining samples from different sources, our method effectively improves the accuracy of the text standardization process, outperforming existing methods by achieving a 2% higher F1-score on a dataset of 5,000 documents. Furthermore, using the TaF2A dataset, which includes 1 million sentences from academic papers, our method significantly surpasses the baseline by 3% in F1-score.

This paper demonstrates a Faber-Krahn type inequality for the first eigenvalue 
of the Hermite operator when bounded by Robin type conditions, showing that 
the optimal configuration remains a half-space, and resolves an open question.

This study introduces NFT-K, a non-exchangeable tangent space-based model that
can be trained on continuous datasets without using graphical representations.
Trained models using NFT-K can generate non-exchangeable, continuous tangent
spaces for any given input, enabling the construction of complex, hierarchical
structures. Tangent spaces derived from hierarchical data such as texts or
audio-recollected signals can be visualized to show connections between
contextual points after being labeled by an unsupervised process. NFT-K's
performance is demonstrated through classification and clustering tasks using
both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our research with NFT-K utilizes a flow
of unsupervised and supervised phases to develop complex, non-exchangeable
representations from raw, continuous data. NFT-K's source code is publicly
available on the GitHub platform.

Research on non-Hermitian topological phenomena is becoming increasingly prominent in the physics community due to their distinctive characteristics and promising applications in the realm of heat transport.
The theory of non-Hermitian point-gap topologies is relatively new and sophisticated, yet the influence of interparticle interactions within these systems has not been thoroughly studied.
In our research, we investigate how interactions affect a chain of bosons connected by a non-Hermitian lattice structure, specifically the extended Hubbard model on a one-dimensional complex lattice with nearest-neighbor interactions.
Using a combination of the density matrix renormalization group method and lattice formalism, we explored the thermodynamic properties and transmission coefficients of these systems.
Our results indicate that interactions diminish the extended non-Hermitian point-gap topology by suppressing the extended Z2 topological phase in the non-interacting system and introducing a finite but variable transfer rate.
The findings provide valuable insights into the extended non-Hermitian point-gap topology and serve as a starting point for investigating other related topological phenomena in related systems.

This study's primary goal is to examine speaker personality and its relationship to speech content. We sought to achieve this by gathering acoustically relevant personality traits from a crowd-sourced study and developing a training method to integrate these traits into a limited-liability speech generator. We based our analysis on the Big Five personality traits, specifically extraversion, agreeableness, and conscientiousness. Our research reveals that certain aspects of speaker personality are linked to specific speech characteristics, such as tone, pace, word choice, and sentence structure. We found that acoustically-expressed personality traits, such as speaking rate and sentence complexity, are characteristic of extraverted, agreeable, and conscientious individuals. Additionally, we discovered that certain traits, such as loudness and pause frequency, are distinctive of agreeable and conscientious speakers. While the results we obtained are intriguing, it's essential to note their limitations. The data we collected is subject to several constraints, and our analysis may be influenced by statistical biases. Nevertheless, the insights gained from this study provide a solid foundation for future research, potentially including the development of more sophisticated models to record speaker personality and incorporate this information into synthetic speech systems.

A fundamental approach incorporating a modular $A_4$ symmetry in the standard model with an extra $Z_2$ symmetry is presented, based entirely on high-energy expectations. In this framework, two types of charged fields are allowed, resulting in a rational value for the modular coupling of the right-handed neutrino, while its partner remains free of charges. As a consequence, the model predicts the existence of luminous dark matter, consisting of a nearly mass-degenerate state paired with the right-handed neutrino, which is accessible to experimental verification through its effects on the neutrino oscillation spectrum and the properties of charged lepton fluctuations.

In-depth studies of low-lying states in deformed nuclei, specifically in a triaxial shape, utilize a Hamiltonian derived from Gogny wave functions, where eigenstates are obtained through diagonalization. A collective degree of freedom is introduced via the Peierls map, enabling the investigation of triaxial nuclei across the valley of the total system's minimum. Results for nuclei such as $^{134}$Ba and $^{140}$Ce reveal intricate properties and demonstrate the substantial impact of configuration-mixing on triaxial collective states.

This paper introduces a novel class of Golay complementary structures, utilizing 4-phase, 8-phase, and 16-phase complementary arrays. These arrays are referred to as G4-CS, G8-CS, and G16-CS. The proposed structures are differential, circulant, and periodic in nature, with the ability to generalize any number of entries within any interval. The paper demonstrates several properties, showing the G4-CS, G8-CS, and G16-CS are pairwise, pairwise circular, and periodic complementary structures. Due to their unique properties, the G4-CS, G16-CS are differential Hadamard, circular Hadamard, and periodic Hadamard codes. Additionally, the paper presents constructions of pairwise, circular, and periodic codes from the G4-CS, G8-CS, and G16-CS. The paper also presents a method of constructing pairwise, circular, and periodic codes from the G4-CS, G8-CS, and G16-CS, with the latter offering the best results.

This research introduces an unsupervised method for detecting image alterations in hyperspectral images, which are images comprising a spectrum and color data. A novel deep convolutional autoencoder is proposed, capable of learning and representing both the hyperspectral and color aspects of an image simultaneously. A contrastive loss technique is integrated with the original reconstruction loss to emphasize similar features and suppress non-similar ones. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method performs as well as a supervised method, while operating at a significantly lower computational cost.

Our research focuses on understanding how entropy varies with temperature in molecular fluids and relating it to particle interactions. Typically, molecular dynamics simulations utilize Diatomic models that don't account for heat, yet molecules have internal energy even at absolute zero. This discrepancy motivates our project. Initially, we analyzed models with a fixed structure, then moved on to more intricate systems consisting of NPT ensembles with temperature and pressure adjustments. This allowed us to assess models with varying complexity, including those with simple, semi-empirical, and more realistic potential types. Our findings indicate that a relationship exists between thermal entropy and molecular dynamics viscosity, which is most pronounced in more realistic models with extended motion. These outcomes have significant implications, as they enable us to estimate thermal entropy using a narrower ensemble, which is crucial in thermodynamic studies of molecular fluids. Moreover, we discovered that a linear combination of higher derivatives from the reduced potential can be used to approximate a landmark expression for thermal entropy, which was first proposed by Born and von Karman. This approximation showed an average discrepancy of less than one percent for semi-classical models with extended motion.

A cosmological model is proposed where a universe filled with dark matter and dark energy alternates between periods of geometric expansion and contraction. It's suggested that cycles of the universe's expansion and contraction could be triggered by a mechanism of particle decay. The phase transition hypothesis implies that particles which were once dark but now emit light is not a viable option to explain the current state of the universe's acceleration. Observational constraints from the values of the cosmic density parameters and Hubble constant are used to test a new cosmological model which suggests that the cycles may be happening at the same rate. The model also predicts that the universe's expansion is expected to continue into the future, rather than reversing the current state. The model is named LambdaCDM cyclical cosmology.

The invariant-set concept has been proposed to address quantum nonlocality, which is a challenge to the causal order of events in reality. This study introduces a hidden-variable formulation of the invariant-set theory known as Invariant-set concealed variables (ICV). By analyzing the properties of the ICV model, it was found that this paradigm inherently possesses a global causal order, thus naturally resolving the nonlocality issue. Furthermore, the research demonstrated that the ICV model retains consistency with the statistical outcomes of the Bell, Collins, and Braunstein protocols. In addition, the study examined the distinct features of the ICV model, which distinctively differ from other theories such as local hidden variable theories, quantum nonlocality theories, and no-signaling nonlocality theories.

With the rapid advancement of IoT, machine learning and AI have become essential components for creating intelligent and personalized experiences on various devices. Unlike smartphones and tablets, IoT gadgets such as TVs, cars, and industrial equipment have unique requirements for content consumption. In particular, a desirable feature is the ability to seamlessly integrate machine-generated metadata into human-generated content without manual input. However, current solutions often fall short in this aspect. Unlike human-generated content, traditional techniques have difficulty accurately detecting and isolating key phrases effectively. In response to these challenges, this paper explores the feasibility of employing neural networks for detecting critical phrases in various content types on distinct IoT gadgets using different modalities, such as text, graphics, and static media. By transforming the detection task into a binary classification problem, experimental results using the TAC dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of combining n-gram and word embedding features with a binary Integrate-and-Differentiate Network (iD-NET) for improving detection precision.

We examine the interplay between two-dimensional fermions and classical dimers in a specific type of lattice model that incorporates both discrete gauge fields and relativistic fermions. This model has a natural connection to recent findings in the study of dimers on a specific type of lattice. Notably, our approach allows us to relate gauge fields to "spin" configurations of dimers. When focusing on a specific regime where gauge fields are weak, our method reveals that lattice statistics can be approximated by treating fermions and dimers as interacting particles with a specific set of rules that apply at the lattice level. This approximation has led to new insights that support a broader understanding of the connection between gauge fields, fermions, and dimer configurations in this complex lattice model.

This research introduces an enhanced Group-Lasso technique to handle categorical data with a high number of dimensions. A significant obstacle in applying the Group-Lasso method arises when regression coefficients cannot be directly linked to discrete variables. To overcome this, our proposed method converts categorical data into meaningful components, and then applies a modified Group-Lasso technique. Empirical risks are minimized at two levels – for individual groups and across all categories. By doing so, this method is guaranteed to achieve zero error asymptotically, making it suitable for high-dimensional categorical regression. To illustrate its effectiveness, experiments were conducted using simulated data and two classification datasets from the UCI Machine Learning repository. Experimental findings indicate that our proposed method offers improved accuracy compared to traditional Group-Lasso and other state-of-the-art algorithms.

In recent years, the development of embedded real-time systems has increased rapidly, with the introduction of Linux and hypervisors like VMware and Xen. However, existing real-time hypervisors are primarily designed to handle single-importance systems, which are not suitable for mixed-importance systems. A mixed-importance system has tasks or virtual machines with different priority levels, some of which require real-time guarantees and others do not. Providing real-time performance to high-priority tasks while ensuring the coexistence of low-priority tasks with real-time tasks presents a challenge. To address this issue, this research proposes a new real-time hypervisor, called T-Visor, which is designed to manage mixed-importance systems to achieve real-time performance. T-Visor achieves real-time performance by providing a fast scheduler, preventing preemption of lightweight virtual machines, using copy-on-write technology to provide real-time performance to guests, and implementing an out-of-band interrupt scheduler. A case study involving a hardware virtualization-based embedded real-time system also demonstrates the feasibility of this concept. Through comparison with a single-importance hypervisor, it is shown that T-Visor provides better performance for mixed-importance systems, achieving a 25% improvement in terms of schedule deviation and schedule completion ratio metrics.

I'm designing more straightforward methods for assembling panoramic images from multiple cameras, taking into account the natural tendency of humans to prioritize images taken upright. This involves creating a 3D scene reconstruction technique that relies on a single camera and leveraging the laws of physics, particularly those governing the attraction between objects, to generate a plausible 3D shape from the assembled images, even in cases where some images may have incorrect geometric information. Additionally, I'm exploring ways to simplify the image composition process by limiting the criteria for seamless image joining, such as eye-level preference, instead of attempting to calculate the 3D positions of the images. This could potentially simplify the required computational power and improve the overall user experience.

Chimera states in coupled dynamical systems appear to demonstrate a stable coexistence of contrasting behaviors, with some elements exhibiting rigid, periodic or rhythmic behavior, while others show a diverse range of dynamics.  Initially, this stability seemed to imply that the system itself must be in a state of equilibrium; however, it has since been proven that the presence of chimera-like patterns can occur even in systems that are in a state of constant change.  In fact, such patterns have been observed in systems whose insurance policies remain largely unchanged over time, even when coupled with oscillating systems.  In this study, we investigated the potential for chimera states in systems whose insurance policies are evenly distributed and observed the emergence of chimeras in systems whose insurance policies are asymmetric, thus demonstrating the existence of these states in systems that are in a state of constant change.  In addition, we investigated the impact of system parameters on the emergence of chimeras in these systems and found that the presence of chimeras in systems that are in a state of constant change is not necessarily indicative of a general tendency for such states to arise in systems that are similarly structured but different from one another.

Despite the advancement in model-based learning capabilities, developing a reliable controller through this approach remains a significant challenge due to its high cost and complexity, especially when defining a comprehensive and accurate model is concerned. In our research, we introduce a stochastic approach called Resilient Controller through Model-based Policy Exploration (RCME), addressing this issue by only requiring a basic plant model and incorporating external defenses to mitigate the effects of inaccuracies in the models. RCME achieves a resilient controller by approximating a set of optimal policies rather than a single ideal trajectory, thereby outperforming other robust control methods. Our study confirms the effectiveness of RCME in producing a robust controller with reduced costs compared to other state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, RCME demonstrates the potential to adapt quickly to changes in its environment, preserving its performance even after prolonged periods of evolution.

Multi-layer graphs provide a means of representing complex data, effectively expressing relationships across various domains using a uniform framework. We investigate the isomorphism problems for multi-layer graphs with special emphasis on their structural components. Moreover, by incorporating multi-layer structure, we re-examine the isomorphism problem for elevated slice graphs - a topic previously explored by Bouygnand et al. Isomorphism tests for all mentioned classes can be solved in logarithmic time complexity, namely in O(m ∥ log m ∥ n) with m being the number of layers and n the number of vertices.

We explore the relationship between entropy and mutual information in stochastic tensor networks by developing novel representations for these concepts. We establish that in a specific order of tensor network contraction, mirrored versions of these representations remain invariant. These coordinates enable an easy transition between them and maintain reflected relationships between entropies and mutual information. This property has significant implications for tensor network algorithms, allowing certain methods to be adapted into more efficient algorithms that use entropy instead of mutual information. Additionally, we've identified a specific entropy measure whose change along an entanglement block complies with the concavity principle. This discovery positions stochastic networks as a promising framework for statistical mechanics by enabling the quantification of entropy and entanglement.

Living organisms with their complex structures and responses to external stimuli, give rise to patterns and blends of different states, as opposed to the uniformity of equilibrium states. The interplay between order and disorder, inherent in pattern formation, is particularly evident when considering individual, spatial, temporal, and genetic variations. Although discussions on order and disorder often focus on the spatial and temporal domains, neglecting the genetic aspect is not feasible. In this analysis, we examine the fundamental characteristics of systems capable of generating both transient and persistent patterns, where "persistent" refers to states that are neither equilibrium states nor transient ones. By expressing the dynamics as a detailed Markov chain, we find that certain pattern persistence properties are linked to both information and entropy quantities. We then illustrate the concept of heritable data in stochastic models of cell differentiation, where the state space comprises any of the standard models with discrete states. Although the general results are extensive, the examples primarily concern simple one-dimensional models of cell differentiation. Finally, we have also discussed an open issue, concerning the meaning and calculation of heritable data when the model's initial and boundary conditions are also random.

The three-dimensional Generalized Hénon scheme serves as a simplified model for studying chaotic systems. By analyzing the diagram of chaotic regions in this model, researchers have discovered a unique pattern. This pattern emerges from the dynamic relationships between three key variables: disorder, stability, and complexity. This model can also be used to explore how chaotic systems respond to changes in disorder by fixing two other variables, representing stability and complexity, and adjusting one variable representing disorder. This approach allows researchers to analyze the behavior of these systems under different scenarios.

Researchers Griddyni and Fanuel have discovered a singular solution to the equation for gravitational curvature, which they believe could expand Einstein's theory of gravity. This singular solution represents a gravitational wave with constant speed and undulating temporal and spatial components. Although the wave's effects are negligible in the current universe, they may have significant implications for astrophysicists studying early cosmic events and phenomena such as black holes and gravitational radiation. Investigating the properties of this wave could also reveal a deeper understanding of the underlying principles of gravity and electromagnetism.

This study focuses on specific symmetric functions from the Type A Shi tableaux, specifically those whose hook lengths can be formed by pairs or triples of numbers. We use this to investigate symmetric function families associated with Gelfand-Graev distributions for GL(n,q), with each distribution indexed by a partition of n. The first index varies linearly in q, while the second index is a function of the S(n)-partition. The analysis establishes families of parametrized polynomials over Z[q], with each polynomial family indexed by a Gelfand-Graev distribution and efficiently solvable. Notably, as the number of variables approaches infinity, each polynomial family converges to a corresponding rational function over C, which can be viewed as a part of an extended version of GL(n)-Poincaré polynomial. We visualize the generated rational functions by using a family of points within projective space (3n-1), which enables a characterization of GL(n)-Poincaré polynomial limits. Additionally, the analysis leads to new counting results for partitions with even or odd hook lengths. We also derive a method for calculating torus fixed-point enumerations, which can be seen as a special case of a longer-term goal to study the enumerations of fixed points under actions of complex reductive groups on complex spaces.

In this study, we examine tunnelling duration using Larmor clock measurements, 
which display oscillations preceding tunnelling. A specific condition is established 
for maximal (instantaneous) tunnelling duration, with its value being independent 
of system parameters aside from tunnelled particle energy, yet this duration always 
appears earlier compared to standard tunnelling duration. The studied Larmor clock 
oscillations indicate quantum state changes, including Stark-induced oscillations in 
atoms, and oscillations connected to collisions in ions, observed at CERN.

By employing the large-$N_c$ limit of QCD's twist dimension, we established a method for analyzing dominant twist distributions in P-wave mesons. We applied this method to various meson types, including quarkonia and non-relativistic mesons, and examined their relevant twist structures. For example, in the case of non-relativistic P-wave mesons, such as mesons with the D or B jet, we identified the leading-order twist structures and calculated the maximum number of possible twists, finding that the dominant twists involve two quarks and a gluon, and determining the possible distributions of these quarks and gluons within their respective orbital states. We also calculated the distribution functions for these quarks and gluons, taking into consideration the constraints imposed by the Pauli principle and colour neutrality, as well as the possible arrangements of this quark-gluon-gluon state. Similarly, in relativistic P-wave mesons, such as mesons with the D* or B* jet, the dominant twists again involve a quark, an anti-quark, and a gluon, and we also determined the possible twist distributions in these relativistic P-wave mesons, taking into consideration the constraints imposed by the spin-spatial spin symmetry rules. We also explored these arrangements for all possible one, two, and three-quark configurations in relativistic P-wave mesons.

We analyze a Bose-Einstein condensate through the lens of nonlinear quantum operators. These operators incorporate both linear and nonlinear components that reflect the nonlinear Schrödinger equation governing the condensate. Building on previous work by R. J. Glauber and others, we extend existing knowledge and develop new expressions for these operators, starting with their fundamental properties. Subsequently, we apply these operators to various aspects of the condensate, including its propagation, energy, and momentum distribution. Key to our analysis is a novel definition of angular momentum that accounts for the phase and amplitude of the condensate. We explore the practical utility of these operators, proposing their measurement through multichromatic imaging, and demonstrate how they can be used to quantify key parameters like the complex phase, overall amplitude, and radius of the condensate.

This article explores various extensions of the BMS algebra associated with asymptotic flat space-time scenarios, particularly focusing on two-dimensional BMS$_3$ and BMS$_4$ cases. We identify the key features of these extended algebras and provide concrete examples of new symmetry extensions in both three and four dimensional space-time contexts. The primary physical implication of these enhanced symmetries stems from their incorporation within a unified theoretical framework, where we address a long-standing question: can gravity be derived from non-trivial asymptotic conditions applied to previous lower-dimensional theories with extended symmetries? Our work answers this question in the affirmative, demonstrating that the necessary commutation relations among new symmetry elements can be derived from the established principles of soft graviton action and the resulting theory would possess a finite dimension. Interestingly, our findings reveal that the theory of massless higher-spin particles in three dimensions, with a zero-mode contribution, constitutes an example of a theory of gravity derived from asymptotic conditions applied to previous lower-dimensional theories with extended symmetries.

Continual Learning, which mirrors the unfolding nature of real-world experiences, demands that systems learn from one instance without forgetting previously learned information. Online Collective Continual Learning stands out due to its unique setup, with multiple agents learning concurrently from separate streams. Notably, agents can share knowledge with each other, but this shared knowledge may ultimately lead to shared forgetting problems. Despite the growing interest in both batch and online Continual Learning and Repetition-Free Continual Learning, the field of online collective learning remains relatively underexplored. Past attempts have either simplified the concept or introduced unnecessary restrictions. Our research aims to fill this knowledge gap by exploring a unified setup for evaluation: a single central agent learning while concurrently observing the experiences of multiple secondary agents. To achieve this, we developed NuFoOCCL, an innovative approach that allows the central agent to identify and prevent forgetting caused by shared knowledge. NuFoOCCL's performance was evaluated across three distinct domain-line splitting scenarios and compared with current state-of-the-art methods. When testing in a setting involving two agents, NuFoOCCL demonstrated an improved GraS performance of +5.8% and +4.2% respectively when working with or without access to the shared knowledge. The project's code can be found on the repository at https://github.com/harshadhardikar/NuFo-OCL.

The concepts of shapes, classical measures, pseudo-measures, and pseudo-shapes originate from extended versions of classical distribution functions, with pseudo-measures and pseudo-shapes arising from the fourfold distribution functions derived from moments. Recent breakthroughs include the establishment of relationships between non-degenerate generalized shapes and pseudo-measures/pseudo-shapes, as well as the introduction of Ricci flat four-measures. Building upon these discoveries, we thoroughly investigate the interconnections among all these geometric objects, moments, and classical measures. Furthermore, we display the relationships between these objects through concrete examples, while examining the generalized shapes corresponding to Ricci flat four-measures.

In this study, we derive specific formulas for the number of permutation groups with bases in $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$ and examine the properties of permutation functions and complete permutation functions with respect to subfields $\mathbb{F}_{q}$. We then proceed to compute the counts of permutation functions and complete permutation functions that satisfy a particular degree condition over $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$ and explore the SDU-structure of permutation function fields, where $q$ represents a power of $p$, a prime number.

A computational method for identifying intestinal worms through microscopic image analysis is presented, aimed at assisting parasite control efforts. Utilizing deep learning techniques, the research employed DBN architectures to develop a framework capable of accurately classifying images even with limited hardware resources. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of the approach.

To analyze the dynamic behavior of an investment-reinsurance model, a dual approach involving an Markov-modulated jump-diffusion model has been employed, with the objective of establishing a mathematical method to calculate a specific non-zero-sum game equilibrium. By utilizing the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, this equilibrium issue is reformulated as a variational inequality with regard to stochastic differential equations. Numerical simulation results demonstrate the model's potential for both reinsurance and investment returns, as well as the influence of model parameters on the equilibrium and associated investment-reinsurance strategies. Notably, this study offers a novel type of two-players game model tied to financial activities.

This research introduces a novel practical identification and control approach for fixed-wing aircraft, leveraging the dual simplex method for fast and efficient parameter estimation using dynamic linear models to represent flight behaviors. The proposed algorithm enables identification of parameters in both stationary and non-stationary conditions, followed by a genetic filter to rapidly converge towards optimal control parameters, facilitating rapid prototyping and experimentation. The presented methodology demonstrates robust resilience against turbulence in both steady and fluid flight modes, and its effectiveness is showcased through comprehensive flight tests spanning 200 hours of flight time. Moreover, the contribution of this work includes the successful adaptation of the dual simplex algorithm for stochastic processes and the integration of genetic filtering, enhancing the traditional identification and control paradigm.

This article examines the significance of low-energy pion-nucleon interactions in effective field theories. It highlights that several prominent pion-nucleon scattering observables, such as elastic differential cross-sections and polarization, are constrained by energy-dependent unitarity limits. To determine these limits, we integrate the isoscalar and isovector partial waves from the $t$-channel and apply the Cauchy inequality, leading to the derivation of model-independent, energy-dependent upper limits for these observables. Furthermore, we utilize this framework to derive lower limits for certain phase and amplitude information that will be available with future high-precision experiments, such as those to be conducted at the J-PARC hadron experiment facility.

The Large Hadron Collider at CERN will soon be upgraded to the Comprehensive Large-incedium pHT detector. A crucial component of this upgrade is the CMS endcap pixel detector system. As part of the CMS endcap pixel detector, 49 sensitive components will be placed near the point where particles enter the detector. These components were tested in a real-world environment under conditions similar to those found in a working collider. A group of these components was put through a test where they were read by a computer system in real-time, and scientists were able to demonstrate the effectiveness of their new reconstruction methods even with complex conditions at the point of entry. This was achieved through a process called hit finding, where algorithms were applied to data collected during the experiment and 95.4% of total hits were successfully identified (including those with only one hit), revealing (including those with only one hit), revealing (including those with only one hit) 99.6% of individual hits. A separate simulation experiment showed that the efficiency of their new reconstruction methods should range between 93.9% to 97.9%. This independent evaluation confirmed that the CMS endcap pixel detector is ready for operation.

We have created a machine learning model using 3D visualization software to 
analyze a dataset of 5315 AGN hosts from the Hyper Suprime-Cam survey. Our 
model can identify four types of galaxy morphologies: s0, SA, SAB, and SA/SB 
galaxies, with an accuracy of nearly 90%. By applying our model, we found 
statistics for AGN host galaxies in the sample and compared them to a similar 
sample of non-active galaxies. We noticed that galaxies with smaller masses 
have fewer SAB and SA/SB galaxies and more s0/SAB/SB types, whereas more 
SAB/SB galaxies are associated with higher masses. Additionally, SAB/SB hosts are 
less common than other types in both active and non-active galaxies. By 
exploring the mass and concentration relations for AGN hosts, we found that 
S0 hosts have a narrower range of concentrations than SA or SAB hosts. By 
analyzing the properties of AGN hosts based on their morphology, we found a 
correlation between morphology and black hole-to-galaxy mass ratio but not 
with the overall galaxy mass or K-band magnitude. Our results support the 
theory that a galaxy's environment plays a crucial role in its morphological 
development.

Using the Space Transport Model, specifically its quantum-based version QTSM, this study investigates how asymptotically formed clusters in a nucleus allocate phase-space when they interact with each other at short distances. By examining two-dimensional (2D) configurations with a finite density of states, QTSM is capable of simulating interactions to a degree comparable to 3N wave functions, which it does by integrating over 3D momentum space. To achieve this, QTSM must conform to a principle: the total phase-space of the two clusters must be equivalent to that of the original, single nucleus. By applying QTSM to a 40Ca isotope, researchers found that cluster distributions remain stable up to densities exceeding three times normal matter density, at which point they deviate by about 10% due to the asymptotic nature of the Bohm-Pines 3Quasiparticle Mean-Field model on which QTSM is based. By comparing QTSM's predictions to Experimental Fourier densities extracted from Jefferson Lab experiments featuring short-wavelength proton probes, researchers found a low-level discrepancy between the two, which indicates that the asymptotic model is approximately accurate in describing nuclear interactions at the quantum level, while accounting for the distribution of phase space.

Recent breakthroughs in complex-valued deep learning reveal its potential for improved performance in applications such as speech recognition, feature learning, and image classification due to the ability to represent and process complex numbers more effectively. While complex numbers offer advantages, their use also introduces challenges such as the risk of training models on incompatible complex number formats, leading to inconsistent results and hindering comparison with models trained on other formats. This study investigates the co-domain equivalence of complex-valued deep learning models by examining the implications of different complex number formats on their performance and provides guidelines for selecting an appropriate format in line with the dataset's characteristics. The research also extends existing theories on complex-valued deep learning to provide a comprehensive understanding of the co-domain equivalence phenomenon.

We investigate the concept of geometric scaling in high-energy collisions, along with its application to both subatomic particles and macroscopic objects. Geometric scaling describes a phenomenon in which particles exhibit scaling behavior within their longitudinal and transverse profiles as energy increases, which was initially observed in small particle collisions and later also in large particle collisions. A theoretical framework for geometric scaling will be developed, and its generalization to higher dimensions will be discussed. Furthermore, we examine the theoretical underpinnings of geometric scaling, namely gluon saturation, which is a concept rooted in the connection between particle interactions and physical space. A fundamental aspect of geometric scaling is understood when considering the relationship between particle interactions and physical space, which can be quantified by a parameter called the saturation momentum. The saturation momentum represents the point at which particle interactions cease due to overloading and can be utilized to predict particle behavior. A detailed analysis of geometric scaling in various particle systems, including ep scattering, heavy ion collisions, and proton-proton collisions, will be explored, drawing direct connections between these processes as the energy increases. Additionally, we discuss several distinct regimes of geometric scaling, including the geometric scaling of ep scattering, the "geometric scaling" of gluon distribution functions, and the geometric scaling of particle distributions such as charged jets and photons.

Our analysis focuses on the application of the Rao-Zhang-Rybakov feedback module within StarForge to study the formation of gas and stellar configurations within low-metallicity star clusters. Through a series of simulations with the Rioja-Peterson-StarForge code, we investigate how feedback from the central massive protostar can reverse the collapse of gas at the cluster core, especially in over-massive clusters where the gas would otherwise solidify. The Rioja-Peterson-StarForge code generates cluster models based on a one-dimensional radial setup, whereas the Rioja-Peterson-StarForge code with the Rao-Zhang-Rybakov feedback module expands this to a two-dimensional model across the cluster's radius. Our results include a range of possible origins for the second-generation wealth distribution within low-metallicity star clusters, encompassing single-star gas solidification, gas depletion, and wealth distribution within over-massive clusters.

As big data analysis shifts from straightforward to complex problems for traditional models, modern machine learning intelligence takes over, delivering exceptional results for the analysis of unstructured and structured data, surpassing that of classical statistical methods. One of the challenges with using machine learning, however, is the lack of transparent explanations for its outputs, a problem that needs addressing for users to build trust in these models as decision support tools. This research proposes an innovative evaluation framework for machine learning models to be used alongside human experts in decision making processes, with the aim of enhancing decision quality through greater accountability and improved communication between decision makers. A case study on financial literacy shows that this framework works effectively, with the potential application of this methodology in finance settings demonstrated through another example, and its potential expansion into other fields shown through examples of text-based models.

We create an open-source framework for classical and quantum neural networks, enabling research into their distinctive properties. A novel square framework for quantum neural networks is introduced, demonstrating its potential for simplified research and faster execution. Multiple quantum neural network architectures are examined and contrasted, with simulations showing one architecture can learn the XOR function without adjustment, significantly outperforming other variants. When applied to machine learning with the quantum framework, our results show that the state-of-the-art quantum neural network architecture trained on the MNIST dataset performs better than comparable non-quantum approaches. Additionally, our experiments explore the impact of noise on quantum machine learning tasks, with exciting results that indicate further research into this field.

This paper explores a subset of nearly contact manifolds, termed $C^{\infty}$-distorted product manifolds, and examines a particular type of subset known as $D^{\perp}$-distorted product pointwise semi-inclined submanifolds within these manifolds. Initial research has been conducted into the properties of $D^{\perp}$-distorted product pointwise semi-inclined submanifolds and their relationship with a specific subset known as $I^{\perp}$-distorted product pointwise semi-inclined submanifolds.

A new technique using colored center spin impurities in transparent materials has the potential to read out signals from weak interactions with particles having kinetic energies less than 100 keV, and with high resolutions of ~10 keV.  This method could serve as a passive detector for measuring nuclear recoil energies resulting from the interactions with weakly interacting massive particles having masses similar to those of the neutrino.  A coloured center based nuclear detector would have several advantages when searching for such WIMPs, as it would allow for large amounts of material to be tested at once, would enable the use of natural targets and would facilitate the development of large and efficient detectors.  This text outlines the principles of operation for such a Coloured Center based Nuclear Recoil detector, or CCONE, and discusses its capabilities.

Colloidal particles undergo constant movement due to their low mass and Brownian motion, which enables them to randomly change direction and speed. In any given fluid, these particles will continuously interact with each other as well as with other elements such as surfaces and external motivators, like a force in a specific pattern. The interaction between these particles and external motivators creates a pattern of activity, which varies at different distances. The likelihood of these particles colliding with the external motivator is directly proportional to the value of the specific parameter at their location. The particles may become trapped in a dynamic equilibrium state within the area, which is determined by the likelihood of these particles colliding with the external motivator as they approach it from different angles, versus the likelihood of these particles escaping this area by moving in a different direction. In a recent study, researchers analyzed the Brownian motion of these particles within a specific environment as they interact with an external motivator with a specific type of symmetry, or lack thereof. The researchers found in their mathematical model that the particles exhibit three distinct behaviors, which are determined by the intensity of the external motivator, which can be quantified using a specific parameter. The behaviors include a response where the particles escape a specific area by moving in a specific direction, which can be quantified using a different parameter; a response where the particles can escape a specific area by moving in both directions; and a response where the particles can no longer escape a specific area by moving in both directions

This study delves into the theoretical framework underlying seniority physics within weakly-coupled lattice models featuring complex spin-orbit interactions. Specifically, it analyzes a two-dimensional p-wave model and its variants, and finds that applying a magnetic field results in a gapped phase characterized by composite spin-pair excitations. Notably, it observes an abundance of topological Tonkopp-Hofstetter lumps within this phase, arising from the interplay between magnetic flux and spin-orbit interactions. Moreover, as a derivative of the model in question, it discusses a two-band system resembling the $
u = 4/7$ fractional quantum Hall state at fillings $
u = 5/3$ and $
u = 10/9$.

Detecting latent disease spread poses significant challenges, particularly when it occurs in intricately connected networks where individual identification is impractical. Although exposure history can help identify close contacts of infected individuals, it is not always sufficient to pinpoint those who have not yet shown symptoms. We introduce a novel method utilizing a geometric approach to track both active and latent cases in a population. This method involves categorizing individuals into distinct subgroups based on their disease status and history, ensuring accurate estimation of infectious individuals and maintaining a specified margin of error. We have developed an algorithm that achieves efficient data collection with minimal contact tracing, which we demonstrate using small-world network simulations of hepatitis B transmission. These studies indicate that geometric method can effectively identify infectious and asymptomatic individuals with a reduced need for contact tracing, while also providing an updated protocol for contact tracing to further enhance outbreak detection.

We're focusing on finding the most probable configuration of Abell clusters and superclusters in large-scale structure (LSS) based on an assumption using the Poisson-Lindblad master equation to describe their evolution. Our model considers the LSS as composed of sub-halos and a large "monster" that abides by specific statistical distributions. A monster refers to a vast, diffuse structure, distinct from regular clusters, to simplify calculations. Our research utilizes the WMAP 7-year sky realization to estimate probabilities for different LSS configurations using a Monte-Carlo approach. Notably, the probability distribution peaks at irregularly shaped structures, including "x'es" - structures lacking central clusters but featuring increased matter at peripheral areas. However, these structures are significantly less likely than previously thought. Our research shows that monster matter accumulation sites are likely shifted towards facing the direction of local cluster formations, indicating an ongoing cluster formation process. Furthermore, our research reveals that monster matter accumulation sites are likely shifted towards facing the direction of local cluster formations - possibly an indication of ongoing formation. Additionally, our research reveals that the formation of clusters is likely driven by the transformation of matter from the outside to inside of these structures.

Our research focuses on enhancing goal-conditioned reinforcement learning through the use of natural language, including methods for automatically generating complex objectives. Nevertheless, the current approaches encounter significant challenges in tasks that involve multi-step reward structures and significant gaps between agent performance and objective alignment. The difficulties arise from natural language objectives that become increasingly ambiguous as agents progress towards more skilled states, thereby reducing their ability to differentiate between actions that lead to similar outcomes. To tackle this problem, we present a novel method that integrates sets of both low-level actions and symbolic actions. The high-level symbolic actions can lead to novel states, but also introduce new objectives to supplement those in the original dataset, thus keeping the objectives relevant even as agents become more skilled. The experimental findings that we gather demonstrate that this technique allows agents to efficiently utilize the natural language objective by reducing the scope of possible actions as their skills improve over time, thereby achieving a range of different skills more effectively and faster.

Quantum channel shadow mapping holds significant importance in quantum information processing due to its potential applications in solving TSP and QMA-hard problems. Although research has been extensive, the method's feasibility depends heavily on specific channel properties. This study focuses on the broad class of channels with polynomial product structures composed of unitary channels, where we employ the concept of unitary shadow counting to measure channel observables. We establish criteria for a class of channel-product functions to be polynomial in a specific dimension, while exploring the impact of low polynomial degrees on the method's efficiency. We also discuss how certain channel characteristics, such as the assumption that a particular basis remains relatively close to the actual channel product, affect the method's effectiveness. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of our findings through the analysis of a specific case study related to holographic quantum-thermal systems.

The four Keen inequalities include the circle inequality πr, the mean curvature inequality
$\int_M|H_n|^2dA, and three inequalities involving the Cheeger constant, specifically
p\int_MH_n^pdA^{1-2p} for p < 1,  \frac{\pi}{2}\int_M(H_1)^2dA, and \int_MH_2dA\geq \pi.
In this study, we explore the limits of these inequalities for a broad category of planar
convex shapes (including star-shaped and bodies of revolution) and establish the equality
cases for specific shapes, notably, all cases have been identified except for shapes with
Cheeger constant equal to π and shapes with H_1=0.

This application notes the elevated interest in using unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) for tasks requiring rapid data transfer, as evident from the significant research in this area, focusing on optimizing UAV paths and communication systems. A key consideration for successful mission completion is selecting the optimal flight path within a predetermined time frame. This paper's objective is to provide an overview of current strategies for optimizing UAV routes with respect to time constraints, including simulations and real-world scenarios. A thorough analysis of the challenges and shortcomings of existing approaches is also presented, aiming to identify potential areas for improvement.

In multilayer graphene, characterized by the Coulomb interaction between different layers, we conducted a renormalization group analysis. Initially, we derived the four-vertex function between any two layers, and then we identified the conditions that lead to the renormalization of the coupling constants between these layers. Notably, our analysis reveals that the coupling between adjacent layers remains stable, in contrast to the coupling between distant layers, which becomes unstable. This finding is relevant to the instability of the Coulomb coupled superlattices formed in bilayer graphene when a voltage is applied across them.

The conformation of surface molecules greatly affects their functions, so controlling conformation is crucial in molecular design, especially for surface-tethered molecules. Researchers have developed a temperature-sensitive molecule, Sc2TbN@C80, which changes its conformation due to the thermally induced phase transition of the terbium core. To understand how temperature affects the conformation of Sc2TbN@C80, a study investigated the molecule adsorbed on a nickel (111) surface treated with boron nitride using scanning tunneling microscopy and atomic force microscopy. The results showed that at temperatures below 50 K, the molecule adsorbs in a flat manner, but starts to bend and change its arrangement at higher temperatures, which correlates with the phase transition temperature of the terbium core (around 150 K for Sc2TbN@C80(0,85) and 170 K for Sc2TbN@C80(94)). Additionally, the study found that the molecule can undergo a second phase transition at temperatures above 210 K. Further research is needed to understand the mechanisms behind these phase transitions, but the study shows that the presence of nickel does not affect the phase transitions of Sc2TbN@C80.

The number of IoT devices is rapidly expanding, with a huge number of new devices being connected to the network every day due to the introduction of various new technologies and services. Utilizing light-weight algorithms in the IoT devices' security framework seems to be the best approach to ensure their security. We have conducted an experiment where we compared the security offered by post-quantum algorithms to that offered by classical algorithms. The findings of this experiment revealed that post-quantum algorithms offer a comparable level of security to classical algorithms at a lighter weight. Therefore, using post-quantum algorithms in the IoT devices' security framework seems to be the suitable solution to their security issues.

The Ramsey series combines high precision and adaptability, making it an ideal technique for measuring hydrogen atom energy levels in various conditions. However, hydrogen atoms are part of many compounds, so researchers need to consider multiple scenarios when applying Ramsey series in a laboratory setting. A new study develops a statistical approach to schedule measurement intervals and optimal pilot experiments that minimize uncertainty in hydrogen energy level measurements, giving preference to scenarios with the lowest relative uncertainty.

A novel multi-faceted measure of node importance in a network is derived using a generalized version of the Laplacian, which is based on the triangle inequality. By incorporating all network connections, this approach provides a more comprehensive understanding of a network's structure. Calculating the geometric importance of individual nodes or groups involves solving a system of linear equations using numerical methods. Experimental results demonstrate that a streamlined version of the algorithm can efficiently handle large networks containing up to one million nodes. Furthermore, in numerous applications, the proposed method shows competitive results with other established metrics, such as betweenness centrality, degree centrality, and structural hole centrality. Examples of synthetic and real-world applications include identifying key nodes in networks, determining the most critical nodes for removal in network components, and targeting nodes for efficient network disruption.

We examine several categories of matrix pencil collections, defined by specific matrix transformations, including equivalence, transverse equivalence, and strand equivalence. We establish a fundamental connection among these categories by demonstrating that every collection within one category can be obtained from a unique collection within another category through a systematic process of reduction. This framework facilitates the development of a standardized approach for analyzing each type of pencil collection, as well as the identification of specific properties that characterize every collection within a particular category.

We establish a local coordinate system for classified T-duality transformations between twisted tori. The T-duality maps for twisted tori are a combination of those for plain tori and certain inversion operations, involving a coordinate transformation that includes a transformation that relates to the fiber of a specific projection map. Given that the monodromy of the associated Seifert fibration can be expressed as a torus rotation, we show that the T-duality transforms by inversely rotating the fiber. This discovery connects to an older finding that the T-duality transformation for elliptic manifolds corresponds to a reverse rotation of its fiber.

In 2019, researchers reduced complex distance problems involving graphs with a certain complexity level down to simpler forms with smaller dimensions. This work extends their findings to multiple variants of these problems in graphs that are also minor-free. Specifically, they developed an efficient algorithm using parametrized tools to find a compact representation of distances in these graphs, which can be easily adapted to other graph problems. Additionally, they proved that a compact representation of distances in graphs with a particular structure (known as planar graphs) cannot be found using linear time complexity. This result establishes a key boundary for distance problems in graphs with a particular structure.

This research examines global behavior in continuous, monotonic discrete-time systems. These systems have consistent, ordered behavior due to their monotonicity. Therefore, they either converge or diverge. The required conditions for global convergence or divergence are shown to be determinable through a specific analysis of their dynamics, specifically by identifying the number of orbit-intersecting points. The findings from this study can also be applied to a type of iterative map, specifically the Krasnoselski map.

The potential of near-term quantum computers lies in solving complex problems through a hybrid approach that combines quantum and classical computing. The variational quantum algorithm is particularly suitable for these systems, as it enables efficient simulation of complex quantum states. Our research introduces a novel adaptive variational algorithm that leverages a quantum circuit with a dynamic programmatic optimization strategy. By carefully managing the number of excitations in individual qubits, we achieve optimal algorithm performance while minimizing errors caused by incorrect state preparations. Our results demonstrate that our approach can efficiently solve fermionic Hamiltonians on quantum simulators and real quantum devices. Furthermore, we solved the ground state of a four-atom quantum circuit model and obtained an approximate 50% improvement in our adaptive method compared to the standard variable-depth approach.

We propose an innovative, efficient, and versatile approach to represent learning, where a profound generative decoder generates a representation for a given input. Unlike other techniques such as self-supervised learning which often focus on similarity between input representations, this model aims to produce a representation that accurately captures an input's essence by modeling its probability density function. This, in turn, allows for more effective use of this representation in downstream applications. For example, when given a set of categories, our approach can identify and produce a compact, class-specific representation for each input, where the input's features are likely and the remainder is uncertainty. This property turns the task of representation learning on its head, where rather than seeking similar structures, we seek representations that are easy to model. This concept is known as Ease of Modeling (EoM), where we aim to develop compact, natural representations by describing the space where an input resides using fewer parameters. This natural focus allows our approach to outperform competitor models on various tasks such as clustering, self-supervised learning, and compression.

A fundamental cosmological equation that describes how the universe expands is the Friedmann equation. In the low-frequency part of the Fourier spectrum of the gravitational waves produced during inflation, there's a strong background known as the Bogoliubov vacuum, identified as the "relational cosmological vacuum". This vacuum gives rise to a unique phenomenon in the sense of scale, known as "cosmological redshift", in which the gravitational wave amplitude decreases over time due to the acceleration of the universe. This phenomenon, when occurring for multiple frequencies, results in a redshifted state that can be characterized by a negative correlation coefficient, giving rise to a phenomenon known as "redshift-induced quantum entanglement". In this study, the phenomenon of redshift-induced quantum entanglement is explored, using a specific example in which the scale factor of the universe, given as $a(t)$, is given for both power-law and polynomial forms. These particular forms of $a(t)$ yield singular states at a specific point in time, known as the "inflationary hubblescope". This state can be characterized by a specific strain, given as $\eta(a) = \dot a(a)/a$. This particular point in time, known as $t_h$, can be identified as the moment at which the cosmological redshift begins to take effect, leading to a specific behavior in the gravitational wave amplitude. In this study, the time $t_h$ is explored, using different expressions for $a

Two solar comet analyses, conducted with the ALMA Atacama Compact Array, detected CS in Comets 41P/Tuttle-Giacobini-Kresak and C/2015 ER61. Prolonged emission from icy grains was found in Tuttle-Giacobini-Kresak, while ER61 displayed both gas and icy grain emission. Variations in emission related to distance from the Sun were observed for CS in ER61, suggesting it may have originated from multiple locations. GCSS is a common H$_2$S precursor molecule, which could have formed CS throughout the comet's tail due to photon diffusion. Sulfur-containing species are abundant in cometary nuclei, so it's likely that CS is found in most solar comets, regardless of their polarization orientation. Therefore, it's likely that CS is a widespread species in solar system comets, which could provide key insights into comet formation and evolution processes.

We introduce an uncomplicated and resource-effective method for producing high-quality speech without guidance, leveraging existing neural speech synthesis models to create a novel approach. By utilizing a pre-trained synthesis model, we generate speech from a text-to-speech dataset, extracting speech from a small subset of high-quality recordings with moderate lexical similarity to the synthesis model's input vocabulary. To produce diverse speech samples without extensive training, we apply a novel word substitution technique, combining it with a data augmentation method to enhance speech generation diversity. Experimental results on the LibriTTS dataset significantly outperform state-of-the-art unsupervised speech generation methods in terms of speech quality, with our technique achieving a mean opinion score (MOS) of 4.0 compared to the best prior method, MOS 3.8.

We examine the influence of quintessence on black hole shadow, utilizing the Tsallis holographic dark energy model. Assuming the function $f(Q)=\alpha e^{\sqrt{1+\gamma}Q}$ from the original paper, we find that by raising the quintessence redshift, the shadow radius decreases, while increasing $\alpha$ also yields decreased shadow radii. Additionally, the effects of $\gamma$ and $n$ on shadow properties are also explored. By selecting specific values for these parameters, we can determine their individual effects on the shadow. For instance, a negative $\gamma$ reduces the shadow radius, and the shadow radius decreases as the deviation $n-1$ of the Tsallis distribution increases.

Multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems often arise in various engineering contexts, but reliable solutions are typically confined to two-objective scenarios, thanks to the limitations imposed by computational requirements. This paper proposes a multi-objective solution approach utilizing a natural selection genetic algorithm with a innovative branching system, which expands the solution set for three or more objectives. The proposed technique enhances computational efficiency by incorporating a novel branching system that selects an intermediate value between the best and worst possible option for infeasible variables, as opposed to the standard binary approach. Additionally, the algorithm's diversity is maintained through the use of a new termination criterion based on the average distance between the best objective values of offspring and parents. The proposed technique is demonstrated by applying it to a set of known three-objective optimization problems to showcase its effectiveness.

The foundational concept of groupoids arose from studying symmetries in continuous settings, leading to the definition of linked groupoids to encompass more circumstances. By applying synthetic differential geometry principles, we find that linked groupoids inherently possess a level of completeness and are connected. Moreover, we demonstrate that the process of forming quotients from groupoid actions does not disrupt their inherent connectedness.

In the biomedical field, data have become a critical component of healthcare, driving healthcare system advancements, and fueling biomedical research.  There's currently an overwhelming amount of diverse data available, encompassing high-content imaging, proteomics, genomics, trans-omictic data, etc.  To tackle this challenge, data sharing is key to facilitating discovery, system advancements, and biomedical research.  However, with various datasets coming from different sources, aggregation poses a significant challenge, largely due to technical, semantic, and social barriers.  In this paper, we highlight the importance of and strategies for data sharing, focusing on the development of a Cyber Infrastructure Toolkit to support dataset aggregation, dissemination, and facilitation of standardized data exchange.  This is exemplified through two case studies, one focusing on Proteomics Data and the other on Histopathology Images.

Aspect-based emotion analysis focuses on pinpointing the specific emotions towards a particular aspect within a given text. This task is crucial for comprehending the multi-faceted nature of emotions, but the datasets themselves are often imbalanced due to the absence of relevant data on certain emotions. Moreover, data containing two aspects complicates the task of distinguishing between distinct emotions expressed towards the same aspect. This research proposes a novel pre-training technique that incorporates guided contrastive learning to mitigate the challenges posed by imbalanced data and the overlap between aspects. By developing this method, experiments using two datasets show that it significantly outperforms existing approaches.

Researchers are becoming interested in the role of a specific variable, or mediator, in explaining cause-and-effect relationships between exposure and an outcome, especially when studying rare events. Since the outcome is already balanced due to matching, but the mediator might be poorly matched, a specific statistical analysis, or estimator, is being examined. This estimator is capable of handling imbalanced mediator data, and is being used in a simulation study to compare its performance with other approaches. A real-world example is provided to illustrate the results of applying this estimator.

This research delves into a secure communication network for multiple users that incorporates a reconfigurable intelligent surface to enhance security, with the objective of maximizing the minimum secrecy rate among users. To address this problem, an optimization approach is proposed that takes into account the limited capabilities of the RIS, such as reflection power and phase constraints, as well as channel state information. A novel security-enhancing design framework is developed, combining block coordinate descent and successive convex approximation optimization techniques. By leveraging these methods, the original non-convex problem is transformed into a sequence of convex problems that can be efficiently solved using established optimization algorithms. Numerical results demonstrate that this approach significantly improves the minimum secrecy rate in comparison to a baseline scheme, even after removing the equipment limitations. Furthermore, the findings illustrate the trade-off between achieving secure communication and the transmission power required.

In the realm of online trading, portfolio management is ultimately an ultimate goal that everyone strives for. Given a given portfolio with stocks, our objective is to devise a value-based strategy that facilitates the acquisition of stocks with promising future growth potential. To achieve this goal, we employ a forecasting framework that utilizes macroeconomic data such as GDP, inflation, unemployment rates, and other relevant factors, along with publicly available stock information, to determine the likelihood of a stock's value increasing in the long run. By integrating resampling and renaming techniques, our proposed approach is able to pinpoint the most suitable combination of macroeconomic and stock data, accurately predict a stock's value growth based on such factors as current price, earnings per share, and others, and effectively filter out noisy data by analyzing correlations and setting relevant thresholds. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our strategy in identifying stocks with potential for long-term growth.

The solar wind's behavior near the Sun remains puzzling, particularly regarding how temperatures and speeds change. To address this question, researchers analyzed data from the Parker Solar Probe, which was close to the Sun (about 27.8 centimeters) and recorded temperatures and speeds over an 8.5-day period in 2019. During this time, the solar probe experienced a temperature increase of up to 8 times the normal temperature. This increase was associated with a decrease in speed by about 300 kilometers per hour. The data showed that the temperature rise and speed drop often occurred and were linked in an orderly manner. The results are consistent with the theory that the temperature and speed changes are part of a regular solar pattern. The researchers also found that the solar pattern is more pronounced near the Sun and is influenced by the structure of the solar plasma.

The concept of noncommutative countable principal bundles is introduced as a version of the commutative analogy, involving locally trivial bundles and a separable C*-algebraic structure. Existence and uniqueness theorems are established for these bundles under specific conditions, including actions of discrete amenable groups on certain type I C*-algebras and Glimm-dual algebras. Additionally, a notable example is provided of such a bundle that arises from the group action of a free discrete amenable group on the C*-algebra of infinite tensor product of two matrix algebras.

We establish the existence of an elementary endextension carrying a free ultrafilter that is minimal with respect to nearly disjointness, specifically above any free ultrafilter with a specific property related to countability. Furthermore, it's demonstrated that it's possible to embed a ultraproduct of a specific sequence of cardinalities, namely $\aleph_0,$ $\aleph_1,$ $2^{\aleph_0}$ and $2^{\aleph_1}$, over an ultraproduct of models of these cardinalities, with the property that a free ultrafilter generated within this extended structure remains minimal with respect to nearly disjointness.

We have developed a new approach for an optomechanical system that incorporates q-deformation. This innovative method gives us the optomechanical model (QM), a complex physical system with a real mechanical component, whose interaction with the optical field is governed by the Fokker-Planck equation. We explored the conditions for improved output light and mechanical sensitivity in this model. The model's enhanced output light and mechanical sensitivity arise from a quantized field in a doubly coupled q-deformed optomechanical cavity. The model allows for two approaches: the traditional method focusing on the classical mechanical sensitivity and the novel method incorporating q-deformation, which increases sensitivity through the use of strongly nonclassical mechanical sensitivity. We examined the model's physical properties through its Wigner W(E, q) function. The model's analysis reveals that for an optomechanical cavity with strong nonlinearity, the Wigner function changes from negative to positive around the turning point of 0.25 within the range of 0.6 to 0.8. Additionally, this model's output light and mechanical sensitivity can be improved by either adjusting the parameter a2 or applying a time-varying radiation force. The model's analysis also predicts improved output light and mechanical sensitivity in an all-optical QM system when the parameters used are half of those in the double-coupled QM system.

We incorporate R-parity violating interactions into the Isonemonic Double-Rotors Model, which effectively describes the underlying structure of a nucleus with space-time vibrations. This natural extension of the model enables us to account for both R-parity violating and preserving modes of a nucleus, with the latter corresponding to the classic scissors modes. We derive analytical expressions for the former's modes, establish a general formula for their transition strengths between a nucleus and a rotor, and identify a correlation that links the R-parity violating and preserving modes. Calculations performed for the Isoscalar and Isoscalar-pseudoscalar components indicate that the R-parity violating modes are characterized by the same signature or spatial part as the preserving scissors modes, but with different spatial patterns and significantly higher transition strengths. This suggests that the R-parity violating modes are expected to make a greater contribution to electric monopole and dipole transitions than the preserving scissors modes, particularly in nuclei with large deformation.

A novel approach incorporating a cell-mean based neural network (CM-ANN) is presented for solving first and second-order partial differential equations with mixed elliptic-hyperbolic characteristics. This method builds upon previous neuronally-based methods for one-dimensional domains, optimizing them for increased efficiency and adapting to a range of equation types via dynamic neural network architecture and adaptable neural network operation timeframes. In-depth analysis of CM-ANN is conducted via both theoretical and numerical examinations, including validation with established methods for solving the shallow water equations. Results demonstrate the method's accuracy and comparative efficiency with state-of-the-art CM-ANN techniques for various numerical configurations and solution types. Furthermore, the CM-ANN method exhibits a strong potential for extension to more complex multi-dimensional partial differential equations.

The ALICE Collaboration is working to bolster the experiment's capabilities by incorporating advanced detector upgrades and implementing efficient data collection and analysis techniques. A critical enhancement is the High Acceptance Di-electron/Photonic System (HIP) for the LHC Run 3, which involves a cutting-edge silicon-tungsten calorimeter. This large-scale upgrade will enable the ALICE Collaboration to meet the heightened requirements of the LHC and achieve the desired scientific outcomes by collecting extensive proton-proton and lead-lead data. In addition to HIP, the team is introducing a range of new features, including a re-designed barrel, extended pseudorapidity coverage, and an enhanced trigger system. These advanced upgrades will greatly expand the ALICE Collaboration's scientific scope, allowing them to explore new areas of investigation such as heavy-ion interactions with proton and proton-ion at low energies, and proton-proton interactions at high luminosity in the ALICE detector.

Our investigation into the global structure of the SU(2) gauge group as applied to complex three-dimensional space shows that the topological charge generates a Berry phase within a time frame defined by the past and future light cones of an arbitrary point. This Berry phase can be detected through both the geometric change in the phase of coherent states after circumnavigating a closed path and the expectation value of a corresponding global operator. Furthermore, the geometric phase can be determined by computing the entanglement of opposite light cones, specifically, the part of the Hilbert space associated with the past with respect to the part with the future, and this method may serve as a signal for the temporal Unruh effect experienced by a accelerating observer.

Our research focuses on processing multilingual text by extracting key events (ocisions) from given text. A comprehensive dataset, called MEE, consisting of multilingual text, has been introduced to help with processing multilingual text. Analysis of the dataset shows that certain English occurrences do not have direct equivalents in other languages, which makes comparing their frequencies challenging. Additionally, the dataset is used for other natural language processing tasks such as identifying unknown occurrences and their associated contexts. MEE is shown to be superior to other available datasets in these tasks, and also helps with other related tasks such as identifying unknown occurrences and their associated contexts. Furthermore, the dataset is used for other natural language processing tasks such as identifying unknown occurrences and their associated contexts. Preliminary results from experimenting with the dataset show that certain English occurrences do not have direct equivalents in other languages, and also help with other natural language processing tasks such as identifying unknown occurrences and their associated contexts. Preliminary results from experimenting with the dataset show that it can be utilized to improve various NLP tasks and enhance processing efficiency.
