Many languages specify gender for nouns and adjust articles and adjectives accordingly, leading to a connection between the gender of nouns. NLP systems capitalize on this link for automated gender labeling, although the underlying reasoning is somewhat intuitive. Our investigation delves into how grammatical gender affects representation learning for nouns, focusing on the impact in languages that label nouns with a gender: we analyze the effect of gender on noun representations, evaluate the performance of state-of-the-art models, and assess fine-tuning options for gender classification. Our results reveal that representing all grammatical attributes, including number and gender, enhances the accuracy of gender classification models. Our findings and accompanying code can be accessed at \cite{our-paper}.

We demonstrate that if a non-compact, hyperbolic manifold has a non-trivial charm, then its fundamental group must be either a cusp-group or a cusp-norm one. Moreover, our findings extend the work by Biao Ding, Yong Ge, Jin Song and Qiong Ling who previously established a similar result for special metric manifolds, and also generalize the previous outcome by C. Bettoli who proved that having a non-trivial charm implies the finiteness of the manifold's isometry group.

This study focuses on developing a technique for locating objects within an image, a task that is more complex and extends beyond the ability of zero-shot, class-level estimation. Zero-shot object localization aims to determine the class and location of an object within an image without any additional data on the object's original position. To achieve this, we introduce the concept of 'anchors' - predefined boxes that serve as a basis for calculating the object's class and spatial offset. Notably, the number of anchors per class should be optimized to balance accuracy and computational cost. Through analysis, we establish that the optimal number of anchors relative to the class size follows an inverse proportion, and this insight can be utilized to find this optimal number by walking through all classes in a dataset. To address this issue, we developed an anchor selection method based on the dataset dictionary of COCO 2014 Challenge, and it is available at https://github.com/zeyoh/Zero-Shot-Object-Localization. Additionally, we provide demonstrations of zero-shot object localization using the DetectoShips dataset and the COCO 2014 dataset.

Traffic forecasting plays a crucial role in modern city operations, yet the current approaches, primarily designed for sparse areas with little data, are often incomplete for densely populated areas with temporal and spatial complexities. Most existing models, focusing on predicting short-term traffic, neglect the city's spatial-temporal correlations and use outdated data. As cities continue to expand, the initial data for densely populated areas is often sparse and irregularly distributed. To overcome these challenges, we developed a traffic forecasting system for extensively dense areas. This system incorporates a new type of data, called spatial-temporal traffic patterns, which can be extracted from spatially similar traffic data and assist in data augmentation. Our method identifies areas with similar traffic behaviors, using Gaussion Mixture Model and Gaussian Graphical Model, and then uses these patterns to make comprehensive predictions by incorporating temporal and spatial relationships within the city. Our method was tested on various datasets and demonstrated superior performance, especially in areas with sparse data.

This work introduces VACA, a social media platform for exploring variational graph-based machine learning models, including those for causal inference. As such, it serves as a complementary resource to Colab's causal learning tools, focusing on models like Structural Causal Models, Interventialism, Counterfactuals, and Causal Discovery. VACA enables users to generate variational graph-based models, visualize them using NetworkX, and assess model performance with evaluation metrics and tools. Furthermore, it incorporates a synthetic data generator and a COLAB-based VAE model, facilitating data creation and model training. In addition, VACA includes a collaborative interface for shared project access and seamless integration with Colab's platform.

Our recent commissioning of the Irish LOFAR's REALTA system has allowed for the transfer of real-time, 200 Tbit/s data to the Jodrell Bank Observatory, yielding initial findings comprising comprehensive spectral, polarisation, and interferometric data across a 0.0-1.0 GHz frequency band and 0 km to 1 km baseline length. 

A key outcome of this system has been the successful capture and near-instant analysis of a significant transient event on July 1st, 2021, namely the rapid peak of the 2021FI Aug event, a rare Type-IIn supernova, approximately 18.5 hours after the initial explosion sighting. 

The recorded data, incorporating 38,000 s integrations and 128 baseline lengths, was concurrently processed using both standard and AI-powered systems, the latter including UltraFast (UF) machine learning models, the former relying on traditional high-time resolution (THR) spectra, with the former exhibiting an average RMS noise level of 40 Jy at 250 MHz and the latter exhibiting an average RMS noise level of 50 Jy at 200 MHz.

Despite the similarity in noise levels, the UF models exhibited an average spectral line width of 10% w.r.t. the known thermal expansion of the source, a value 25% lesser than that of the traditional THR spectra, further indicating the potential of the UF models in studying the dynamics of various astrophysical objects, most notably supern

We suggest an innovative concept for light guidance and control, combining traditional metaphotonics with cutting-edge artificial intelligence technology. By employing an artificial intelligence-optimized light-manipulation scheme, we demonstrate the effective propagation of light through narrow channels and facilitate the development of novel, highly sensitive photonic devices that take advantage of the photonic nanomembrane's thinness. The artificial intelligence strategy is applied to a photonic nanomembran-based waveguide, with results showing significantly improved performance compared to previously proposed designs and more conventional waveguide structures.

This study significantly expands the size of the FilMTech dataset, presenting a more comprehensive view of the film industry's intricacies. Initially launched in 2019 with 349 films, the updated dataset now includes 1890 more entries, totaling 2389 films. To assess its precision, the new dataset was evaluated against a range of existing film dataset evaluations. Furthermore, the study delves into how utilizing attributes from a pre-existing film dataset can influence the projected box office revenue for upcoming films. To validate this, the research demonstrates how a machine learning model can forecast revenue by considering both new and existing film characteristics. By employing a regression model with variable selection, the results reveal that combining both new and existing features leads to improved box office revenue predictions for new films.

The integration of widespread distributed energy resources has given rise to a necessity for frequency regulation stabilizers. Initially, researchers explored the potential of inverter-based DERs to provide this function, but widespread adoption of auxiliary frequency regulation (AFR) has not been accompanied by a deep examination of its impact on voltage stability. This work aims to fill this knowledge gap by examining the voltage stability consequences of AFR. We begin by determining the conditions under which AFR can maintain the stability of the power system by analyzing the phase plane. Subsequently, we conduct a detailed analysis, taking into consideration the nonlinearity of the system, by means of numerical simulations, and finally, back our analytical findings with numerical evidence derived from actual power system matrices.

Cyber-physical networks of systems, featuring cognitive components, are becoming a promising research area, given that such systems inherently possess both physical and informational attributes. These multi-faceted systems can be found across various applications, including nature, agriculture, and engineering contexts. The complexity of their shared physical environment, along with the dynamic interactions among individual components, poses significant challenges to modeling and controlling these systems. This paper proposes a multi-layer cognitive network of systems, where each layer comprises autonomous entities that interact with their surroundings through both physical and informational interactions. The paper also explores a particular application of these networks in agricultural ecosystems, where it focuses on modeling cotton development as a cognitive system. Furthermore, this research discusses its far-reaching implications for designing and optimizing such complex systems and the potential realization of futuristic cognitive networks inspired by nature.

This study employs a novel method to simulate non-thermal processes in the external inverse Compton mechanism in various astrophysical contexts. Focusing on blazars, a well-established paradigm suggests that their high energy emissions result from the interaction between energetic electrons in the jet and ambient photons emitted by the jet's own electrons. This idea is theoretically supported by a mathematical model where a correlation exists between UV/soft X-ray flux and break energies in the jet's high energy spectrum. This model utilizes Monte-Carlo simulations based on a mathematical framework and addresses the challenges of non-thermal equilibrium in the jet. The simulations reveal that matching the observed high energy spectra of blazars, including their X-ray and gamma-ray components, is feasible using a specific distribution of electrons and photons within the jet. The simulated spectra exhibit a characteristic 'double-break' structure in the jet's high energy spectrum. The first break corresponds to a transition from synchrotron radiation to inverse Comptonization, with a second break corresponding to a transition within the IC mechanism from lower-energy photons within the jet. This is consistent with observed spectral energy distributions of certain blazars. Adjusting the simulations to include more realistic gradients in the jet's photon and magnetic field environments is also possible.

In this study, we investigate the extension of holomorphic functions and function sequences across complex surfaces and examine their compactness. We establish new criteria for extending holomorphic functions and function sequences to all dimensions, offering fresh, dimension-by-dimension theorems. We also explore the terrain geometry and show that these new conditions can be characterized by the geometric properties of level sets. We prove that functions with compact support in complex one-dimensional manifolds can be extended, but this is not the case for higher dimensions. We verify Convergence on Demand (CoD) for harmonic functions across all dimensions, validating CoD for monotone functions previously identified by the first author. Moreover, we demonstrate the CoD for a broader range of functions with positive or monotone sequences than initially proposed by the first author.

We investigate virtual detection in experiments with two-particle states having specific symmetry properties. The analysis focuses on initial states being either polarized or unpolarized, with various potential detections being either direct or indirect, and explicit formulas are given for probabilities of successful outcomes in all these scenarios. Particular emphasis is placed on hidden variable models for virtual detections where initial states are unpolarized, specifically in scenarios involving the Peres--Horne--Horne model.
Baryon creation through the quantization of a complex QCD string phase, exhibiting both twist fields and topological charges, is explored in detail.

The time it takes for seismic waves to travel from the surface to a lower layer, detected through helioseismology, is used to study the movement of mass along the Sun's equator and poles. By analyzing the delay in this time travel due to the Sun's equatorial bulge, scientists have found hints of mass transport in the Sun's interior. However, their new research finds that the equatorial and polar forces affecting the time travel delay are significantly different, leading to errors in interpreting the data. The team used the mock seismic data to test how the Equatorial Bulge Effect model's predictions changed with varying resolution and found that currents parallel to the Sun's equator contributed mainly to the seismic delay, while those running parallel to the poles had an opposite effect. As a result, the difference between these two types of currents was responsible for the observed discrepancy in the travel delay measurements. The new findings indicate that the mock seismic data's accuracy was sufficient to reveal the significance of parallel to the pole currents and their opposing effect on the Equatorial Bulge Effect model's predictions.

High-redshift sources of gravitational waves in the pulsar timing array frequency range can be found in the early universe, originating from the alignment of magnetic fields created by electrons and positrons. These cosmic strings, existing well before recombination, can produce graviational waves with a peak frequency ranging from $10^{-8}$ to $10^{-6}$ Hz. Our calculations predict that at the higher end of this range, a primordial magnetic monopole model is most likely to yield a detectable signal. Additionally, similar detectable signals may arise from the dynamical instability of cosmic domain walls under certain conditions. However, the possibility of observing such a signal does not significantly alter our current understanding of the universe, as the required primordial magnetic fields are consistent with the existing cosmological model.

Achieving high-quality compression of light fields remains a difficult task due to their unique properties with four degrees of freedom. Current approaches primarily rely on existing frameworks for single-image and video compression. In contrast, we present a more suitable framework tailored for light field compression by leveraging insights from established methods and statistical analysis of light field datasets. Our framework encompasses three key components: a disparity-sensitive light field model, a transformed tensor-blockized framework for reduced information representation, and an optimized processing order of sub-blocks within each tensor. These components enable the extraction of substantial geometrical information from baseline methods, resulting in improved overall performance. Our framework's effectiveness is validated through thorough evaluation of its components using comprehensive benchmarks in terms of reconstruction quality and compression efficiency.

A key issue in cross-language information retrieval involves finding a document's translation based on an user-supplied sentence in a source language. This retrieval model can be adapted to the parallel framework, where all pairs of a query sentence and a target document are simultaneously assessed, or to the interactive framework, where a retrieval model and a post-ranking model operate successively with the first identifying a small pool of candidates for the second. Despite the parallel framework's simplicity, it fails to capitalize on potential syntactic relationships between a query sentence and a target document. On the other hand, the interactive framework achieves superior results but at the expense of extra computational resources. This article explores a compromise strategy, known as semi-interactive IR, that allows the incorporation of key features from both IR approaches while minimizing computational costs. An experimental examination of several retrieval models demonstrates the semi-interactive IR strategy's effectiveness. Moreover, a comparative evaluation demonstrates the superiority of the parallel IR strategy when employed in a setting with limited computational resources compared to other IR strategies, such as query translation and the transference of neural cross-attention weights.

In the context of low-and-middle-income countries, survey designers face challenges associated with a limited number of households per cluster, making it essential to account for the variability between regions when conducting small-region estimates. However, standard design-focused methods are not optimized for this goal, as they primarily focus on the variability within clusters. This is in contrast to the potential benefits of a model-focused approach that can incorporate external information and account for the between-region variability. This study aims to contribute to the understanding of a critical issue in low-and-middle-income countries by exploring small-region estimation methods and their applications. Key contributions of this paper involve: (1) a novel simulation model that mimics survey data from a two-level mixed effects model, mirroring real-world survey practices in many low-and-middle-income countries; (2) a comparison of design- and model-focused small region estimation methods, including a random start GLS estimator and a novel semi-ABEC estimator, using the simulated data; (3) an exploration of the extensions to estimate linear regression coefficients and a brief discussion on applying small region estimation methods, including practical implications for survey analysts and designers, with a goal of informing surveys in similar settings.

We've found that utilizing a quantum memory engine can significantly reduce the randomness in wagering games based on the Kelly criterion. By using a quantum memory engine to continuously generate random -1 or 1 bits, which are instantly converted into classical bits, this setup outperforms its classical counterpart in reducing entropy throughout the probability distribution. Even with this quantum advantage, the reduced entropy follows the pattern established by the classical Kelly wagering model. As a result, the number of standard deviations away from the mean (concentration) of the distribution decreases over time, following the formula N(t) = 2^(-2bt), where b is the Kelly betting fraction and t is time.

Recently, two-dimensional superconducting MoSi$_2$N$_4$ and MoGe$_2$N$_4$ have been successfully synthesized and tested. Using the empirical Austin-Heaton model, we created a database that includes the band gaps of over 400 Mo, W, and Ti-based compounds with varying Si, Ge, Sn, P, As, and Bi compositions. From the calculated data, we predicted that many compounds would exhibit quasiparticle alignments near or below the critical alignment threshold of 0.24 eV, thereby supporting the existence of two-dimensional superconducting MoSi$_2$Z$_4$ and WSi$_2$Z$_4$ (Z = P, As). Furthermore, we discovered that the stacking-dependent excitations of charge carriers in these compounds would significantly decrease their energy cost, thereby contributing to their stable superconducting behavior. Consequently, we recommend further study and testing of potential superconductors, such as WSi$_2$Z$_4$ (Z = P, As).

We investigate the rare decay of $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^- $ at both the LHCb and a proposed $\tau$-collider, primarily focusing on these experiments for several reasons. Firstly, this experiment can test the theoretical prediction made by Poshladski et al. in 2017, suggesting that $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^- $ decay occurs via $SU(3)$-members of hadronic octets, thereby constraining a theory that causes CP and is mediated by adjoint SU(3) fields. Secondly, beyond standard model processes resulting in the mentioned decay are predicted to follow specific patterns, with one octet having a preferred alignment and an anti-octet assuming an anti-alignment, both of which can be verified at LHCb. Thirdly, a rare decay of the mentioned type can occur in the context of Pati-Salam model, with the baryon sector of this model experiencing significant tensions, thereby making a rare decay of the mentioned type a high-risk but manageable threat, thereby not being detectable at the mentioned LHCb limits but detectable at $\tau$-collider. Fourthly, a rare decay of the mentioned type can occur in the context of chiral gauge theory, with one of its many realizations being able to make a rare decay of the mentioned type a major threat, thereby not being detectable at LHCb but detectable

A new investigation into the protostar and surrounding protoplanetary disk structure begins with a core collapse, where a pre-existing cloud fragment undergoes a rapid, dynamical collapse. This is followed by a sequential, radiative shock formation. The $24$ models developed for this study, spanning from 1 to 20 solar masses, examine the disk evolution across a wide range of orbital distances and mass ratios between the star and surrounding disk. Key findings from this investigation include: (i) due to the disk's high concentration of angular momentum, it undergoes a complex rearrangement with multiple shock formations and reconfigurations before its eventual accretion onto the star; (ii) the disk's structure undergoes a sequence of evolution phases characterized by different levels of activity and finally achieves a stable, accretion-driven configuration; (iii) the star-disk interface exhibits a stable structure, supported by a clump shaped like a "V', where the pre-stellar nucleus clippings determine the extent of the star's convective envelope and surrounding disk's super-Keplerian layer, where mass accretion is concentrated and where the disk makes its transition from the outer regions; (iv) the disk's outer regions feature large gas and dust fractions, where large particles can grow, leading to significant formation potential. Overall, our investigation emphasizes the importance of accurately representing initial conditions for low-mass star formation models and the importance of the star-disk interface as a site for efficient

Characterizing the complex interactions between upper atmospheric particles and electromagnetic radiation is essential for understanding scenic effects, minimizing interference in telescope operations, and optimizing data processing. To this end, a two-part study employs both observational and computational approaches. Previous research involved collecting data on the intensity of horizontal sky radiation over specific wavelengths, and these findings are supplemented by analytical and numerical assessments of the impact of oxygen molecules and atoms on such radiation patterns. Notably, the results obtained from these analytical and observational methods align remarkably well, and we now use them to develop models of the scattering behavior of these atmospheric constituents.

This paper tackles a key problem in time series analysis: modeling complex temporal sequences with multiple correlated components that cannot be easily observed in real-life scenarios. Traditional models are often restrictive, ignoring the nuances of these temporal sequences or making unrealistic assumptions about their properties. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel approach based on a sparse, low-rank matrix decomposition model, which can efficiently handle high-dimensional data with low sample sizes and complex temporal relationships. By applying prior constraints to both the spatial and temporal dimensions, we can simultaneously identify patterns within the sequences and model their evolution over time. Building on a precise Bayesian model, we develop a approximate inference method using variational free-energy minimization, which yields surprisingly fast and efficient inference. Through comprehensive simulations and real-world case studies, we evaluate the proposed model's efficacy in multi-term time series analysis.

This note starts by proving that certain topological groups have dense subgroups within their continuous duals, before expanding on a related idea of Pontryagin duality to develop a new continuous reasoning framework. A key theorem is that every topological group with a certain level of continuity has a corresponding dual group with dense subgroups across every degree of continuity, and this leads to a dense network of subgroups in the relevant product space. Building on this result, a continuous reasoning methodology is proposed, and several examples are provided to demonstrate its underlying principles, including a complex number system. Furthermore, a central role is attributed to the concept of hypercompleteness, and various theorems are formulated to illustrate its significance, including a version of the Specker ideal theorem. Ultimately, the framework is used to establish a fully developed arithmetic, with results such as Fermat's Last Theorem.

The main goal of Federated Learning (FL) is to facilitate machine learning on user devices while ensuring the confidentiality of the data. However, the fact that FL's convergence relies on many participants raises questions, as releasing personal data is not always within the data owner's discretion. To tackle this issue, we aim to establish a framework that upholds individual data confidentiality throughout the FL process, even in scenarios where participants may not have control over their data. To achieve this objective, we explore the potential of utilizing a publicly available dataset for training, thereby granting data confidentiality to individual data contributors even in a shared learning environment. To address the challenges posed by such a approach, we will employ a legally compliant method of quantization to combine justice and differential confidentiality. Firstly, to address potential biases in the training data, we will apply quantized fair clustering (QFC) to group the training data into various sub-datasets and then use a publicly accessible dataset for training, ensuring that no single participant owns the training data. Secondly, to prevent unauthorized data leakage, we will employ differential confidentiality (DIF) to safeguard the training data owners' privacy. Notably, previous methods of quantization indistinguishable to the extent of an individual data record (QUIR) have overcome privacy threats during inference, however, they have failed to effectively address the question of record non-participation during inference, which is a concern we aim to address. To address these challenges, we will employ a legally compliant method of quantization

A proposed model of supersymmetry and a new $U(1)_X$ symmetry, introduced in the arXiv paper 1309.2895, is reviewed. We focus on a specific version of this model which is characterized by the presence of three Lepton-specific Higgs fields, the superpotential being $\omega W + \lambda \frac{|\omega|^2}{3},$ with $\omega$ a $U(1)_X$ broken field and the additional parameter $\lambda$. It has been shown that one of the Higgs fields acquires a vacuum expectation value of the order of the $Z$-Peccei-Quinn mass to break $U(1)_X$, thus providing a natural origin for the dark energy observed at present. It has also been found that both the dark energy density and the universe are decreasing at the present rate due to the effects of the right-handed neutrino dark zebra and the universe's current state. It has been found further that this model is characterized by the presence of a discrete $Z_3$ symmetry, thus prompting the investigation of the model's (non-)empirical, (non-)supersymmetric, and (non-)miraculous natures. The model's (non-)empirical, (non-)supersymmetric, and (non-)miraculous natures are investigated through the analysis of various particle mass spectra, thus confirming prior analyses. We look at how a network that includes an IRS-assisted wireless power transfer and experiences interference from other networks. To improve this network's performance, we develop an unconventional machine learning technique that doesn't need data examples, which allows the IRS to change its reflections in real-time. To begin, we create an artificial neural network model based on a mathematical concept that can be applied everywhere, called the multivariate Gaussian distribution's mean vector. By using this model, our algorithm generates artificial data that represents the input variables with the highest probability. To process this data, we develop a unique filter inspired by a mathematical concept that reduces noise, which effectively estimates the conditional mean of a network performance metric, such as throughput. This process is repeated using an optimization technique, which uses the estimated mean to calculate the conditional mean of the next iteration, allowing the IRS to change its reflections. Simulations show that this technique significantly improves the network's performance compared to other methods like Q-learning and reinforcement learning without data examples.

Historical and theoretical evidence has long suggested that certain nuclei exhibit octupole Wigner symmetry. Our study has confirmed the presence of this symmetry in the very weak beta decay of $^{186}$Hg, whose emission spectrum features a complex pattern of 106 distinct lines. By analyzing this spectrum, we have determined the half-life of this process and the total decay rate, as well as assigning absolute branching ratios to specific unique and double beta decay transitions. Furthermore, our investigation has yielded new information on the energies of several individual decay rates. In addition to this, we have developed a phenomenological model to describe the unique beta decay of this nucleus, whose results have led to the prediction of eight previously undetected transition lines. Many of these predictions align with those made by earlier studies.

We investigate a unified theory combining all interactions of a fermion with different quantum numbers within a single gauge group, which also contains a novel Z6-'Z2' symmetry. This theory's Z2 symmetry protects a massive majorana fermion, while the Z6-'Z2' symmetry influences its mass generation through a variant of the oblique correction mechanism. Furthermore, the same gauge group is found to permit a dark matter implementation of the pecci-quinn mechanism via one set of gauge bosons, while utilizing an 'accidental' Z2-protected vector-like doublet to a different subset of gauge bosons, without impacting either the dark matter or the fermion mass, due to the separate groups of gauge bosons being used. Additionally, the possibility of the fermion being identified as a higgsino in a two-component higgsino model is also considered.

The success of control algorithms using machine learning significantly depends on the quality of available data, and gathering an extensive dataset in a specific environment is often impractical or expensive for many real-world applications. In some cases, gathering relevant data is feasible, but doing so for all possible states and conditions is not possible. Our proposed method, called the One-Shot Multi-Objective Controller, overcomes these challenges by using a single exemplary demonstration to learn and achieve various objectives in diverse conditions. Even with limited data, our OOMO Controller can consistently deliver superior performance compared to leading machine learning control methods, as demonstrated by simulation results using a quad-copter in different environments. Moreover, our method allows for effortless adaptation to a range of applications without the need for additional data, as illustrated by its successful deployment in various conditions of an aerial robot.

ward relations play a key role in Toda conformal quantum field theories. 
The Toda theory based on the A_2 sector of the Toda system possesses a specific set of first-order differential operators whose relationship with the Toda characters involves the translation of the Toda characters into a system of equations for these operators. 
This paper derives an expression for the precesion of these equations, known as the Toda beta-deformation. 
The Toda characters get reinterpreted as special functions, specifically three-point Correlation functions in the Toda conformal quantum field theory. 
The Toda characters' general expression, known as the Toda tau-function, reveals itself as a product of quasi-determinants of the Toda beta-function. 
The Toda characters' specific realization, in terms of the Macdonald polynomials' ratio, results in a system of differential equations whose precision is characterized by the central invariants. 
The central invariants' specific form, in terms of the Hall-Littlewood function, unifies the theory to its finite and discrete versions. 
The Toda characters' specific realization, in terms of the central invariants, results in a system of meromorphic differential operators whose precision unifies the theory to its finite and discrete versions. 
The Toda characters' specific realization, in terms of the beta-functions, results in a system of operators whose precision generalizes the theory to its conformal quantum field theory based on the A_2 sector

We introduce Relation Adversarial Network (RelGAN), a novel approach designed to tackle a significant limitation of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) by leveraging massive amounts of unlabeled data to train effective node and graph classifiers. In contrast to existing methods that focus on optimizing neighborhood representations, RelGAN aims to improve the overall representation of graphs by enhancing its global context. Our proposal involves constructing a GNN-based classifier to maximize its differences from incorrectly labeled graphs, thereby forcing the model to utilize global graph structure information. This innovative method outperforms state-of-the-art methods on various benchmark datasets. Additionally, our solution addresses a long-standing problem in graph representation by developing a scalable and efficient approach to train effective node and graph classifiers on large, unlabeled datasets.

A novel approach to quantum key exchange, utilizing twin-field states, was introduced in a previous study. This method eliminates the need for synchronization but introduces an issue with noise reduction. This article examines a method to address this challenge. The proposed technique involves splitting the shared entangled state into two distinct sections, employing one for communication and another as a distortion indicator. By comparing the distortion indicator with an already exchanged classical message, the sender adjusts their transmission method. The receivers then combine their respective information, applying error correction techniques to obtain a shared key. The method's reliability, when two communication links are available, was demonstrated to be theta and omega, based on the general threat models proposed by Lo-Chau. A practical execution of this idea, utilizing linear optics and encoded qubits, is also discussed. The proposed method reduces the reliance on precise control of control qubits, simplifies the required equipment, and improves performance compared to traditional quantum key exchange methods.

In this paper, we establish a complete classification of multipliers for the Toeplitz algebras constructed within Fock and Bergman domains, utilizing reproducing kernel methods. We then derive various equivalent characterizations of multipliers by combining our work with previous research on bounded and meromorphic multipliers. We complete this study by identifying the bounded and compact spectra of these Toeplitz algebras.

In visual object instance recognition, one of the key challenges is associating objects in a scene with their corresponding semantic meanings. Lexicon-based methods leverage a dictionary of class terms to bridge this semantic gap and gain greater understanding of the scene. However, current methods primarily focus on coarse-grained object categories like 'dog' or 'car', whereas efforts to identify finer-grained classes such as 'terrier' or 'Hatchback' remain limited due to a shortage of high-quality annotations. We introduce a novel framework known as LIBAO, which combines a lexicon-based approach with pseudo-labeling to identify both coarse and fine-grained object classes without relying on cumbersome manual annotations. By incorporating this method, we also create two new datasets – PASCAL-LLOI and ImageNet-LLOI – that accommodate fine-grained class labels, thereby facilitating evaluation on previously unsolved tasks. Our approach sets new records for accuracy on PASCAL-LLOI and ImageNet-LLOI, outperforming baseline methods by a significant margin in both fine-grained and coarse-grained object classification tasks.

The region around Rho Ophiuchus is a prominent dark cloud in the process of dispersal within a larger molecular cloud complex, located at a distance of 125 parsecs from Earth. It is exposed to the impact of a nearby early B star, which in turn triggers star formation within the surrounding material. This interplay gives rise to various dynamic phenomena. High-resolution spectroscopic analysis of the star and its surrounding environment has helped in understanding how different gas components spatially distribute and their connection to both the star's radiation and the larger interstellar medium, which in turn is shaped by external factors such as a nearby high-speed outflow. This analysis has revealed that different gas components spatially distribute as follows: an outflow with an outflow rate of approximately five times 10 to the power of negative 2) solar masses per year, an outflow with outflow rate of approximately five times 10 to the power of negative 2) solar masses per year, a surrounding external stationary photo dissociation region, an ionized stationery region, an ionized outflow with a rate of approximately one times 10 to the power of negative 11) grams per year, an accretion rate of approximately two times 10 to the power of negative 7) solar masses per year, an accretion rate of approximately five times 10 to the power of negative 6) solar masses per year. This three-dimensional model helps in understanding the relationship between the different gas components

In the field of Natural Language Processing, Transformer models have achieved remarkable breakthroughs, surpassing traditional architectures like RNNs and LSTMs in many areas. This review provides an in-depth examination of the advancements and applications of Transformer-based models, covering their fundamental principles, adaptations, and pioneering works leading up to current developments. By analyzing the successes and limitations in multiple areas, such as language understanding and generation, machine translation, and text classification, this work identifies gaps and suggests future directions. Various applications of Transformer models are discussed, including their use in modeling visual data and structuring knowledge for tasks beyond language understanding. The challenges associated with these models are highlighted, and potential solutions proposed, including combining related tasks, using pre-training for strength augmentation, and addressing complexity issues for deployment. Finally, this review outlines promising areas of improvement, such as adapting these models to semi-supervised and few-shot learning scenarios, and achieving end-to-end deployment of these models on large-scale platforms.

The purpose of this study is to develop and introduce a mortality model based on factor models that incorporates both time-varying factor loadings and scores. We focus on the significant impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on mortality rates and aim to incorporate this event into our model. To achieve this goal, we incorporate a additional factor, the pandemic shock, which is linked to historical mortality levels and can be estimated in advance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our model using data from 52 cities across Europe, comparing its performance to established models such as Lee-Carter, Cairney, and models based on factor models with time-varying factor loadings. Our findings indicate that incorporating pandemic shocks leads to improved short- and long-term forecasting performance, especially during catastrophic events like the pandemic, and suggest that using time-constant factor loadings provides a suitable base for modeling complex phenomena like those observed during the pandemic.

Designing neural architectures is a pivotal yet still unresolved aspect of AI research. Due to its high stakes and time-consuming nature, comprehensive exploration of all possibilities is generally impractical. As a result, researchers must rely on sampling techniques to design architectures, which inevitably introduce uncertainty and uncertainties skew the results. Moreover, the impact of disruption is often overlooked in the evaluation of these sampling methods, which hinders the accuracy of the outcomes and confuses the direction of the improvements. To address this issue, we investigated the effect of disruption on neural architecture sampling by conducting an in-depth analysis of its occurrence, influence, and consequences. Based on our findings, we proposed an innovative transformation technique utilizing Style Tokens, which effectively minimizes disruption and significantly boosts the state-of-the-art sampling methods for designing architectures, particularly in finding top-performing models and reducing the gap with the current best achievements in architecture search.

Time series data analysis is a rapidly growing field with numerous applications in fields such as finance, sports, and music. However, the traditional approach to time series analysis, centered on forecasting and smoothing, neglects the intrinsic value of these data. A new method, attribute-based time series analysis, seeks to characterize a time series through its attributes, offering the potential to both derive new insights and improve forecasting. This study aims to introduce a novel method for attribute-based time series analysis and make it accessible to the R users community. Leveraging the theft R package, which implements various thefts (homologous empirical transfer of parameters and hypotheses), the paper provides an empirical case study on its capabilities.

Given a proper, geodesically complete CAT(0) space with an infinite
$\delta$-thin value set, we establish a lower bound on the
$\delta$-thin value norm in terms of the CAT(0) distance between the
chosen point and the set. We further demonstrate that the established
lower bound can be achieved by selecting an appropriate point within
the $\delta$-thin value system. Subsequently, we extract a subsequence
from the sequence of Alexandrov distances, and demonstrate that the
corresponding sequence of reparameterized distances converges to 0.
Notation and conventions: Throughout this analysis, the 1-parameter family
of reparameterized distances will be denoted by $d_\theta$, with
corresponding length-metrics given by $\ell_{\theta}$.

Translators play a vital role in assessing the reliability of human translators by evaluating their work. A new Bayesian method aims to achieve this by using a subset of available data. Unlike traditional evaluation processes that rely on qualitative feedback, this approach relies on a translator's entire body of work to determine their reliability. A key component of this proposed method is the "reliability scale", which measures a translator's consistency in using clear and concise language. Prior research has established a reliability scale with a proven effect on translation quality. 

The proposed method considers two factors: a translator's consistency in using the target language and the ease of understanding their translations. Translators working on samples of texts, such as news articles and software descriptions, allow the evaluation of their "reliability scale" using a statistical model. This model combines the translator's translation abilities and difficulties to form a distribution of their overall reliability scale. 

When new assessments become available, the translator's "reliability scale" is recalculated by combining it with their updated translation quality, which is then determined using the maximum likelihood estimation. This process is further refined with the inclusion of a normal distribution, representing the uncertainty of the "reliability scale" and translation difficulties. 

The method has been tested on two small datasets and shown to effectively update a translator's profile with new assessments, with the added bonus of estimating their "reliability scale" and translation difficulties. A comparison with a previous iterative method demonstrated that the new method

We demonstrate the existence of specific eigenchannels through which a scattered wave passes with minimal energy loss, and derive mathematical expressions to calculate the total energy absorbed by an object regardless of its orientation and position in space. These expressions simplify to a fundamental principle for three-dimensional scattering scenarios. Furthermore, we utilize these findings to create an algorithm for computing the total energy absorbed by an object placed within any given incident wave environment. The proposed method is a practical solution for calculating the total energy absorbed by an object scattered through any type of wave, present or incident.

We've shown that reducing the parameters of a fully connected neural network by trimming unimportant weights results in a smaller network with comparable performance to the original. This approach enables us to determine the triming margin: the number of weights that can be safely removed without affecting the model's accuracy. Furthermore, the reduced network is often a simpler, more interpretable model with more regularized characteristics. Notably, when we apply this trimming method to a convolutional neural network, the resulting model exhibits similarities with well-performing subsets of a neural network's connections, known as "lottery tickets." This suggests that the model's ability to yield a successful subset only under specific conditions is not unique to convolutional networks, as it can also be observed in fully connected networks.

This study examines the behavior of randomly generated thin ticket strings and their connection to the anticipated value of a lottery ticket, which is determined by the string's probability of winning as calculated by the ticket's coupon collector's problem. We analyze the ticket string's anticipated value and its fluctuations over numerous draws, aiming to identify optimal moments to purchase lottery tickets and effective strategies for doing so, with the example of Spain's national lottery (El Gordo de Navidad) used to illustrate our findings.

Our research focuses on capturing the intricate nature of spatially distributed electron-phonon coupling within and between valleys in 2D materials, specifically those with and without center of symmetry. We find that this interaction results in a particular phonon distribution which in turn significantly impacts valley dynamics. The earlier work on 2D electron-phonon coupling in a single valley is extended here, specifically to two valleys, which allows for the inclusion of two more mechanisms of electron-phonon coupling: deformation potential and polar mode interactions. The Visual Domain Adjustment (DA) contest at NeurIPS 2022 highlighted the difficulty of adjusting a style to match a reference dataset, as seen in the ubColor challenge where multiple, diverse colors need to be matched. We present ubColorUBD, an effective approach to tackle this problem, explaining why it outperformed other methods and how it achieved first place in the contest.

Maps of complex 3-D structures, like the surface of a sphere, are fundamental in biology, biology-inspired computing, and neuroscience. However, using 2-D plots like those employed in Principal Component Analysis to interpret high-dimensional complex data can be misleading due to rotation ambiguities when dealing with 3-D structures like the surface of a sphere. To rectify this issue, we introduce Virtual Multivariate Normalization for t-Distributed Stochastic Encoding (VMF-SNE), a novel encoding method derived from a spherical probability model. By leveraging the geometric properties of spheres, VMF-SNE is able to visualize 3-D structures in a more accurate and reliable manner without the presence of rotation ambiguities. Our research demonstrates that VMF-SNE outperforms previous methods like TriSNE by better preserving the structural characteristics of data sets, especially in its ability to recover nearby points and avoid edge cases in low-dimensional representations. Furthermore, VMF-SNE offers improved interpretability of neural connections in better-quality 1-D representations, revealing significant and distant neural contributions that are often difficult to distinguish as a result of long-range connections and noise in the data.

We investigate the properties of the Fermi polaron on the honeycomb lattice using diagrammatic Monte Carlo, focusing on the polaron mean field energy, the critical polaron density for phase separation, and the dynamics of the quasi-particle residue. Our results reveal that the lattice gives rise to complex intrachain and interchain interactions, resulting in a more substantial critical polaron density compared to the 3D and 2D cases. Furthermore, we observe a non-equivalent critical polaron density between the intrachain and interchain interactions due to the lattice structure. Our research demonstrates that the lattice significantly affects the polaron's spectral and dynamical properties, providing a possible route for experimental realization of the Fermi polaron in graphene and honeycomb superconductors.

Our research focuses on simulating quantum phenomena for distinct particle systems 
using a hybrid digital-analog quantum computing approach that integrates digital 
qubits and an analog channel. Digital qubits serve as hubs to represent fermionic 
systems, whereas the analog channel facilitates interactions and connections among 
these digital qubits. Crucially, this method allows us to represent complex 
interactions between fermions accurately without encountering issues related 
to fermionic anti-symmetry. Furthermore, this technique enables efficient modeling 
of fermionic systems in a more compact space compared to general systems, 
thanks to the application of Fermi operators. We demonstrate the effectiveness of 
our approach by simulating both the quantum annealing process for a system without 
coupling and the analog channel dynamics in a two-hoppfield model, observing exact 
results that conform to known solutions. Our simulations highlight the distinct 
characteristics of simulating quantum phenomena in fermionic systems.

Graph polynomial families like Piauer and Ikeda--Tomita exhibit intriguing properties, with their individual members connected by a clear transformation, but the overall structure remaining unclear. Conversely, the Lascoux polynomials demonstrate a cohesive pattern through exponential corrections, as revealed by a generating function. Similarly, the Lascoux polynomials can be reinterpreted as a specific case of generalized Hessenberg polynomials, which show an analogous pattern. We propose a function to capture these exponential corrections for various graph polynomial families, including the Ikeda--Tomita polynomials, by utilizing techniques from combinatorial mathematics and Laguerre bi-polynomials. Furthermore, our study of the Ikeda--Tomita polynomials leads to a discovery of a novel formula involving two variables, as well as a dual series expansion for Laguerre bi-polynomials.

We establish a connection between the 1-teichmüller space and a determined moduli space by identifying a determinant form that expresses the second symmetric power of the first Chow group of a genus g curve. This form, defined as a product over points of algebraic degree 2, matches a previously known expression from Borel's free Lie algebra. As a result, we obtain an explicit description of the 2-cocycle appearing in the Teichmüller space's transition form, which also relates to the 1-cochain representing the degree of the Veech arc in the 1-teichmüller space's orbit space.

As the global shift to remote work accelerates, companies are increasingly adopting distributed teams using Agile project management frameworks like Scrum. This transition to remote work brings up new difficulties for Scrum teams, prompting a crucial question: how can remote working influence the achievement of Scrum project goals? To investigate this impact, we've put together a comprehensive study combining quantitative and qualitative methods with real-world data collected from Scrum team members. Our exploration of remote working's effects aligns with existing research, offering a comprehensive view of its impact on Scrum project success. We've analyzed data from over 300 respondents across 9 countries via a quantitative survey, complemented by qualitative interviews involving 21 Scrum team members. Our study reveals the complex consequences of remote working on Scrum project success, often resulting in unpredictable, variable effects. We've identified a range of factors contributing to these impacts, including communication challenges, personal struggles like maintaining a work-life balance, increased stress levels, differences in cultural approaches to work, opportunities for flexibility and freedom, and a more efficient use of time. While some factors harm Scrum project success, others enhance it, highlighting various factors that can shape remote working experiences. To improve the success of Scrum projects in remote teams, we recommend managers and leaders address communication challenges head-on, implement effective data-sharing protocols, foster open relationships among team members, enable flexible work policies, and develop adaptable strategies for navigating remote working. The norm of a positive matrix is defined as the maximum row sum, and the Gau-Wu value of a matrix is its norm minus the trace. This study determined the Gau-Wu norm for all choose arrowhead matrices of size 4, and established relationships between these matrices and their multiplicative and irreducible properties.

Our research involves examining electron trajectories resulting from the decay of open-charm and open-barrion mesons, produced within a significant magnetic field and at high temperatures in central Pb-Pb collisions at a 5.02 TeV collision energy. By incorporating magnetic force into the Standard Model, we have derived an amended Dirac equation, which includes equations of motion to track both charge and spin changes in electrons under the influence of a strong magnetic field in a non-linear regime. Furthermore, we have employed magnetic field fluctuations to simulate the formation of quasi-particles, which undergo thermalization in the Quark-Gluon Plasma. By modeling this, we have tracked the development of electrons within a high-temperature plasma and then upon entering a hadronic phase, where we have accounted for fluctuations in magnetic field intensity and probability distribution. Subsequently, we have analyzed the obtained electron spectra and compared them with those observed in ALICE using a 20-30% central Pb-Pb collision dataset at a 5.02 TeV collision energy, while also examining the polarization and spatial movement of electrons within a non-uniform magnetic field in both the Quark-Gluon Plasma and hadronic phases.

Computationally extracting topological features from discrete, filtered datasets is a pressing need within data analysis. The weighted persistence diagrams generated through this process often present their results in a non-intuitive format with significant dimensions spanning across various scales of $\rho$ values, where $\rho$ denotes a predetermined threshold. The complexity of interpreting these diagrams increases in direct proportion to the size of the input data. To mitigate this issue, the proposal involves developing more concise and refined representation of persistence diagrams, specifically tailored for colored dataset analysis. The proposal draws inspiration from recent research highlighting the effectiveness of using $k$-nearest-neighbor distances to determine optimal $\rho$ values. To this end, the method uses color-based distances to determine a refined representation of persistence diagrams, thus circumventing the need to present entire scales of $\rho$ and instead focusing on the most informative $\rho$ values. The experimental evaluation includes two datasets: (i) an artificially created dataset with known topological features and (ii) a real-world dataset consisting of MRI images of brains with tumors, along with healthy brains. The results show that the proposed method yields more concise diagrams while capturing the overall structure of the data, including tumors in the MRI image analysis.

This work utilizes the strong law of large numbers and the extreme value theorem to determine the extreme generalized degrees of freedom (GDoF) differences between binary and optimally controlled power management schemes for interference networks with multiple users. Calculating the average GDoF differences for each network size $K$, we find that the absolute difference in GDoF is affected by a $\Theta(1/\sqrt{K})$ factor, thus proving that the extra GDoF from optimal management for any interference network with $K \geq 2$ users is positive but diminishing with increasing $K$. We further demonstrate that for networks with $K$ users and any channel gain distribution, the resulting GDoF loss for binary power management can be approximated by the expression $K - 2\sum_{i=2}^{K \lceil \sqrt{2} \rceil} \ln \frac{\ln i}{\ln \sqrt{2}}$. Moreover, we show that the previously proposed bound based on a Gaussian interference network as a benchmark is tight for networks with $K$ users and any channel gain distribution, yielding a GDoF value of $K$. Finally, we extend our findings from networks with $K$ users and any channel gain distribution to multi-hop interference networks with $L \geq 2$ jumps and derive similar results for their GDoF analysis.

Auditing is a foundational aspect of data analysis, ensuring the data accuracy meets specific criteria it's supposed to serve. This research focuses on developing a versatile classification system for auditing data. The proposed solution utilizes formal concept analysis to create conceptual classes, and then applies Dempster-Shafer theory to address the data labeling process, including instances where there are no labels, some data points are missing, and there are conflicting labels. The introduced approach also handles uncertainty by calculating the probabilities of different labels. Furthermore, this study explores the applicability of MIQP optimization for determining the most likely label, given a given state of data points. The proposed method's efficiency was evaluated using HDI datasets, and compared to other existing approaches. The experimental results demonstrate that this solution achieves promising performance.

In the context of continuum mechanics, the method of fundamental solutions is a mesh-free and time-efficient approach for solving partial differential equations. Researchers, including Strauss in the 2010s, introduced several variants of this method. One of the most notable adaptations is the generalized meshless method, which incorporates a non-uniform fundamental solution to support a wider range of nonhomogeneous jump conditions. Notably, this variant includes the original meshless method as a subset, making it a more extensively applicable technique. This study compares the meshless method, the extended point source method, and the generalized meshless method, highlighting their distinctions and similarities. Further analysis involves an in-depth review of these methods' convergence, emphasizing the significance of using properly designed source distributions in practical applications to ensure solution convergence. Additionally, some numerical examples demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods in solving PDEs with nonhomogeneous jump conditions.

We find relationships for transformations between canonical momentum and position, as well as canonical momentum and time, taking into account a generalized uncertainty principle. This investigation establishes new relationships between canonical momentum and position, as well as canonical momentum and time, in both Galilean and special relativistic frameworks. In the galilean framework, our analysis leads to the discovery of a power transformation, while the relativistic framework yields a logarythmically linear transformation. We further observe that in the relativistic framework, a shift in momentum by $\Delta p_0$ leads to a corresponding increase in time $t$ by $\Delta t_0 /2 + (\Delta t_0^2/(4t_0^2)+\Delta p_0^2/(4p_0^3))$. Our study provides explicit expressions for the new positions and times in terms of the original and the corresponding canonical momentum and position, as well as canonical momentum and time, taking into account a generalized uncertainty principle.

When working on multiple tasks simultaneously, switching between tasks can significantly increase overall computation time. Many real-world applications, such as image editing and web development, benefit from using shared computation where executing a new task can reuse results from previous tasks. Current online scheduling algorithms for managing multiple tasks in the presence of shared computation often focus on minimizing the total computation time and information acquisition costs separately. In contrast, we have developed a new online scheduling algorithm that simultaneously accounts for both computation and information costs. Our proposed algorithm is shown to achieve a 4-5 times faster running times compared to previous state-of-the-art scheduling algorithms for both single-server and multi-server settings. Additionally, we have demonstrated that, in many practical scenarios, our new algorithm is likely to perform near-optimal when the communication costs are comparable to the computation costs and the total number of tasks is relatively small. Our results highlight the effectiveness of our algorithm as it provides a more unified framework for managing computation and communication costs in complex online multitasking systems.

This research project involves creating a mathematical model and simulation for a one-legged jumping system that moves across a yielding surface. Our main objectives in this study are to demonstrate the effectiveness of a validated reduced central mass model in predicting the movement of a one-legged jumper moving across a flat surface. Additionally, we are investigating the possibilities of extending existing control theories for one-legged jumping on an inert surface to control a jumper moving across a yielding surface. To achieve this, we are exploring strategies to maintain a specified posture in the jumper and achieve control using inclination adjustments. We have conducted simulations using the Hopper3 robot from Harvard Robotics to test these concepts.

In the context of IoT multi-hop mesh networks, where nodes retransmit packets to enable connectivity for their peers, we're studying the process of software upgrades within these networks. A new package needs to be installed on a few selected nodes, called the'seed nodes,' along with their descendants, to optimize network performance, as introducing changes on these nodes allows better packet forwarding. This concept is being tested with real-world mesh networks in various environments, including urban areas, by evaluating the time it takes for software upgrades, its success rate, and how it affects the network's overall size. Our experiments show that the time it takes for software upgrades on mesh networks is significantly longer than in flat networks. Furthermore, we found that the mesh network's scale and the percentage of seed nodes influence the upgrade duration, with the time it takes for upgrades increasing exponentially as these factors change. By comparing our results to theoretical models, we discovered that the time it takes for upgrades on mesh networks can be predicted using an accurate model that considers the network's structure. Contrary to expectations, the work presented here is the first extensive real-world evaluation of software upgrades in IoT mesh networks, addressing an issue of dependency packages present in software upgrades, as the process involves complex interactions between nodes.

We examine the multifractal nature of entanglement within one-dimensional, non-generating random spin-1/2 chains of length L, transitioning from ergodic to localized phases. We investigate how multifractal properties change as L varies and the system approaches criticality, as well as the role of symmetry in these changes, observing no'multifractal gap' in critical regions for symmetric interactions. The emergence and disappearance of complex multifractal behavior in both critical and non-localized regimes correlates with the shift from ergodic to localized phases, where the degree of fractalization reaches its maximum at the upper critical disorder value. Notably, the multifractal spectrum does not follow a typical logarithmic pattern across the system's entire phase diagram, unlike the'multifractal gap' in critical regions. Instead, the logarithmic leading exponent varies in a non-linear fashion with disorder, reaching its maximum at the upper critical disorder value. This result has significant implications for the use of analytical tools rooted in a fractal structure in the study of complex many-body systems.

This paper introduces a pioneering research contribution in the area of Data
Interactive Exploration (DIE) for a new scenario where there are numerous
targets within the dataset. In this scenario, the algorithm starts with a
dataset partitioning that initially yields one relevant result and many
irrelevant ones, and then obtains new data samples by questioning the oracle
while considering a time expenditure constraint. Next, it takes the acquired
samples as the focus of attention within an expanded dataset partitioning,
ultimately aiming to refine the initial relevant results and minimize the
number of irrelevant results. Furthermore, the study proposes a novel
evaluation method for assessing search algorithms' effectiveness and introduces
a benchmark suite of synthetic datasets that facilitate research on this new
DIE challenge. By applying the well-established MaxMin Loss First strategy,
the evaluation demonstrates its ability to attain superior outcomes in terms of
both the cost and performance metrics.

The success of quantum machines as multi-class image classifiers is to be proven 
through an ongoing experiment where they will be presented with images 
containing objects from multiple classes, as well as with images created to 
deceive them, until such time as the validation of the results is required.

We establish a lower bound for the $n$-th Steklov eigenvalue of a domain that approximately aligns with a sphere, with its boundary featuring $n$ evenly spaced holes. Additionally, this lower bound matches the known lower bound for spherical domains exactly.

When businesses or systems don't operate as expected, it can lead to difficulties and losses. To prevent such issues, it's essential to ensure that real-world data matches the predicted behavior, based on simulations or models. We've developed a new approach for checking if actual data adheres to the expected behavior by using alignments, which identify and explain deviations from expected traces. Our method includes a general scheme for checking conformance, along with a new approach using prefix alignments that demonstrates better performance compared to existing methods, especially for reducing false alarms. We've also discussed how our results can be utilized to further study the properties of such systems or find their optimal settings.

Radio propagation modeling plays a vital role in evaluating the performance of future wireless systems. This work presents a novel approach to estimate the attenuation of downlink co-site paths in homogeneous urban scenarios, leveraging a large openly-licensed dataset of measured radio signals. We compare two distinct neural architecture designs, focusing on their ability to predict signal attenuation and verify their validity through extensive cross-validation techniques. Our findings demonstrate the potential of these models in surpassing established propagation models under certain conditions, while highlighting the significance of data quality and quantity in neural-based approaches.

Our approach creates precise definitions for the behavior of agents within time-based environments and establishes a comprehensive framework combining agent semantics, planning, and validation. By establishing a formal framework, we can design and analyze a validation method that rigorously verifies path completeness and ensures agent behavior conforms to the specified time constraints. The effectiveness of this methodology is demonstrated through the application of a fine-grained adversary model that incorporates properties from game theory. The entire development process of our methodology was executed using the Interactive Theorem Prover (ITP), with the final derivation of our semantics and validation algorithm being manually verified and proven correct.

These assumptions, which vary widely in terms of the results they produce,
have yet to be systematically examined in-depth in the broader literature.
In this study, we take various assumptions for coal-based technologies and
apply them to established energy system models (REMIND/MESSAGE and hybrid
routines within Igcc), thereby generating a range of different energy
paths that arise from the same initial circumstances. Our analysis reveals
the underlying causes for these discrepancies, pinpointing the specific
assumptions that drive the models' differences.
Ultimately, our research highlights the necessity for greater transparency
regarding the assumptions made in energy system modeling and suggests a
number of potential areas for investigation. These areas include further
refining the parameters for low-grade heat use, assuming high-grade heat
will continually meet decreasing demand, exploring efficiency advancements,
and accounting for high-grade heat demand in scenarios with low-demand and
limited energy services as societal progress factors into consideration.

generation loses market share due to increased competition from other coal-
