In this paper, we perform an experiment to evaluate the accuracy of two summary qualification assessments and how they compare to incorporating a qualification question that tests the task's skills. Our results show that using all four methods to filter workers leads to similar results, but using qualifications alone is not enough to ensure high-quality workers. Based on our findings, we offer guidance on setting up effective MTurk assignments.

Our proposed TS2-Net is a sophisticated retrieval framework for text-clips
that leverages the strengths of both text and clip models. We deviate from the
conventional approach of directly utilizing pre-trained models, instead
integrating token-level shift and selection mechanisms to refine final outputs.
Such token-level adaptations significantly enhance model resilience to token
ambiguity and token distribution imbalance. Experimental results confirm that our
token-level shift and selection methods significantly boost text-clip retrieval
performance across a range of challenging scenarios. Furthermore, our TS2-Net
achieves state-of-the-art retrieval performance on the largest available dataset
, outperforming other top models by substantial margins, up to 8.8% RoP@1.

We present an original flavor-changing interaction model, where a neutral current affects
the taste of flavors without altering the strong interaction legacy. This model can be
characterized by a new flavor-changing parameter, $\hat{b}_t$. As a result, our model
influences taste-changing transitions among the first and second generations of
quarks, and also allows for a relationship between taste-changing and flavor-changing
processes. Specifically, our research identifies novel taste-changing transitions among
s- to d-quarks and u- to d-quarks in addition to the previously known s -> d transition.
Moreover, theoretical predictions for naive dimension-five, weak eigenstate transitions
s -> d with a quark mass of approximately 1.25 GeV are provided along with constraints
derived from existing data and future projections from the future Belle II experiments. 
Lastly, our research explores how this model can be validated through taste-changing
transitions in top quarks and combines theoretical expectations with available Higgs
production data from the CMS and ATLAS experiments along with anticipated results
from forthcoming high-energy colliders.

This research introduces and examines a novel type of random graph, referred to as \emph{asymmetric oriented hybrid random graph}, which integrates directed preferential attachment with directed degree-corrected hybrid graphs. Specifically, new incoming vertices affiliate with existing vertices in proportion to their outcoming connection counts, yet prevent self-loops. Simulated statistical properties of this new family of random graphs align with theoretical forecasts, indicating that they closely resemble large-scale real networks in both structure and dimensionality. Additionally, it has been observed that this hybrid family of random graphs effectively combines the beneficial characteristics of directed degree-corrected hybrid graphs and directed preferential attachment graphs.

The growth of wireless communication systems has led to increased interference from unauthorized devices and electromagnetic radiation, which in turn poses risks to equipment and human health. Therefore, monitoring and detecting these wireless disturbances are essential, particularly in sensitive environments. This research focuses on developing a multi-faceted disturbance detection system using Convolutional Neural Networks. Our approach involves two key components: a Convolutional Neural Network that learns the spatial features of wireless signals, thereby identifying detection boundaries and patterns within time-series data; and a Transformer model that utilizes the insights gained from the Convolutional Neural Network to generate predictive models for various wireless disturbance types across multiple networks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through experimental analysis of multiple wireless signals, showcasing its ability to accurately locate signal patterns and outperform baseline random forest models by at least 76% in terms of accuracy.

Using the numerical scheme in the context of Som-Raychaudhuri cosmic string spacetime, 
the investigators examine the impact of cosmic string on the properties of particles with both spin and charge. 
By solving and analyzing a nonlinear Klein-Gordon equation with an attractive self-action, wave function localization, and an explicit potential, 
the researchers investigate the role of cosmic string in particle interactions with an emphasis on energy states. 
Their findings reveal how cosmic string influences the spectral and dispersion profiles of particles with both spin and charge, 
as well as the interplay between these particles' physical properties. 
In particular, the investigators discover certain energy-state patterns in odd and even modes, 
which can be attributed to spin and charge relationships. 
Moreover, the locations and multiplicities of these energy states demonstrate discrete spacing, 
which can be understood as a form of band-gap effects resulting from particle interactions with both cosmic string and charge. 
Finally, by achieving full localization through wave function, the investigators demonstrate the feasibility of particle creation and annihilation within the confines of cosmic string spacetime, 
which has significant implications for related phenomena in quantum cosmology and particle physics.

We're investigating a fundamental issue within the field of ergodic theory, specifically the theory of measure algebra generated by ergodic measures. Our research focuses on ergodic measure-algebras $(M,\mu)$, where $(X,\mu)$, an ergodic system, serves as the foundation. Our primary goal is to identify whether every such ergodic measure-algebra shares a key characteristic with the majority of ergodic measure-preserving systems, namely, ergodicity. To this end, we define a locally ergodic measure-algebra and establish that it possesses ergodicity. Moreover, we delve into the underlying reasons for the occurrence of the locally ergodic property and explore the broader implications of this phenomenon. Additionally, we investigate how the properties of ergodicity and locally ergodicity intersect with other established principles, such as Cohen-Kopf lifting, in the context of ergodic measure-algebras.

This study introduces a novel observable in Deep-Inelastic Scattering with a Nuclear Target, specifically derived from the recoil proton's polarization, which can be measured in experiments at a level of detail not possible with observable momentum distributions alone. Our analysis via quasi-elastic ep scattering focuses on its construction, distinct characteristics, feasibility on current experimental equipment, and the potential for enhancement with the PRC project at Jefferson Lab.

Artificial Intelligence has become an integral part of everyday life, encompassing numerous sectors such as industry, medicine, transportation, and education. Despite its vast applications, the concept of Artificial Intelligence remains shrouded in ambiguity. Within the context of this study, a distinctive model is proposed, termed Enhanced Artificial Intelligence (EAI), aiming to bridge the gap between theoretical computer science and practical AI practices. A novel aspect of EAI is its potential to be quantitatively evaluated through the creation of a virtual AI agent, facilitating simulation-based assessments of intelligent behaviors within virtual environments. Furthermore, EAI's benefits extend to fields such as Natural Language Understanding, computer vision, sound profiling, and automated diagnostic services, among others. To substantiate EAI's applicability and versatility, eight case studies are presented, highlighting various applications and benefits in different domains.

Our study explores how quantum fluid behavior in a complex lattice changes with temperature for a specific type of bosons interacting with spin-orbit coupling and neighboring interactions. We used the density-matrix renormalization group method to simulate this system's thermal properties, particularly its phase diagram, near the critical point of superfluidity. Upon increasing temperature, this system exhibits shifts in its phase transitions, where the critical exponent changes from 0.67 to 1 for two bosons interacting with the highest order coupling strength considered. However, the presence of further-neighbor interactions tends to reduce thermal shifts by increasing the critical temperature. In contrast, thermal shifts are expected to decrease with the number of interacting bosons, according to our predictions, where the critical temperature is inversely proportional to the boson density for two bosons interacting with the highest order coupling strength considered. Furthermore, our predictions show that thermal shifts in this system can be reduced by manipulating the spin-orbit interaction strength, which affects the system's symmetry and phase transitions.

Research into the properties of interlinked and knotted molecular structures has seen significant advancement in recent years. When describing these molecular knots and links using a mathematical technique known as graph theory, which expresses them as groups of interconnected elements, different types of intermolecular relationships are represented as distinct operation chains acting within the molecular structure's underlying space. The complexity of these mathematical expressions is directly related to their level of compactness. By examining the various levels of compactness, this study aims to explore the inherent hierarchical nature of these knotted molecular structures and to establish a systematic approach to decomposing these mathematical expressions into their fundamental components. We begin by applying a novel method of graph decomposition, based on the concept of splitting groups logically and efficiently, to identify and understand the underlying cause of these complex mathematical hierarchies. This cause lies in the distinct patterns of intermolecular linkage present within individual molecules. These relationships are modeled as four-dimensional spatial connections between molecules, even in cases where they do not physically interact. The significance of these observed patterns lies in the fact that they also exist across a broader range of complex organic compounds, not just isolated molecules. By studying the mathematical expressions of these molecular structures, we gain valuable insights into their molecular patterns and relationships, and this research has the potential to be expanded into a much broader field of applications.

Building on our prior work, we explore AdS/CFT correspondence in reduced spatial dimensions. By adhering to previously established principles and methods, we investigate a significant case study based on Type IIA AdS/CFT. The resulting findings not only enhance our understanding of existing concepts but also provide novel insights into this complex theoretical framework. In particular, we grapple with the challenge of its apparent universalization at low energy levels and, as might be anticipated, we identify some discordant notes within this theoretical framework.

Simplifying complex mathematical functions can often provide deeper insights, but reducing the complexity of a Gaussian Process prior, which underpins a Bayesian model, can be challenging. Established techniques for creating Gaussian Process kernels are frequently ad-hoc and lack a fundamental theoretical basis. In an effort to establish a more universal approach, researchers have applied mathematical principles to derive new kernels from well-established models. By analyzing the characteristics of these kernels, the authors have developed a method to create Gaussian Process models with improved conceptual clarity and transferability to related problems. This framework encompasses widely used kernels, such as the squared-exponential kernel, the matrix-valued kernel, the low-rank kernel, and the kernel representing a non-Gaussian random field. The authors' approach involves reducing Gaussian Process observation equations to a minimum of two non-linear equations using approximation theory, providing a framework for analyzing kernel characteristics and evaluating their effectiveness.

This study examines strategies to reduce beam-induced background noise in future high-energy muon colliders. It focuses on utilizing fully integrated, very high resolution Landau distributions to model the emitted muons and their effects on collider design, particularly regarding plosecond time-scale beam-induced background noise. Various potential noise alleviation techniques are discussed, along with their relevance to collider design parameters. Finally, this work explores the feasibility of achieving acceptable levels of background noise via enhanced Landau distribution modeling.

Neural networks' inherent ability to learn and adapt is fostered by their
flexible, differentiable design. However, traditional computing frameworks often
struggle to efficiently process data with inherent sparseness, typically found in
images, graphs, and sequential data. Overcoming this challenge and promoting
sparseness within models can significantly reduce computation time and reduce the
amount of data that needs to be stored. We introduce a novel approach to
incorporate sparsity into neural networks by drawing from transport theory and
proposing differentiable models that can efficiently represent various forms of
sparseness. This innovative method, Spartan, enables neural networks to learn from
reduced data and store more efficiently on equipment with limited storage and
capacity. Spartan's potential is showcased through experiments on graph, vision, and
language tasks, where it achieves state-of-the-art performance with substantially
reduced parameters and data.

According to quantum mechanical principles, certain spin configurations of particles cannot exist simultaneously due to the accompanying phase obstruction, as dictated by the spinor wave function's global gravitational anomaly. While this phenomenon typically manifests in extremely correlated systems, it is possible for it to occur in less correlated systems under specific conditions. Our study examines this situation in a dilute Bose fluid near its critical point of phase transition from a superfluid to normal fluid state. The analysis reveals a distinct separation between the critical behavior of the phase obstruction and the critical exponents of the second-order phase transition transition in the Bose fluid.

Previous studies have identified "code smell" as a indicator of poor design, but the extent to which programmers consider it a valid detection method is unclear. We carried out an empirical study among active Java developers to explore their perceptions of using "test smells" as a means of identifying issues in their code. We provided 32 programmers with 28 short Java code snippets, including 8 with test smells and 20 without, and asked to indicate the likelihood of these codes requiring refactoring. Our results show that programmers are somewhat effective at identifying test smells, but are less successful at distinguishing between normal code and code that simply needs further refinement, suggesting that test smells are only a somewhat reliable indicator of areas for improvement. Furthermore, our study reveals that programmers consider certain test smells more significant than others, and that the likelihood of perceiving a smell as serious correlates with the extent to which it breaches coding conventions rather than design principles.

This paper investigates the resolution of variational inequalities that incorporate a non-differentiable, integrated mapping, with applications to problems with obstacles that involve pseudo-monotone, non-convex functions. It establishes semicontinuity properties for the integrated mapping, demonstrating its applicability in a sweeping process with an integrated force. The findings are then extended to quasi-static problems with integral forces. Additionally, aiga-hama and aiga-hama consider two instances of evolutionary variants, with the former leading to the study of differential inclusions with integrated forces, while the latter examines a situation similar to Siguerdid's integro-differential inclusion. The ordered halving method is proposed as an iterative solution technique for the evolutionary problems, with local stability being analyzed for the generalized sweeping problem and various other results derived in the paper.

We introduce a novel Monte Carlo event generator, specifically designed for 
lepton collider experiments, which efficiently simulates the creation of 
lepton and quark pairs, even accounting for lengthy branching ratios. By 
incorporating Monte Carlo methods, we accurately model the weak decay processes 
of heavy particles like Z bosons and top quarks, taking into consideration 
the inherent uncertainties of these decay pathways. In addition to its core 
functions, our event generator offers a range of useful features, such as 
realistic statistical distributions for heavy particle lifetimes and spatial 
distributions within beams. Further details and simulations are presented in 
this paper.

Measuring inter-beat interval data from unattended individuals can provide essential health indicators, such as stress levels and cardiovascular risk. This research targets improving estimates of inter-beat interval data derived from accelerometer and photoplethysmography signals, using raw data from wearable devices. We propose a novel approach, incorporating the Tiramisu framework, to enhance signal processing and enforcement of a constraint on inter-beat interval variations. Experimental results reveal that our method surpasses competing techniques, such as those relying on heart rate variability, and provides highly accurate estimates of inter-beat interval.

The tensor singular value factorization is a matrix decomposition with widespread applications in various fields, including data compression, approximation, and prediction. It consists of three components: a low-rank tensor, a singular value tensor, and two component tensors that multiply with the former to produce the original input tensor. The singular values in the tensor determine the rank of the low-rank tensor, which can be identified by finding the point at which the trailing singular values begin to disappear. Since high-rank structures in data often signify meaningful connections, accurately determining the tensor's rank is essential. As the computational cost of classical methods increases exponentially with the tensor's rank, they become impractical for large datasets. In the absence of specialized hardware, such as GPU accelerators, further challenges arise from the computational demands of recent deep learning solutions. This study presents a flexible stochastic algorithm for computing the tensor singular value factorization, allowing for the use of arbitrary numbers of passes, even on single-threaded environments. The proposed algorithm also provides an efficient means of estimating the tensor's rank through random projections, which takes advantage of the additional available passes. The efficiency of the proposed algorithm is demonstrated by experimental comparisons of its runtime, accuracy, memory usage, and adaptability with the number of passes, as well as its ability to estimate the tensor's rank using variable passes.

Real-world networks often exhibit dynamic properties, such as new connections forming and others dissolving, either periodically or indefinitely. Research in network embedding, which involves converting these complex graphs into meaningful representations for machines, has largely focused on static graphs. However, several prominent algorithms weren't designed to handle growing networks by incorporating new nodes and edges over time. To address this limitation, we evaluated various existing graph embedding techniques using a scaled version of a benchmark dataset, mimicking an evolving network by incrementally adding new nodes and edges to static networks. Our experiments revealed that some benchmark algorithms performed poorly in this scenario, while others showed significant improvements by leveraging new edges to refine node representations. Ultimately, we proposed a new framework for embedding evolving graphs, and our empirical results confirmed that our approach surpassed several baseline methods.

A theoretical study aimed to identify the $^7$H ground state, with researchers suggesting that this $^7$H state might be a resonance of $^3$H attached to 4 neutrons. To test this hypothesis, a $^3$H + 4n continuum was constructed and coupled to the $^7$H bound state, with the resulting results indicating that this $^7$H ground state resonates at 4.8 MeV above the $^3$H + 4n threshold. Furthermore, analyses using SU(3) quark symmetry suggested that this $^7$H resonant state would be of D-wave nature. Additionally, as a reference point, similar approaches were applied to the $^5$H isomer, with results confirming that it remains stably bound at 11.1 MeV above its $^3$H + 2n threshold.

Research into the Nirenberg problem with a semilinear equation has concentrated on the maximal rigidity of this type of problem. A previous study, 'Maximal Rigidity of the Nirenberg Problem with a Semilinear Equation', demonstrated the maximal rigidity of this type of problem when occurring in a bounded domain of a Euclidean space, using blow-up solutions. This article employs a similar approach to investigate the Nirenberg issue on the boundaries of half spheres.

This research introduces a novel learning method, called SDORep, which uses the Sinkhorn distance to acquire a deep optimal representation from data. Unlike other distance metrics, the Sinkhorn distance has been proven to be more favorable for various learning tasks due to its improved robustness. However, implementing the Sinkhorn distance in deep learning models has been complicated due to its computationally intensive nature. To overcome this limitation, we developed a scalable framework based on PyTorch to efficiently train models using the Sinkhorn distance. As a result, our proposed framework enables the training of robust deep learning models that outperform others on multiple datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR10, and SVHN, in terms of various evaluation metrics.

In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, many cities and regions in England established their own contact tracing efforts in 2020.  These individual efforts were integrated into a national contact tracing program by the National Health Service, operating under the NHS Test and Triage system.  Our study assessed the performance of eight regional contact tracing initiatives and their impact on the pandemic's progression, considering the inherent trade-offs between contact tracing efforts and economic restrictions.  Through the use of mathematical models, specifically individual-based and deterministic models, we analyzed available data to evaluate several metrics associated with contact tracing operations, including the quality of test facilities, collaboration with the NHS Test and Talaris, and the resulting contact tracing efficiency.  Our findings revealed that regional initiatives contributed substantially to the national contact tracing effort, with some cities accounting for up to 20% of all traced contacts.  However, the variability in data quality from these regional initiatives could result in a four-fold disparity in estimated infection numbers as predicted by our models.  Additionally, our research indicated that the achievement of a contact tracing efficiency of 70%, a goal of the NHS Test and Talaris, requires the efforts of both the NHS Test and Talaris and the regional initiatives.  Ultimately, our mathematical analysis quantifies the influence of regional collaboration on the effectiveness of the national contact tracing effort, providing valuable insights for future pandemic preparedness and response.

Determining the fundamental parameters of star clusters is a complex task that has been ongoing for nearly a century. Advances in recent years have still left gaps in the information sought by astronomers. With the release of the Gaia DR2 survey in 2016, new data have further refined our understanding of astronomical matters. This research presents the findings of a comprehensive study on the Melotte 72 star cluster, utilizing Gaia DR2 and selecting 352 cluster members. The results of this analysis provide the cluster's new radial distance as 3.2 plus or minus 0.5 kiloparsecs, and a revised estimate of its age as 1.0 plus or minus 0.25 gigayears, with a projected initial mass of stars around 20 solar masses, and a R24 index of 2.5, signifying it as a semi-distinct cluster. Additionally, this research confirms Melotte 72's binary ratio as around 0.55, and a mass segregation presence despite the cluster's relatively young age.

We examine Betti numbers in the context of sampling continuous random variables with a given mean and deviation from the mean. Previous work has established that Betti numbers based on geometric properties (like those resulting from random Voronoi patterns or sectioning half-spaces) are generally decreasing. In this study, we consider the impact of a different probabilistic model on Betti numbers in a space defined by a finite number of linear equations with random coefficients. Our analysis, which involves the coefficients being independently generated according to a normal distribution), relies on using'regular patterns' to define regions in this space. Our results, uniquely derived for each domain type, show how the patterns of change in Betti numbers differ based on variance from the mean and other factors. Additionally, we present complementary results regarding distributions of area, volume, and more, including how these traits relate to deviations from the mean. Our findings also extend to covering problems, which involve the number of smallest-sized spheres required to cover the resulting domains with diameters of $r$. Our results regarding patterns of change, deviation from the mean, and other aspects are established through precise mathematical expressions for the rates of change in these patterns.

Researchers have created numerous algorithms to guide robots' manipulation of objects using visual data, yet defining the robot's hand position and scaling is particularly challenging. To address this issue, this study proposes an innovative method, '3DIE', which learns hand positions and object sizes by analyzing two-dimensional images taken from an eye-in-hand camera. 3DIE utilizes a technique called Differentiable Renderer, employs a dataset of simulated image-object pairs, and trains a neural network that can calculate three-dimensional object dimensions and the hand's position necessary to create that image. Furthermore, we have developed an adaptation of this method, treating the hand's position as a relative measurement, which can be applied to real-world scenarios using standard two-dimensional image sensors without direct depth perception. Experiments using both simulated and actual world data reveal the efficacy and efficiency of this approach.

Reinforcement learning serves as a suitable model for numerous applications, but several factors complicate its use: first, developing a well-crafted reward structure is often laborious and requires significant reward design expertise; second, ensuring the reward function is transferable across settings can be difficult due to reward function instability and a lack of domain knowledge; third, the interaction cost associated with the exploration process often poses a substantial obstacle; and lastly, the quality of the learned policy may not always meet the desired standards. On the other hand, inverse reinforcement learning is capable of learning an optimal policy for a specified task by using a demonstrated expert trajectory, but it too has its limitations, particularly when it comes to the availability and quality of the expert trail. This research proposes a novel IRRL framework that aims to mitigate these challenges by learning a transferable, dynamic reward function, but one that is subject to changes in partial optimization. The proposed method not only manages to learning the dynamic reward function but also achieves a stable and consistent policy output through several experiments on multiple tasks.

The GAIA mission will create a detailed 3D map of the Milky Way region by tracking nearly a billion stars across the visible light spectrum and multiple photometric bands. As the most distant object that can be observed is about 520,000 light-years away, the mission will focus on understanding the Galaxy's structure and activity. By releasing preliminary data in 2016 and full data in 2018, the mission will utilize DR3 to release additional information in 2022 and DR5 to release information in 2023. DR3 and DR5 will utilize information from the 66,000-degree-angle sky to create 2D maps, but will then create 3D information through asteroseismology, as the diameter of the studied area will increase from 0.1 to 20 degrees. DR and DR5 will then release the results of the gravitational field's radial component and the magnetic field's B total, but will not create the magnetic field's B component maps due to the limitations of the current data. DR and DR5 will then release the results of the DR3 to study the velocity of the stars across the 520-degree-angle sky, but will not create the maps due to the limitations of the current data. The results will then create three new datasets including Gaia DR5 proper motion covariance, Gaia DR5 raw photometry, and the Gaia DR5 pseudo-counts list, as the mission will then create the 3D map of the

Vertex divider pairs serve as a crucial concept in graph structure theory and are closely related to tree-width. Every vertex divider pair includes two vertices connected by an edge within a tree-shaped subgraph structure. Research has focused on creating vertex divider pairs without the need for edge selection preprocessing, an important concept that has been thoroughly explored using various criteria. A key finding in this research involves identifying a subset of these pairs that can effectively capture the tree-width characteristic of a graph, and is efficiently processable on an O(n) space boundary. To the best knowledge available, this is the lowest space-effective measure achieved so far in graph structure theory. Additionally, this research further explores the maximum number of vertex divider pairs that can be created from a single graph, and demonstrates that this number can be quantified using the characteristic function of the n-exponent, an exponential function with base e.

Network analysis involves directing a limited number of links or connections between items in a set of data, which can be used to discover relationships, make predictions, and offer insights that cut across multiple fields. Researchers have proposed various approaches for setting the direction and strength of these connections. In this study, we explore three distinct applications for such connections: finding relationships within data by eliminating unessential information, understanding the data collectors' intentions, and making connections based on the data's value to the collectors. While these uses differ, they all rely on varying the connection strength between pairs of items. We identify three distinct requirements for these applications: (1) defining a family of effective networks that reflect specific properties, (2) ensuring that objects within subgroups exhibit similar relationships with other objects, and (3) ensuring that objects that don't belong in those subgroups don't show correlations with those they shouldn't be associated with. We discuss these needs in the context of synthetic and real-world examples, and provide a comprehensive evaluation of existing and proposed methods for setting the direction and strength of these connections.

We introduce an approach for evaluating the errors of machine learning models in their predictions for physical phenomena. Currently, researchers rely on an ad-hoc method to estimate a model's potential error. However, this unofficial method is not considered valid for confirming a model's accuracy in the physics community. Our proposed technique is based on a fundamental concept in experimentation called a "fuzzy boundary." We utilize this idea to establish a specific range of predicted values for a model's output, derived from an analysis of measurement uncertainties. By providing an estimate of potential errors, this method allows for the determination of a model's reliability. We demonstrate the application of this technique to a specific scenario - predicting the electromagnetic fields around a charged conductor using a physics-informed neural network. Although the technique is illustrated with a physics-informed neural network, it is not specific to this particular type of model and can be applied to other types of machine learning applications that involve physical phenomena.

Epidemiological research benefits from integrating geospatial methods, which enable the use of diverse geospatial data to identify and investigate patterns, correlations, and risks. Additionally, machine learning can be incorporated to enhance research by extracting, visualizing, and preprocessing data for analysis, offering a range of data analysis opportunities through interactive visualizations and machine learning-driven investigations. This study highlights the potential of combining geospatial and machine learning methods for research purposes by providing background information, presenting a framework for conducting epidemiological research, and showcasing their application in a real-world scenario. Specifically, we explain the importance of geospatial data analysis and machine learning in epidemiology, discuss their integration, and outline a research framework. Then, we identify and discuss challenges in epidemiological research, followed by a case study demonstrating how geospatial and machine learning methods were applied to investigate the spread of COVID-19 in a particular city (Porto Alegre, Brazil), resulting in the creation of a risk map for contracting the disease and identifying risk factors based on various urban activities. Finally, we identify areas for future research and provide concluding remarks.

In searching for Majorana modes within a semiconductor-based system, engineers have developed a new tunneling spectroscopy technique to distinguish them from other particles. A previously utilized method of distinguishing Majorana modes, which relies on the non-Lorentzian shape of zero-bias conductance, is insufficient on its own. This insufficiency results in the difficulty of identifying Majorana modes, which is particularly challenging due to the overlap of their spectral signals with those of other particles. To overcome this limitation, a new methodology has been proposed that utilizes ohmic contacts with high electrical resistance. This technique can detect the non-equivalent behavior of the zero-bias conductance found in Majorana modes, which may hold the key to identifying these particles. To confirm the utility of this technique, researchers performed simulations modeling the processes of zero-bias tunneling spectroscopy for both normal fermions and Majorana modes. These simulations demonstrated that ohmic contacts with a certain, relatively narrow range of resistance (approximately 0.05 to 0.15 Ohms) can facilitate notable distinction between the two types of particles. This technique has the potential to provide substantial utility in identifying Majorana modes within topological superconductors, which are essential components of topological quantum computing systems.

Linear bandits, a type of contextual bandits, assume that context and action effects are linear, resulting in a well-defined posterior model after sufficient data collection. However, when actions vary significantly, resulting in vastly different magnitudes of observed context, the model's posterior may become ill-defined due to distinct scales. In this study, a diverse group action set is defined as one in which a linear policy consistently generates infinite regret over a finite time period against an exponential number of arms, indicating a scenario where a learner is consistently out-performed by a sub-optimal arm in both expectation and posterior models. It is shown that action set diversity impacts posterior model definition, resulting in a posterior that effectively characterizes data collection only under specific conditions, and that even with data collection, inference becomes challenging in these diverse action sets. Two commonly used inference methods are analyzed: Bayesian credible intervals and Thompson sampling, demonstrating that these methods fail to offer effective bounds, regardless of posterior computation time, and that these bounds can be as poor as the Whittle's paradox in the context of Gaussian variance. Thompson sampling is shown to fail in these diverse action sets, resulting in a policy that may perform worse on average in the long run. An alternative method that addresses these limitations through a novel regularization approach is presented, resulting in improved bounds and the potential for improved long-term performance when applied to a real-world recommendation system dataset.

Researchers have identified unique properties in graphene that result from its gapless energy spectrum and specific molecular arrangements. The family of graphene-based materials, known as moiré superlattices, can be engineered to exhibit certain characteristics within the energy spectrum, such as the responses to magnetic fields and the behaviors of orbital magnets. The presence of multiple energy valleys within these materials facilitates the occurrence of the valley Hall effect, where different energy states cause charge movements in specific directions. However, it has been found that when these materials undergo a transition to a gapped state under a strong magnetic field, their energy spectrum becomes reorganized, eliminating the concept of valleys and instead giving rise to a new phenomenon. The gapped state of these materials is home to a unique behavior that can be accurately described as an orbital Hall effect, where charge movements are directed by the orbital states. Our study has demonstrated that this new effect shares key differences and distinct properties with the original valley Hall effect, and it has also highlighted several key characteristics that can be utilized to identify and study this effect, such as its response to magnetic fields, the presence of orbital states, and the specific mathematical equations that describe its behavior. By advancing our understanding of these properties and effects, researchers can continue to push the limits of what is possible in materials science and physics.

Stochastic graph neural networks exhibit stochastic variability due to data contamination issues, causing a concern for users who prefer deterministic outputs. Our research focuses on the development of a reinforcement learning-based method that utilizes the agent's actions to eliminate data contamination, applying its knowledge to select the most suitable datasets for network training. Our experiments include reinforcement learning-based approaches, assessing their efficacy in eliminating data contamination on existing neural networks and comparing their results with current state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, we introduce a new training technique that integrates maximum likelihood estimation with the reinforcement learning-based approach, yielding promising deterministic output generation capabilities.

The process of aligning surveys involves matching points of interest across various datasets to create a unified map. This is a crucial step in merging data from different sky maps, which is essential for training AI models that need large, joint datasets to perform accurately. The traditional approach to survey merging relies on cross-matching objects based on their positions. This is done by selecting the best match at a specific angle of alignment below a certain threshold. Generally, the best match is chosen by selecting objects with the closest approach based on their angular separation. New methods have been introduced that use proper motion and distance information to improve survey merging. However, these methods still utilize only one piece of information when determining the best match: the angular separation. In this study, we present an advanced technique that makes two types of information available when selecting the best match: angular separation and the total brightness of each object. We use synthetic data to develop the initial model, and then test the new approach using real sky maps created with Gaia EDR3 and the All-Sky Photometric Survey. The results show that our technique outperforms existing methods by reducing errors in the alignment of the surveys by up to 40%. This breakthrough allows us to achieve accurate results even when the best match is chosen based on the largest angular separation between the datasets to be aligned.

In this paper, the smallest subsets of indices that ensure the presence of a specific edge in an infinite hypergraph are studied, with research yielding general lower and upper bounds for such sets. Moreover, the lower bound is achieved in a particular class of hypergraphs, specifically those generated by almost-regular motions within 2-dimensional Cantor space, with countably infinite outcomes. We demonstrate the existence of a unique minimal subset of indices in this specific type of hypergraph that define each edge, with odd multiplicity occurring only for the minimum element of the hypergraph's range.

The continuous expansion of ontologies in various domains has intensified the need for improved visualization tools, especially given their complex nature, encompassing thousands of concepts and extensive interconnectedness. This has led to the development of several fully immersive visualizations and interactive interfaces aimed at simplifying ontology comprehension, but they largely overlook or underemphasize non-hierarchical connections. To address this gap, this research presents OntoPlot, a novel visualization method that showcases both hierarchical and non-hierarchical aspects of ontologies. By integrating Sunburst and Sankey diagrams, OntoPlot allows users to explore the comprehensive structure of ontologies. To facilitate seamless navigation, this system incorporates a high-level zooming mechanism, enabling users to zoom in on specific components and factors influencing their relationships. Furthermore, OntoPlot allows users to filter out less significant interactions as needed. The test of visualizing an extensive biomedical ontology, representing nearly 400,000 interconnected concepts, has proven OntoPlot to be an effective tool for comprehending large-scale ontologies.

Automated Speech Transcription using deep learning technology shows great promise, particularly when large amounts of labeled speech data are available. However, the high cost of creating such datasets due to the need for human annotation limits their adoption. A recent approach to addressing this challenge involves leveraging cycle-consistency training to create large amounts of unlabeled paired data through unsupervised domain translation. This method, combined with an regularization technique, can improve end-to-end automated speech transcription performance in real-world settings. In this study, we first examine the effectiveness of this approach using a German speech dataset and compare it to a baseline method of using labeled data alone. Next, we investigate the impact of combining several cycle-consistency-based penalty methods to identify the most efficient way to utilize these techniques in improving ASR performance in inter-domain scenarios. A recently developed Inter-domain Test Set Separation dataset is utilized to create unlabeled data for each domain using a cycle-consistency-based penalty method not previously associated with ASR. A comprehensive evaluation of our approach based on multiple, diverse datasets is presented in the accompanying jupyter notebook.

A new approach combining proven I-deduction with an innovative self-sustaining
mechanism is proposed, enabling long-term navigation planning for robots through
repeated deduction sessions. These repeated sessions facilitate a shift from
quasi-axiomatic to quasi-horn clauses within the knowledge base, ultimately
enhancing solution search efficiency. This hybrid method is termed Proactive
Deduction. Our study examines Proactive Deduction's performance in sustained
reasoning, focusing on its ability to learn and exploit new representations.
Furthermore, we explore its effectiveness in generating navigation plans with
greater detail and robustness. Empirical evaluations using the Pedestrian-
Navigation Domain demonstrate the proposed method's capacity for improved
resilience against unexpected events and enhanced overall performance.

The Soret effect, which describes the separation of components within a thermal gradient, has received considerable attention in soft matter research. Although flexibility in soft molecules can hinder this separation, by allowing internal structural changes that counteract the temperature-driven interventions, its impact on the separation process remains under-researched. This study investigates how flexibility in molecules affects the Soret coefficient, which characterizes separation phenomena. Using the lattice model, which mimics molecular structures composed of polymerized monomers, we explored how changes to the monomer and bond parameters affect the lattice dynamics and structural organization in relation to the thermal gradient. By calculating the Soret coefficient for the lattice model and related systems, such as monomers and bonds with limited flexibility, we gained insights into the relationship between molecular flexibility, chemical interactions, and separation phenomena. This investigation concludes that the flexibility in molecules, which allows internal structural changes, can either enhance or suppress separation phenomena depending on the circumstances.

In the music technology domain, there's currently a scarcity of tools utilizing natural language processing (NLP) techniques, which are established in other creative fields such as text-based arts and design. Our research focuses on exploring NLP models and developing an automated evaluation tool that provides valuable critique and suggestions to improve composed music. We've successfully adapted existing NLP-based critique models to apply to music, and have collected and annotated a substantial dataset of natural language critiques related to music. Our proposed automated evaluation tool not only generates more informative and relevant feedback compared to existing models, but also produces more consistent and concise suggestions.

Domain shift significantly impacts deep model performance; thus, achieving adaptation between a model trained with labeled data and an unlabeled target domain is crucial. Unlike unsupervised domain adaptation methods that utilize similarity metrics or generative models to reduce false positives, we present a novel approach that eliminates false positives by reordering box predictions within each anchor box. This technique incorporates an hard example mining-based priority target assignment, prioritizing the top label for each anchor box, and re-ranking the remaining targets based on their original labels. We integrate our box reordering method with a novel loss, priority hard example mining loss, and implement it on a pedestrian identification model to achieve the highest known performance on the benchmark dataset LaSOT-Pedestrian without using any labeled target dataset.

This paper presents an innovative approach to enhance music by leveraging image processing and audio representation. A newly developed technique for Music Image Enhancement involves analyzing a musical image through rotational and scaling transformations to distinguish between foreground and background elements. Furthermore, this method's applications extend to detecting instrumental entries in orchestral music and identifying rhythmic patterns in various musical genres. Moreover, this approach's potential lies in its broader applicability to vision-based musical analysis problems. Building on this concept, we explore the connection between musical notes and numerical patterns by creating a custom encoder to translate MIDI data into fixed-length vectors. This sequence-to-sequence model utilizes a transformer architecture, which it will learn to represent the temporal relationships between notes for a range of guitar melodies.

In recent years, the task of predicting the dynamics of object throwing has gained significant traction within the field of physics-based simulation. Researchers have not only delved into the physics of throwing but have also explored the simulation's implications for human movement, ultimately aiming to create realistic, three-dimensional animations of throwing motions. However, most studies have focused on the overall throwing motion, neglecting potential errors in input data. Conversely, we actively introduce artificial mistakes into specific task inputs, examining how discrepancies in the point of release affect not only the trajectory of the thrown object, but also the movement executed by the virtual character, and ultimately, the overall appearance of the simulated throwing motion. By incorporating these artificial mistakes, we demonstrate the existence of multiple, physiologically plausible throwing motions that correspond to a single point of release, thereby shedding new light on a long-standing, yet rarely investigated aspect of throwing animations.

Traditional machine translation decoding methods focus on predicting the likelihood of the next token, resulting in inefficient interpretation and interpretation errors. A notable exception is the tree autoencoder, a method that uses a bottom-up approach to generate syntactically accurate sentences. However, this approach has several limitations, such as the inability to learn from prior predictions and resulting sentence representations that lack the structure of the underlying syntax. To address these issues, we have developed a novel top-down tree form decoding framework that uses a set of predefined rules to build sentences from the root to the leaves, incorporating syntactic relationships into the sentence representation. A new type of neural module has been created to analyze the sentence representations and produce interpretations by identifying the root node and breaking down the sentence into constituent parts. Experiments have been conducted on two datasets. The results demonstrate that our method outperforms similar approaches in multiple metrics, including automatic and human evaluations of sentence interpretation.

Accurate binding energy data are necessary to understand which molecules can form on icy cosmic dust grains and remain intact under interstellar conditions. We created a platform that collects and reports binding energy data of different types of molecules on grain surfaces, based on quantum chemical calculations. We evaluated the strength of hydrogen bonds between small molecules and water on grain surfaces, including water dimer, monomers, methanol, formic acid, ammonia, phosphorus oxide, and phosphorus dioxide. The platform provides a comparison of binding energies on different grain surfaces, including those with water, organic compounds, and phosphorus-containing substances. The results show that in many cases, the lowest energy state of a molecule adsorbed on grain surfaces is more stable than the ground-state, the water dimer is more stable than water, and other molecules are more stable in a particular environment. The platform's data can be accessed at https://cebp.app/.

Typically, multiplicative stochastic models based on log-normal distributions assume that a particular critical value, below which birth events cannot occur, is constant across all samples. In contrast, the proposed model relaxes this assumption, allowing the critical threshold to vary between samples. A new stochastic model has been introduced, its parameters derived and analyzed in terms of exponential representation. The model's ability to fit actual data has been demonstrated. Furthermore, we have developed methods for generating stochastic models that can simulate the overall dynamics of large systems while neglecting minor details, as well as detecting whether a stochastic model is suitable for modeling phenomena that occur over long periods of time. Lastly, we have devised methods for creating sets of stochastic models that can simultaneously fit multiple datasets.

Subsystems and their representations play a crucial role in quantum field theory descriptions of low-entropy states through density matrices, which can be modeled with finite-depth random unitary operations, imitating random Clifford circuits. However, random unitary operations are expensive, driving research into shorter, yet still effective protocols. This paper proposes shallow shades, utilizing random Clifford circuits of depth 7 to model subsystems, efficiently applying them to any given state. Previous studies show that these shallow shades efficiently approximate valid density matrices with low subspace entropy, despite working with fewer qubits than the original circuit. Additionally, the cross-entropies of shallow shades and original density matrices are shown to be efficiently approximated within a small margin. As a result, the cross-entropy can serve as a metric for complexity classification. With further analysis, the paper addresses methods for determining density matrices corresponding to shades and discusses potential applications to derive density matrices from shallow shades of various quantum systems. Furthermore, the paper investigates shallow shades localization in translationally symmetric systems and discusses its implications using an example model. Using the cross-entropy as a complexity classifier, the paper shows that there's a clear link between the entropy of the shade cross-entropy and the entropy of the reduced density matrix, providing ground-state complexity bounds. Lastly, the paper discusses how the proposed algorithm can be applied to recent quantum computing complexity studies.

We are studying the reflection and scattering of water waves generated by a point source at great distances from the source.  We use the Davey-Stewartson II equations, a model for how water waves move in a shallow sea, to study this system.  We found that for two regions far away from the source, the strength of the scattering increases as the wavenumber (a measure of how quickly the source is moving) increases, in one direction it increases at a regular rate, in the other direction it increases at a faster rate.  We also found that the amount of wave reflected back at the source also increases as the wavenumber increases, though in a different way than in both other regions.  We used this information to study how sources interact with each other when they are in different phases, a question that is related to how water waves move in a shallow sea.

To ensure text classification models operate safely and responsibly in real-world contexts, addressing attacks such as text-to-text transformations that seek to deceive the model is essential. Recent research on defending against such attacks has proposed countermeasures, but a concurrent need exists to evaluate the efficacy of these measures in detecting the most sophisticated forms of attacks. Unlike methods limited to testing individual samples, our proposed method involves a comprehensive evaluation approach that generates diverse variants of attack instances through a combination of three techniques. Three datasets, including IMDB, Stanford Sentiment and SST, were utilized to demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in identifying attack instances for both semantic and syntactic attacks. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing countermeasures, with notable successes in detecting approximately 33\% to 87\% of attack instances.

Our research focuses on the meta-learning domain, specifically addressing the task of linear transfer. This involves identifying a linear model that best represents how different data distributions relate to one another. Typically, linear transfer problems have been experimentally defined by manually designing both the source and target distributions. In contrast, we propose an innovative, fully automated approach that utilizes only the source data to simultaneously determine both distributions and the linear model that would be most adaptable when switching between them. By implementing this method, known as 'Meta-Learn Depiction', we successfully achieved significant enhancements in the transfer performance on various common machine learning tasks. Furthermore, 'Meta-Learn Depiction' showcases an impressive ability to demonstrate its effectiveness through intrinsic and extrinsic understanding capture metrics. 'Meta-Learn Depiction' source code is available on GitHub.

Successful applications of model compression through distillation have motivated the exploration of leveraging pre-trained knowledge to improve cross-language learning and reduce language processing costs across multiple tasks and resources. We examine the utilization of knowledge from a high-resource source to aid in learning a target model with limited data, investigating either a reduced number of parameters or a lighter model. The compression of the target model is achieved by analyzing a framework of knowledge-based multilingual learning, specifically through an assistant model that utilizes its knowledge to guide the student model. We test the student models under various parameter counts as well as in a no-knowledge setting to evaluate the effects of model complexity and the transfer of knowledge from the pre-trained model, while also evaluating the student models' performance with different weight priors on a low-resource machine translation dataset. Furthermore, we compare the student models' performance to a pre-trained and fine-tuned model on a no-knowledge and a high-knowledge benchmark, discovering that model compression that incorporates the transfer of knowledge outperforms the model without knowledge. Conversely, the student models' performance with a limited number of parameters that relies on the pre-trained knowledge falls short when compared to the model without knowledge. Consequently, the results suggest that model compression that relies on the transfer of knowledge is too fragile to handle in low-resource scenarios, whereas the pre-training of knowledge can offer more robustness and achieve state-of-the-art results, even in cases where the target model is lighter and more fragile.

The maximum number of these colorings that maintain a specific property is denoted as f ( G, k ) or simply f ( G ) when the value of k is clear.
